## Liberty Next — Screen Creation Assistant
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/screen-assistant/

A guided wizard that turns a set of database tables — or an existing connector query — into a working screen, dialog and menu item in one pass. Pick the source, choose the grid columns (default shared view), optionally lay dialog columns into tabs, review the dictionary, place a menu entry, create.

The **Screen Creation Assistant** is a guided wizard that builds a complete screen in a single pass. Two starting points are supported:

- **Database table** — a base table and any joined tables. The assistant writes a fresh `SELECT` on the connector.
- **Existing query** — a read-only reuse of a connector query already in place. The assistant reads its columns and builds the screen on top; no duplicate query is generated. A catalog preset that names a query goes through the same path.

Once the source is picked, you choose which columns the grid shows (that becomes the screen's default shared view), optionally arrange columns into dialog tabs for editing, review the dictionary entries and drop a menu item — the assistant writes the read query (when from tables), the screen, its dialog, the default view and the menu entry together.

It is the fast path to a working screen: what you would otherwise assemble by hand across the Connectors, Dictionary, Screens and Menus pages, the assistant produces in one reviewed step.

:::info[Superuser tool]
The assistant is a **superuser** tool. Open it from **Liberty Next → Build → Assistant**, or from **A new screen, with the assistant** on the [Overview](../studio.md#overview) page. It opens as a window over the current page — there is no separate route — and closes only with its **×** or **Cancel**: a click outside or Esc does not wipe a half-built screen.
:::

:::note[Not the AI chat]
This wizard is **deterministic** — it reads your schema and generates standard SQL and config; it does not call a model. It is a different feature from the [AI Assistant](../ai-assistant.md) chat drawer, which proposes the same kinds of artifacts conversationally. Use the wizard when you already know the tables; use the AI chat when you want to explore.
:::

---

## The steps \{#steps\}

The header switches between **A screen** (the seven steps below) and **A module** ([a whole module](#module)); **↺** resets the assistant. The steps are shown as a row at the top — a step done is ticked, and **Next** is enabled once the current step is complete; **back** returns to the previous one.

### 1 · Target
The **Source connector** (a SQL connector) and the **App (for the screen + menu)** — pick an application or type a new one.

### 2 · Tables & joins
Two mutually-exclusive choices:

- **Database table** — type a filter (e.g. `F009%`) to list the tables, pick the **Base table**, then optionally **Add a joined table** (choose the join type and the ON conditions). A [catalog preset](#catalog-presets) can pre-wire the joins in one click.
- **Existing query** — pick a read query already defined on the connector. The assistant introspects its columns instead of writing a new `SELECT`; the screen reads through the existing query.

Either way, the assistant introspects live columns so the next steps have real fields to work with.

### 3 · Grid view
The read query selects **every** column of the source; this step chooses which of those show up on the grid. The picked set is written as the screen's **default shared view** — a shared view a regular user can override with their own [saved views](../saved-views.md).

### 4 · Dialog columns *(optional)*
Skip it to ship a read-only screen — no dialog. Otherwise, a two-pane layout: **Available columns** on one side, your dialog **tabs** on the other. Assign columns into tabs, add / rename / remove tabs, and tick the **key** columns (the ones that identify a row): they drive the update / delete queries. Only the columns you place here appear in the edit dialog; the grid keeps whatever step 3 defined.

### 5 · Dictionary
The assistant scans the source and proposes the [dictionary entries](../dictionary.md) the screen needs. Entries that already exist are shown but greyed out and left untouched — only the **missing** ones are pre-ticked to be created. For each proposed entry you can set the **Label**, **Format**, **Rule**, **Rule value**, **Lookup params** (for a UDC / lookup rule) and **Default**. This is the same scan table used by the Dictionary editor.

### 6 · Menu
Tick **Add a menu item under this app** to place the screen in the navigation, then set the **Menu label**, an optional **Parent menu** and an **Icon**. Leave it unticked to create the screen without a menu entry — useful for a screen reached only as a nested tab.

### 7 · Review & create
Name the **Table / query name** and the **Screen label**, check the *Will create* summary and the generated read-SQL preview, then **Create screen**. On success the assistant reports *Screen … created and live.* and offers **Open the new screen** or **Create another**.

The scaffolded screen has **`auto_load` on**, and the workspace refreshes on close — the new screen opens right where the menu points, no manual browser reload needed.

---

## What it creates

In one validated pass — nothing is written unless every piece validates — the assistant adds:

| Artifact | What lands |
|---|---|
| **Connector query** | *Database table* — a new table on the source connector with a `get` query, plus `post` / `put` / `delete` write queries so the screen is editable. *Existing query* — nothing added on the connector; the screen reads through the query you picked. |
| **Dictionary entries** | The proposed entries you kept (existing ones are never overwritten). |
| **Screen + dialog** | The screen under the chosen app, its grid columns and — if step 4 was filled — an embedded dialog whose tabs hold the form fields. |
| **Default shared view** | The grid selection from step 3, saved as the screen's default shared view. |
| **Menu item** | Optional — a leaf under the app's menu pointing at the new screen. |

A table or screen whose name already exists is refused rather than overwritten. Because the assistant **snapshots the configuration before it writes**, the change is captured in [config history](../configuration/config-history.md) exactly like a manual edit, so you can review or roll it back.

---

## Catalog presets \{#catalog-presets\}

A **catalog preset** is a ready-made starting point: a base table plus pre-wired joins, so an operator skips browsing the schema. When the connector has presets, the *Tables & joins* step shows **Start from a catalog preset** and a **Browse catalog** button that opens a searchable list grouped by family. Selecting one introspects each table's columns and wires the joins — including resolving each join condition from its data item to the real physical column.

Presets are operator-managed files under the deployment's `presets/` directory; each file holds one or more `[[presets]]` entries with a base table and its joined tables. They are configuration, not code — add your own to seed the screens your team builds most often.

:::info[JDE-specific]
Liberty Apps ships ten JD Edwards catalogs, built from the Oracle E1 data models: **Address Book**, **General Accounting**, **Accounts Payable**, **Accounts Receivable**, **Inventory**, **Sales**, **Procurement**, **Manufacturing**, **Product Data Management** and **Product Costing**. **Procurement** covers purchase orders, receipts and voucher matches, receipt routing, the P.O. detail ledger, supplier / item relationships, the supplier price catalog, landed cost rules and order addresses, combined with the supplier, the item, the branch and the A/P voucher. The *full* presets of each area (the A/P ledger with supplier, address and company; the sales order with lines, customer, item and branch…) also give the [Data Explorer](../explorer/model.md#preset) a ready-made model.

The **Address Book** catalog (`config/presets/jdedwards/address_book.toml`): the `F0101` master left-joined to who's-who, phones, email, addresses, customer and supplier, plus each related table as its own base preset. The join conditions are written by **data item** (e.g. `F0101.AN8`); the assistant resolves the JDE prefix to the real column (`ABAN8`, `AIAN8`, …) so the joins auto-fill. A preset table can name a `query` (a `SELECT * FROM <table>` already defined on the connector) so the assistant reads its columns by describing that query — much faster on a large JDE catalog.
:::

---

## A whole module \{#module\}

**A module**, beside **A screen** in the assistant's header, builds an entire functional module in one go — several screens linked to each other, their menu folder and their dictionary entries — from a **module catalogue** shipped with the presets.

1. Pick a module in the list — searchable, grouped by area (*JDE · Address Book*); each shows its application, its connector and its number of screens.
2. The preview reads the live tables at once and shows the screen tree, the details indented under their parent: **Screen**, **Table**, **Prefix** (the column prefix found in the database), **Columns**, **Not in the table** (the items the table lacks), and the **State** of each — *new*, *exists* or *replace*. The **Menu** line shows the folder and its items the same way. A table or a key that cannot be found stops the module, with the reason.
3. **Apply the module** writes everything at once: *Applied: 7 queries, 7 screens, 4 menu entries, 244 dictionary entries.* The sidebar shows the new folder at once, and **Open the new screen** opens its first screen.

What a module creates:

- one **read query** per screen, ordered by the key, with the lookup tables joined for their descriptions;
- **read-only screens** whose dialog carries the module's tabs, and one tab per related table — a list for a one-to-many link, a form for a one-to-one link —, bound on the parent's key;
- the **filters** the module names, applied in the database;
- the **menu folder** of the module, with an item per main screen;
- the **dictionary entries** of the columns, from the source's data dictionary — labels, formats, value lists.

Applying is additive: what already exists is kept. **Replace the module's existing entries** rewrites the module's own queries, screens and menu items — a change made to them since is lost. When everything exists already, there is nothing to apply. The three files are validated before anything is written: everything is written, or nothing. Superusers only.

Liberty Apps ships the **Address Book** module for JD Edwards EnterpriseOne: the address book with its contacts, phones, e-mails and dated addresses, the customer and supplier masters — see [Nomajde → Address Book](../../nomajde/master-data/address-book.md).

## Column picker

The pickers of the Grid view and Dialog columns steps are built for wide sources — a full JDE `F0101` scan is not fun in a flat list. They share a few conventions:

- **Tree-style parent grouping.** Columns are grouped by their source table, and a parent menu row folds every column of that table underneath. Collapse the tables you don't need.
- **Searchable groups.** Each table group has its own filter — type the column name (or its label) to narrow just that group; other groups stay expanded as they were.
- **Per-table Add all.** Beside each table group, a button pushes every column of that table into the layout at once. Useful when you want a full parent table on the grid and only the child records in the dialog.
- **Full-height scroll panes.** Both panes take the modal's full height and scroll independently, so a picker with thousands of columns doesn't collapse the other side.
- **Loading spinners** while the schema is being read — visible on a slow catalog / slow query.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Start from a preset when one fits.** It is the difference between picking one entry and hand-wiring five joins.
- **Mark your keys in the Dialog columns step.** The key columns drive the update / delete queries; a screen without keys is read-only by construction.
- **Reuse an existing query for read-only reports.** *Existing query* is the shortest path when the SQL already exists — no duplicate query gets added and the screen still gets a dialog / dictionary review.
- **Skip the Dialog columns step for read-only screens.** Leaving *Dialog columns* empty ships the screen without an edit dialog — useful for observability screens where nothing should be editable.
- **Review the dictionary, don't rubber-stamp it.** The scan infers the format from the column type (or, on JDE, from the data dictionary); a quick pass over the Format and Rule columns saves a round-trip later.
- **Open the screen and refine it in the Designer.** The assistant gets you a working screen fast; nested tabs, conditional fields and actions are then yours to add in the [Screen Designer](screens/overview.md).

---

## Liberty Next — Connectors
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/connectors/

A connector is how Liberty Next reaches a data source: a SQL connector holds the named queries of a database pool, an API connector the named endpoints of a web API, its server an HTTP server pool. Pools — databases, HTTP servers, LDAP directories — are set up in Liberty Next → Administer → Pools; connectors in Liberty Next → Data → Connectors.

A **connector** is how Liberty Next reaches a data source. Every screen, chart, dashboard, action, job step and assistant answer names the connector and the query — or the endpoint — it uses.

| Type | Reaches | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL** | A database, through a [pool](#pools). | Named **queries**, in four kinds: tables, queries, sequences, lookups. |
| **API** | A web API (REST, JSON), through an [HTTP server pool](#pool-http) or its own address. | Named **endpoints**: method, path, headers, body, response mapping. |

A connector with a menu and **Show in the application list** on is an **app**, picked in the switcher — see [Apps](./apps/overview.md).

---

## At a glance

---

## Liberty Next → Data → Connectors \{#page\}

The left list has a filter and two groups: **Apps** (connectors with a menu) and **Data sources** (the others). Each line says what the connector holds, each kind under its own name — `sql · 118 table(s) · 34 query(ies) · 19 sequence(s) · 14 lookup(s)`, `api · 68 endpoint(s)`. The page header holds **＋ Connector** (a name, the type SQL or API), **Discard** (drops the pending changes), **Save** (writes `connectors.toml` and applies the change without a restart) and **Reload config**. The picked connector opens on the right, its buttons in its header — **Find usages**, **Clone** (with its dictionary scope, screens, menu, charts and dashboards), **Rename** (every reference rewritten), **Delete** (with everything that belongs to it).

### Pools \{#pools\}

A pool is a connection of the installation, defined in **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools** and named by whatever uses it. What belongs to the installation — an address, an account, a password, a key — is set there once, and nowhere else. The beginning of its URL says what the pool reaches:

| Kind | URL | Named by |
|---|---|---|
| **A database** — PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Db2, Db2 for i (IBM i, AS/400), SQLite | `postgresql+asyncpg://…`, `oracle+oracledb://…`, `mssql+pymssql://…`, `db2+ibm_db://…`, `ibmi://…` | SQL connectors, job steps, the environment a screen runs on. |
| **An HTTP server** | `http://…` or `https://…` | API connectors and each of their environments — see [An HTTP server](#pool-http). |
| **An LDAP directory** | `ldap://…` or `ldaps://…` | The `ldap_sync` step of a job and the code of an application — see [An LDAP directory](#pool-ldap). |

The list says what each pool reaches — `postgresql · host:5432 / database`, `http · host:8443/api/v2`, `ldap · host:636 / dc=example,dc=com` — and its header holds **＋ Add pool**, **Discard**, **Save** and **Reload config**. A field of a screen can offer the pools as a list: the dictionary rule [`POOL`](./dictionary.md#rules).

#### A pool, stage by stage \{#pool-stages\}

The picked pool is drawn as stage cards, each saying what it holds: **Database**, **Account**, **Schemas**, **Database links**, **Tuning** for a database — **Database** and **Account** only for an HTTP server or a directory, which run no SQL. Its buttons are **Test connection**, **Find usages**, **Rename**, **Reload from disk** and **Delete**.

| Stage | Fields |
|---|---|
| **Database** | The address, typed as an address: the **Database type** (PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Db2, Db2 for i (IBM i, AS/400), SQLite, *LDAP directory*, *HTTP server (an API)*), **Host**, **Port**, and the one name the type needs — **Database**, an Oracle **Service name** (a **SID** when the URL is written with one), a SQLite **File**, a directory's **Base DN**, a server's **Base path**. Picking another type moves the pool to it: its driver, its usual port; the type also chooses a query's [per-dialect variant](./build/queries/per-dialect-sql.md). **Advanced: driver, options, URL** holds the **Driver**, the **Options** (what follows the `?` of the URL) and the **URL** composed from the fields, which stays editable (`${VARIABLE}` accepted). A URL the page cannot show field by field is kept exactly as written. |
| **Account** | The **User** and the **Password**, kept out of the URL and encrypted when saved; the password field has a show / hide button. A password written in the URL is flagged, with **Move it to the password field**. A directory's account is the **Account (bind DN, DOMAIN\user or user@domain)**, typed as it is; an HTTP server's is the **Account**, with its **Signing key**, **Certificate** and **Verify SSL** — see [below](#pool-http). |
| **Schemas**, **Database links** | The values of the `#SCHEMA.<NAME>#` and `#DBLINK.<NAME>#` tokens — see [below](#schema-and-db-link-tokens). |
| **Tuning** | How many connections the pool keeps, when it renews them, what it logs, and what each database needs (rows per round trip on Oracle, trailing spaces, empty values, query compilation on PostgreSQL) — see [Tuning](#pool-tuning). |

**Test connection** opens one connection with the pool as it is on the page — saved or not — and answers *Connected in N ms* with the server's version, or *Could not connect* with the driver's own words. A directory is bound to once with its account. An HTTP server receives one request at its address, and any HTTP status is an answer: *Connected in 85 ms — http HTTP 404 The server answers at this address, whatever the status…* — whether its account is accepted is checked by the **Test** of the API connector, which knows how it signs in. Nothing is saved and the running pools are not touched.

On Oracle the test runs `SELECT 1 FROM DUAL`, on Db2 and Db2 for i `SELECT 1 FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1`, elsewhere `SELECT 1`.

#### Tuning \{#pool-tuning\}

The **Tuning** stage of a database pool. Each field shows a one-line hint under its label; **more** unfolds the full description.

| Field | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Connections kept open** | 5 | How many connections stay open, ready to be used. |
| **Extra connections** | 10 | How many more connections may be opened when the server is busy. |
| **Test before use** | on | Checks that a connection still answers before handing it out. |
| **Renew after (seconds)** | -1 | A connection older than this is replaced; -1 keeps it for ever. |
| **Log every statement** | off | Writes every statement to the server log. For a diagnosis only. |
| **Let PostgreSQL compile queries** | off | PostgreSQL only — see [below](#pool-jit). |
| **Rows read at most** | empty (1 000) | How many rows a screen reads from this database unless it says otherwise. |
| **Rows per round trip** | empty (driver default) | Oracle only: how many rows are fetched at a time. Raise it to 500–1 000 for large reads. |
| **Trim trailing spaces** | off | Removes the spaces a fixed-width text column adds at the end of its values (Oracle `CHAR`, JD Edwards). |
| **Fill empty values** | off | On a write, puts a space or a zero where a value is left empty, for columns that refuse empty (Oracle `NOT NULL` text columns). |
| **Log statements and values** | off | Writes each statement with its values to the server log. For a diagnosis only. |

##### Query compilation on PostgreSQL \{#pool-jit\}

PostgreSQL compiles (JIT) a query it estimates to be heavy before running it, at every run. On the short queries of screens, searches and dashboards the estimate is often wrong, and the compilation then costs far more than the query itself — measured on a search: 145 ms of compilation for 4 ms of work, and seconds on a server with one processor. Each PostgreSQL pool therefore turns JIT off for its own sessions; the database's other users keep the server's setting. The collections and the Nomaflow jobs run on the same pools, and their heavy reads are as fast or faster without it.

Switch **Let PostgreSQL compile queries** on to leave the database's own setting to the pool's sessions. The field has no effect on the other databases.

#### SQL Server, Db2 and IBM i \{#pool-sql-server-db2\}

A pool reaches these databases like any other: the screens, the queries, the jobs and the applications read it the same way. Their drivers do not ship with the base package:

| Database type | Driver (URL) | Usual port | Database field | Driver to install |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SQL Server** | `mssql+pymssql` — `mssql+aioodbc` is also offered under *Advanced* | 1433 | **Database** | `liberty-next[mssql]` — nothing else to install on the server. `mssql+aioodbc` needs Microsoft's ODBC driver on the server. |
| **Db2** (Linux, UNIX, Windows) | `db2+ibm_db` — `db2+pyodbc` is also offered | 50000 | **Database** | `liberty-next[db2]`. IBM publishes the driver for x86-64 Linux, macOS and Windows, not for arm64 Linux. |
| **Db2 for i (IBM i, AS/400)** | `ibmi` (through ODBC) | none | **Database** — the system's own name | `liberty-next[ibmi]`, plus unixODBC and IBM's *IBM i Access ODBC Driver* (IBM's download, under its own licence) on the server. |

The Docker image carries the SQL Server driver, and the Db2 driver on amd64 only; the IBM i driver is not in the image. On a [Python install](../installation/python-server.md#install), add the extras that match the pools. When the driver of a pool is missing, the pool's error and the result of **Test connection** name the extra to install — *no driver for a 'db2+ibm_db' database is installed — install it with: pip install 'liberty-next[db2]'*.

#### An HTTP server \{#pool-http\}

A pool whose URL starts with `http://` or `https://` is the server an API connector calls — `https://svc_liberty@api.example.com:8443/api/v2`. The API connector names it in its **Server** field, and so can each of its environments: the address, the account and the secrets are then the pool's, and the connector keeps how it authenticates and its endpoints — see [The server of an API connector](#api-server).

| Stage | Field | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Database | **Host**, **Port**, **Base path** | The address the endpoints' paths are added to. The scheme (`https` or `http`) is the **Driver** under *Advanced*. |
| Account | **Account** | The account the connector signs in with. Blank when the server takes a token: the **Password** field then holds the token. |
| Account | **Password** | The account's password — or the token. Encrypted when saved; `${VARIABLE}` accepted. |
| Account | **Signing key** | For a connector that makes each call as the signed-in user: the private key that signs the tokens — the PEM text, or the path of a PEM file on the server; an `ENC:` value is accepted. Whoever holds it can act as any user of that server: protect it like the master key. |
| Account | **Certificate** | Optional: the certificate of the signing key (the PEM text, or the path of the `.cer` / `.pem` file given to the server); its fingerprint is then written in the token's header. |
| Account | **Verify SSL** | Checks the server's TLS certificate. Turn it off only for a test server with a self-signed certificate. |

An HTTP server runs no SQL: a query, a screen or a copy that names it is refused, with the reason.

#### An LDAP directory \{#pool-ldap\}

A pool whose URL starts with `ldap://` or `ldaps://` (over TLS) is a directory — an Active Directory, an OpenLDAP. It is created like a database, with the kind **LDAP directory**: **Host**, **Port** (636 for `ldaps`, 389 for `ldap`), **Base DN** — where the searches start, optional —, the **Account (bind DN, DOMAIN\user or user@domain)** typed as it is (`cn=liberty,ou=services,dc=example,dc=com`, `EXAMPLE\svc_liberty`, `svc_liberty@example.com`), and the **Password**, kept like any pool's (`ENC:` or `${VARIABLE}`). **Test connection** binds once with the account and lets go.

Whatever reads a directory names the pool instead of carrying a server and an account of its own: the **Directory pool** of a job's [`ldap_sync` step](../nomaflow/steps.md#ldap-sync), and an application's code through `connectors.pools.directory(name)`. A directory runs no SQL, and a database pool is not a directory: either mistake is refused by name. `connectors.pools.where(name)` tells where any pool points — host, port, database or base — without its account, which is what a report prints of a system.

The directory client is an optional part of the server: when it is missing, the test says so and names the `ldap` extra to install.

### Tables and queries beside their list \{#list-beside\}

A SQL connector's sections are stage cards with their counts: **Settings** (its pool), **Tables**, **Queries**, **Sequences**, **Lookups**. Picking one lists its content; **＋ Add queries** (Tables), **＋ Add query**, **＋ Add sequence** or **＋ Add lookup** is in the connector's header.

Opening a table keeps the list beside it: the list narrows to a column — each table's four statements as dots — and the table opens next to it, so going from one table to the next is one click; the same for a query, a sequence, a lookup. The connector's sections and the table's stages then fold to one line each, so the statement starts high on the page. A table is drawn as its stages — **General**, then **Read**, **Update**, **Insert**, **Delete** — each saying whether the statement is *set* or *not set*, and in orange *not writable: refused at run time* when a write statement is there but not allowed. Its actions are a row of icons beside **Open visual builder** (find usages, rename, change type, move, clone, delete). The **Build a SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE** dialogs write the statement from the table's columns, with a preview. See [Queries — overview](./build/queries/overview.md).

## SQL connector \{#sql\}

A SQL connector has five stage cards: **Settings**, **Tables**, **Queries**, **Sequences**, **Lookups**. The four query sections are described on [Queries — overview](./build/queries/overview.md).

### Settings \{#connection-fields\}

The **Settings** card of a SQL connector holds its connection settings.

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Database** | The pool the queries run on — a dropdown of the pools defined in *Liberty Next → Administer → Pools*. The connector takes the pool's address, credentials and database type. |
| **Other databases** | Extra pools the same queries may run on — see [Multi-pool connectors](#multi-pool). |
| **Show in the application list** | Shows the connector as an application in the switcher at the top of the sidebar — together with a menu, see [Make a connector an app](./build/menus/make-connector-an-app.md). |
| **Home page** | The menu entry opened when the application is picked. |
| **Home page per role** | A landing menu entry per role: a user lands on the entry of the first of their roles listed here, otherwise on **Home page**. |
| **Rows read at most** | Default row limit of a read; otherwise the pool's, then 1 000. A screen's or a request's limit wins. |
| **Column prefix length** | Length of the table prefix in column names (JD Edwards: `2`, so `ABCO`, `MCCO` and `SDCO` all carry the dictionary item `CO`). Used by a role's [data scope](./build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md#data-scope). `0`: column names are the items. |

### Query editor

**＋ Add query**, or a click on a query, opens the query editor beside the list. Its header holds **back**, the query's name and its buttons — **Find usages**, **Rename**, **Change type**, **Move**, **Clone**, **Delete** (described on [Create a custom query](./build/queries/create-custom.md)). The query is drawn as three stage cards:

| Stage | Fields |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **Label** and **Description** — shown in the pickers, and read by the AI assistant to choose its queries. The name used in the URL (`/api/sql/billing/<name>`) and the permission (`sql:billing:<name>`) is the one in the header. |
| **Statement** | **SQL** — the statement, with `:name` parameters and `{{TOKEN}}` server values; one text, or one variant per database (see [Per-dialect SQL](./build/queries/per-dialect-sql.md)). **Writable** — off: only a SELECT is accepted; on: INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / CALL / MERGE. |
| **Parameters** | The declared parameters, one line each: **Name**, **Label**, **Default**, **Help**, **Example**, **Choices**, **Required** — see [Parameter binding](./build/queries/parameter-binding.md). |

The SQL editor highlights the syntax and completes table and column names from the pool. Above it, **Token** inserts a server value (`{{LOGIN}}`, `{{SYSDATE}}`…) or one of the pool's schemas, **Wizard** opens the SELECT builder, and **Run** tries a read statement on the connector's pool.

### Schema and DB-link tokens \{#schema-and-db-link-tokens\}

A SQL query can carry two placeholder tokens that let the same text run against any pool — local or remote — without maintaining a per-environment variant of the query:

| Token | Resolves to | Where it's configured |
|---|---|---|
| `#SCHEMA.<NAME>#` | The pool's mapping for schema `<NAME>` (e.g. `SY920.`). Empty when the pool has no entry — the token drops out and the table name is written bare. | The pool's **Schemas** stage. |
| `#DBLINK.<NAME>#` | The pool's DB-link suffix for schema `<NAME>` (e.g. `@ORCLPROD`). Appended **after** the table name, so a `#SCHEMA.SY#F0092#DBLINK.SY#` resolves to `SY920.F0092@ORCLPROD`. Empty when no entry — nothing is appended, and the query stays local. | The pool's **Database links** stage (`SY` = `@ORCLPROD`). |

The two are position-independent: `#SCHEMA.…#` prefixes the table, `#DBLINK.…#` suffixes it. The same query works locally (both mappings empty), against a remote schema without a link (schema mapped, dblink empty) or via a database link (both mapped) — the pool decides which shape to emit.

A non-empty DB-link value must be a bare `@link` reference (starts with `@`, letters, digits, `_`, `$`, `#` and `.` only). Anything else makes the query fail when it runs — a guard against a DB-link value that would try to smuggle SQL into the statement.

### Oracle thick mode \{#oracle-thick\}

The Oracle driver runs in *thin* mode by default: no Oracle client needed, every call on the server's event loop. Two cases need the *thick* mode, which goes through the Oracle Instant Client:

- **Native Network Encryption** (NNE) required by the database — thin mode fails with `DPY-3001`;
- reading a **LOB across a database link** — thin mode fails with `ORA-22992` / `ORA-03149`.

Tick **Oracle thick mode** in **Liberty Next → Administer → App** (section *App*) and restart the server: every Oracle pool then runs in thick mode — the setting applies to the whole server, not to one pool. PostgreSQL pools are not affected. The Instant Client is included in the Docker image (amd64 and arm64); a Python install needs it on the host.

---

### Multi-pool connectors \{#multi-pool\}

One SQL connector can serve **several pools** — several database or JDE instances — without cloning the connector or duplicating its screens. Alongside the default **Pool**, list the extra ones in **Pools** (both are dropdowns of configured pools on the connector's **Settings** card); the same named queries and the same screens then run against any pool in the set.

The pool is chosen at runtime:

- **In the app** — when the current app spans a multi-pool connector, a **Pool** picker appears in the sidebar, under the application picker (*Default* is the connector's own pool). Picking a pool re-runs that app's screens against the chosen instance. The choice is kept per app in the browser, and it applies only to the connectors that declare that pool — an app's other (single-pool) connectors keep their default rather than erroring.
- **In jobs** — a `sql_copy` step takes `pool` in its `source` or `target` block, a `sql_query` step takes `pool`, to target a specific instance without a new connector ([steps](../nomaflow/steps.md)). These keys are set in `jobs.toml`; the step editor does not show them.

The reachable set is the default `pool` plus `pools`; a request or a job can never reach a pool outside it, and only pool **names** reach the picker — never a URL or credentials. A connector with just a `pool` runs on that pool only.

An API connector called from those screens — AIS, for JD Edwards — can follow the same environments: see [One server per environment](#api-environments).

---

## API connector \{#api\}

An API connector calls a web API. Its server — address, account, secrets, TLS check — is best an [HTTP server pool](#pool-http), named in **Server**; the connector then keeps how it authenticates and its endpoints. It is drawn as six stage cards, each saying what it holds or still lacks — the server pool it names (`→ erp_api`) or the server's host, the kind of authentication and what it still lacks, the environments, the number of endpoints and how many write, the webhooks, the test:

| Stage | Content |
|---|---|
| **Connection** | Section *App*: **Show in switcher**, **Home**, **Home per role** — a different home page for the users of a role: the role and the menu entry are both picked, one line per role. Section *Connection*: **Server** — an HTTP server pool, or *Set on this connector*; with a pool, the address, the account, the password or token and the TLS check are read from it. Without one, **Base URL** (`https://api.example.com`, `${VARIABLE}` accepted) and **SSL Verify** (*true*, *false*, or a variable such as `${API_VERIFY_SSL:-true}`, kept as written) are set here. **Timeout (ms)** in both cases. Section *Default headers*: **Headers**, `Key:Value` pairs separated by semicolons, sent with every request. |
| **Authentication** | **Method**: *None*, *Basic* (username and password), *Bearer* (static token), *API Key* (header name and key), *OAuth2 / JWT* (token endpoint path, body template and Content-Type, token request headers, token field, token lifetime), *Each user as himself (a signed token)* — each call made as the signed-in user, see [Each call as the signed-in user](#api-user-jwt). When the connector names a server, only the method and its own settings are set here: the account, the password or token, the signing key and its certificate are the pool's. Otherwise the method's fields are here; the secrets are encrypted when saved, and the password, the token and the signing key have a show / hide button. The card names the method and what it still lacks: *no user yet*, *no token, no token address*, *no token address*, *no signing key yet*. |
| **Environments** | One server per environment, for a connector used with several JDE environments — see [One server per environment](#api-environments). |
| **Endpoints** | The named endpoints — see [API endpoints](./build/api-endpoints.md). |
| **Webhooks** | Not available yet: external systems cannot push events into Liberty Next. |
| **Test** | Pick an **Endpoint**, fill its **Parameters**, **Run**: the **Result** comes back, nothing is saved. On a connector without endpoints, **Test connection** checks the address and the authentication. |

An endpoint is one named call — **What it is** (name, label, description, *Changes data*, group), **Inputs** (its parameters), **The call** (method, URL path, headers, body, query parameters — or a function or a service that answers instead) and **The answer** (rows, columns, error and warning fields, response field and mappings). Each stage is described on [API endpoints](./build/api-endpoints.md).

### The server of an API connector \{#api-server\}

The **Server** field names an [HTTP server pool](#pool-http): what belongs to the installation — the address, the account, the password or token, the signing key and its certificate, the TLS check — is then in one place, under Liberty Next → Administer → Pools, and a credential is changed there once for every connector that uses it. What stays on the connector is how it authenticates (the method and its settings: token endpoint, user attribute, signature…) and its endpoints.

A connector an application ships holds none of the installation's values: an upgrade refreshes it whatever the address, and keeps the **Server** the installation named. A connector that names no server keeps its own **Base URL** and credential fields.

A server pool that is missing, or that has no address yet, does not stop the server from starting: each call made through the connector fails and says what to set — *the connector names the server pool 'erp_api': there is no such pool — create it under Liberty → Pools (kind HTTP server)*. The connector's **Test** runs with the pool's address and account: it checks that the account is accepted, where the pool's own *Test connection* only checks that the server answers.

```toml
[pools.erp_api]
url = "https://svc_liberty@api.example.com:8443/api/v2"
password = "ENC:…"

[connectors.erp_api]
type = "api"
server = "erp_api"          # address, account, secrets: the pool's
auth_type = "basic"         # how it authenticates: the connector's
```

Endpoints are called by screens (an endpoint with rows is read like a query), screen actions (`call_api`), [services](./build/services.md), menu entries (type `endpoint`), notification rules (`action` channel), plugins (`connectors.api(…).call(…)`), [tests](./build/tests.md) and — when allowed — the AI assistant. A Nomaflow `http` step calls a URL directly, without a connector.

### Each call as the signed-in user \{#api-user-jwt\}

With the method **Each user as himself (a signed token)**, the connector no longer calls the server under one service account: each call is made **as the user signed in to Liberty**. Liberty signs a short-lived JSON Web Token that names the user, and sends it as `Authorization: Bearer`; the server trusts the certificate of the connector's key. No password of the user is kept anywhere. The method is made for JD Edwards AIS — its HTML server's external JWT trust — and works with any server that accepts a signed token.

| Field | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Signing key** | — | The private key: the path of a PEM file on the Liberty server, or the PEM text (an `ENC:` value is accepted). Whoever holds it can act as any user of the server: protect it like the master key. When the connector names a server, it is a field of the [pool](#pool-http) and is not shown here. |
| **Certificate (optional)** | — | The certificate given to the server (its file, or its PEM text). Its fingerprint is written in the token (`x5t`), which some servers pick the certificate by. A field of the pool too when the connector names a server. |
| **User attribute** | `jde_user` | The attribute of the Liberty user that holds his name on the server — set by an administrator in the user's [data-scope attributes](./build/secure/users.md#attributes), never by the user. Blank: the Liberty user name itself. |
| **Name sent** | *In upper case (JD Edwards)* | Or *As written*. |
| **When no user can be named** | *Refuse the call* | Or *Use the service account below*: the **Credentials** section then appears, and the call is made with that username and password. A job or a schedule has no user; a user may have no attribute. |
| **Field that carries the user** | `sub` | The claim of the token that holds the name. |
| **Signature** | `RS256` | `RS256`, `RS384` or `RS512`. |
| **Issuer (iss)**, **Audience (aud)** | blank | Written in the token when the server checks them. |
| **Valid for (seconds)** | `300` | From 30 to 3600. A token is reused for the same user until shortly before it expires, then a new one is signed. |

A call with nobody to name — and the fallback left on *Refuse the call* — is not sent: it fails with a message that says why (nobody signed in, or the account has no such attribute) and asks to see an administrator. The choice is made per connector: a connector left on another method keeps its service account.

### One server per environment \{#api-environments\}

When the screens run on a [multi-pool connector](#multi-pool) — several JD Edwards environments — each environment usually has its own AIS server. The **Environments** card gives the API connector one server per environment; the endpoints stay defined once.

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Environment (pool)** | The environment (pool) of the connector's own server — its **Server**, or its **Base URL** and credentials. Required as soon as there is another environment. |
| **Other environments** | One entry per other pool: its **Server** — an HTTP server pool, whose address, account, secrets and TLS check are then read —, or, set on the connector, **Base URL**, **Username**, **Password**, **Token**, **SSL Verify**. A blank field takes the connector's value. Passwords and tokens are encrypted when saved. The line of an environment shows `→ pool` or its base URL. |

Nobody chooses the server. A call follows the environment the screen runs on — the **Pool** picked in the sidebar, or the default — and a job step's `pool` (any step type). That covers screen actions (`call_api`), plugins, `/api/http` and the AI assistant.

A call made for one of the connector's environments with no server is **refused** ("no target for pool …"); it is never sent to the connector's own server, which is another environment — often production. The environments are the connector's pool plus every pool of the SQL connectors running on it, so a JDE environment added on the SQL side and forgotten here is refused too. The card lists those environments without a server, and so does *Settings → Integrity*.

```toml
[connectors.ais_connection]
server = "jde_ais"                          # the HTTP server pool of production
pool = "jdedwards"                          # the environment of that server

[connectors.ais_connection.targets.jdedwards_dev]
server = "jde_ais_dev"                      # the HTTP server pool of this environment
```

To name the environment before a sensitive call, use `#POOL#` in a `confirm` message: `Reset the password of {INPUT.user} on #POOL#?`. An upgrade of the licensed apps keeps an install's `server`, `pool` and `targets`.

---

## Schema discovery and column hints \{#schema-discovery-and-column-hints\}

A query has no declared column list: the columns are those the database returns when it runs. How a column looks on a screen is decided, in this order, by:

1. the **column settings of the screen** (Columns tab) — label, format, width, rule, conditions;
2. the **dictionary entry** whose key is the column's name, or the one named in the column's `dd` field — label per language, format, rule (Boolean, enum, lookup…);
3. otherwise the column's name and the default display for its type.

A column does not need a setting of its own: a dictionary entry with its name is enough. See [Dictionary](./dictionary.md#column-reference) and [Screens → Columns](./build/screens/columns.md).

---

## Permissions

Each query and each endpoint has its own permission:

| Permission | Allows |
|---|---|
| `sql:<connector>:<query>` | Running the query — read or write alike. |
| `api:<connector>:<endpoint>` | Calling the endpoint. |

They are granted through roles: allowing a menu entry grants what it opens, and **Beyond the menus** grants a query, an endpoint or a whole connector — patterns such as `sql:billing:report_*` are accepted. See [Roles & permissions](./build/secure/roles-and-permissions.md).

---

## Tips

- **Name queries after the entity** — `invoices_get`, `invoices_by_status_get` — the lists read themselves.
- **Describe the queries** the AI assistant should use: label and description (stage *What it is*).
- **Prefer the dictionary to per-screen labels**: one entry serves every screen.
- **Put a server's address and account in a pool**, not on the API connector: one place to change a password, and a connector an upgrade can refresh.
- **Keep secrets out of the files** with `${VARIABLE}` references when a secrets manager is used — see [Encryption & secrets](./configuration/encryption-secrets.md).

---

## Under the hood

Connectors and pools are stored in `connectors.toml`, in the apps configuration folder. The Liberty Next pages are the normal way to edit them; the same configuration is reachable through the REST API under `/admin/config/connectors` — see [REST API](../references/rest-api.md#admin-config).

## Liberty Next — Queries — overview
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/queries/overview/

How the Connectors page of Liberty Next is organised — the Settings, Tables, Queries, Sequences and Lookups stage cards, a table opened beside its list — and the four kinds of queries it holds.

A **query** in Liberty is a named SQL statement attached to a **connector** (which itself points at a **pool**, i.e. a database). Screens, dashboards, charts, dictionary lookups, dictionary sequences and the AI assistant all consume queries — so adding a query is the most common change you'll make in the Liberty Next pages.

The page that manages queries is **Liberty Next → Data → Connectors**. This overview maps it; the next pages walk through each "add" path.

---

## The Connectors page at a glance

Three regions:

| Region | What it carries |
|---|---|
| **Page header** | Global actions — *＋ Connector*, *Discard*, *Save*, *Reload config*. *Save* writes the connector file and triggers a hot reload — no process restart needed. |
| **Left list** | A filter and two groups: *Apps* (connectors that have a menu and are shown in the switcher — the apps users see) and *Data sources* (connectors that supply data but are not shown in the switcher). Each line says what the connector holds (`sql · 3 table(s) · 6 query(ies)`). Click a name to open it on the right. |
| **Right pane** | The editor for the selected connector. Five stage cards across the top, each with its count, pick a section — *Settings*, *Tables*, *Queries*, *Sequences*, *Lookups*. |

---

## The four kinds of queries \{#kinds\}

A connector keeps its queries in four sections; the section a query sits in is its kind:

| View | What lives here |
|---|---|
| **Tables** | One entry per table, holding up to four queries: **get** (read), **post** (insert), **put** (update), **delete**. They are called `<table>_get`, `<table>_post`, `<table>_put`, `<table>_delete`. The list shows a row per table with its slot badges (GET / PUT / POS / DEL). |
| **Queries** | Standalone queries outside a table's set — reports, bulk operations, queries called by actions, charts or dashboards. Example: `monthly_revenue`, `purge_old_logs`. |
| **Sequences** | Queries that return the next number for a dictionary sequence. Typical body: `SELECT COALESCE(MAX(<col>), 0) + 1 FROM <table>`. |
| **Lookups** | Queries that return codes and labels for a dictionary lookup. Typical body: `SELECT <value>, <label> FROM <table>`. |

### A table, opened beside its list \{#table-open\}

Opening a table, a query, a sequence or a lookup keeps the list beside it, narrowed to a column: one click goes to the next. The connector's sections fold to one line, and so do the table's stages — **General** (label and description), then **Read**, **Update**, **Insert**, **Delete**, each saying whether its statement is *set*, *not set*, or in orange *not writable: refused at run time*.

**Change type** moves a query to another section — for example a query written under *Queries* that turns out to feed a lookup. When the move changes the query's name (a table slot becomes a standalone query, or the reverse), a warning lists the new name: screens, actions and dictionary entries that use the old name have to be updated.

---

## The add buttons — one per view \{#add\}

| View | Button | What opens |
|---|---|---|
| **Tables** | *＋ Add queries* | A choice: **Generate from DB** (the CRUD wizard — reads the table in the database and generates the four queries) or **Empty stub** (asks for a table name and creates an empty read query). |
| **Queries** | *＋ Add query* | A name prompt, then an empty query to fill in by hand. |
| **Sequences** | *＋ Add sequence* | The scaffold — pick a table and a key column, see the SQL, save: it writes the query **and** the dictionary sequence. |
| **Lookups** | *＋ Add lookup* | The scaffold — pick a table, a value column, a label column and an optional filter, save: it writes the query **and** the dictionary lookup. |

The next pages walk through each path.

---

## What a query carries \{#fields\}

The query editor draws a query as three stage cards — **What it is**, **Statement**, **Parameters** — under a header with its name and its buttons:

| Stage | Field | Required | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| — | **Name** (header) | Yes | Unique inside the connector. The query's permission is `sql:<connector>:<name>`. Changed with *Rename*, which updates every reference. |
| What it is | **Label** | No | Short name shown in lists. |
| What it is | **Description** | No | What the query returns — shown under the name in the lists. |
| Statement | **SQL** | Yes | The statement, with `:name` parameters. A single text, or one variant per database (`default` required) — see [Per-dialect SQL](./per-dialect-sql.md). |
| Statement | **Writable** | No (off) | Off, only a SELECT is accepted. On for INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE / CALL. |
| Parameters | **Params** | No | Declared parameters, one line each: **Name**, **Label**, **Default**, **Help**, **Example**, **Choices**, **Required** — see [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md#declare). |

The **Statement** card shows the first word of the statement and the databases it is written for, in orange when it is empty or writes without being marked writable; the **Parameters** card says how many are declared and which `:placeholders` the statement holds.

---

## Save and reload — what a click does

Saving on this page is atomic across two files when needed:

| Action you took | What gets written |
|---|---|
| Created or edited a table or a query | The connector file. |
| Used the scaffold for a sequence or a lookup | The connector file **and** the dictionary (the new sequence or lookup in the connector's scope). |
| Cloned a connector (whole app) | A cross-file write that copies the dictionary overlay, screens, menu, charts and dashboards under the new name. Goes through a dedicated server route. |
| Renamed a connector, a query or a table | A cross-file update that touches every reference (screens, menus, dictionary, charts, dashboards). Refuses to run when local edits aren't saved. |

After every save the framework runs a **hot reload** automatically. The new query is callable immediately — no restart, no logout.

---

## What you actually do — quick map

| Goal | Read |
|---|---|
| Generate the four CRUD queries from a real database table. | [Create from a database table](./create-from-database.md) — the wizard path, recommended when the table exists. |
| Write a custom query (standalone, hand-written). | [Create a custom query](./create-custom.md). |
| Make a copy of an existing query or of a whole application. | [Clone a query or a connector](./clone.md). |
| Add a sequence (next id) or a lookup (dropdown source). | [Sequences and lookups](./sequences-and-lookups.md). |
| Pass values to a query — fixed values, other columns, the signed-in user. | [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md). |
| Ship different SQL for Postgres vs Oracle. | [Per-dialect SQL variants](./per-dialect-sql.md). |

## Liberty Next — Create from a database table
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/queries/create-from-database/

The CRUD Wizard — point Liberty at an existing table, tick the columns, get the four CRUD queries auto-generated and saved in one click.

When the table already lives in your database, the fastest path is the **CRUD Wizard**. You point it at a schema and a table, tick the columns you want the screen to see, mark which ones identify a row, and Liberty writes the four queries (`_get`, `_put`, `_post`, `_delete`) for you — including the `:NAME_ORIGINAL` rebind on UPDATE so a dialog's Save knows which row to find. Generated **column identifiers and bind names are upper-cased** (matching the SELECT wizard), so JDE columns come out uppercase.

This is the recommended path for any table that already exists. Skip it only when the table doesn't exist yet or when you want hand-written SQL — see [Create a custom query](./create-custom.md).

---

## Where it lives

The wizard is reached from **Liberty Next → Data → Connectors**:

1. Pick a connector in the left list.
2. Pick the **Tables** stage card.
3. Click **＋ Add queries** in the connector's header.
4. A choice modal opens. Pick **Generate from DB**.

The wizard then walks the connector's pool (`GET /api/sql/<connector>/_schemas`) and presents the schemas it found.

---

## The wizard layout

---

## Step 1 — Pick a schema

The schema picker shows up only when the pool has more than one. PostgreSQL with a single `public` and SQLite skip it; Oracle (many schemas) requires it.

The wizard fetches schemas lazily — the initial open just lists names, the per-schema table walk happens after you pick. On a populous Oracle pool this saves you the 10+ seconds a full multi-schema walk would take.

---

## Step 2 — Filter table names

The **Table** list fills once a filter is typed (*Type a filter to list tables*): a SQL `LIKE` pattern (`customers%`, `F00%`, `%` for all) typed in the **Table name filter** box narrows the table list **server-side**, before the per-table column introspection runs. For pools with thousands of tables this is the difference between a snappy picker and a sluggish one.

The filter is debounced — type freely; the fetch fires ~350 ms after you stop.

---

## Step 3 — Pick the table

Once you pick a table, the wizard pulls its columns and pre-fills two sets:

| Set | Pre-fill rule |
|---|---|
| **Include** | Every column is ticked. |
| **Key** | Every column the database marks as `NOT NULL` is ticked. |

These are guesses — uncheck the columns you don't want surfaced (BLOBs, audit columns, computed fields) and confirm the keys. The **Base name** (*queries become `<base>_get / _put / _post / _delete`*) is filled from the table's name; change it to name the queries differently. The **Columns** heading counts what is included and how many keys are ticked.

---

## Step 4 — Tick columns and keys

Each row in the **Columns** list carries:

| Element | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Include checkbox** | When unticked, the column is dropped from `_get`'s `SELECT` and from `_post`'s `INSERT`. The dialog will not see it. |
| **Column name + type** | Read-only — comes from the live database. |
| **KEY checkbox** | Beside each column. When ticked, this column drives the `_put`'s `WHERE` clause (with `:NAME_ORIGINAL`) and the `_delete`'s `WHERE` clause. |

A row with **at least one** key is required for UPDATE / DELETE to emit anything. The wizard refuses to save without one.

---

## Step 5 — Pick which queries to emit

Four checkboxes under **Which queries to emit** — **SELECT (`_get`)**, **UPDATE (`_put`)**, **INSERT (`_post`)**, **DELETE (`_delete`)**. Tick the ones the table needs.

| Pattern | Tick |
|---|---|
| Read-only reference table. | SELECT only. |
| Standard CRUD table. | All four. |
| Append-only (audit log). | SELECT + INSERT. |
| Reference table edited only via INSERT-then-purge. | SELECT + INSERT + DELETE. |

The **SELECT** query is always emitted — at the very least the screen needs to read the table.

---

## Step 6 — Read the preview, override if needed

Under the choices, one editor per ticked CRUD slot shows the generated SQL, live, with its **Token** menu. Edit any preview directly — your edit wins over the auto-gen until you change the column / key selection again, which restores the generated version.

### The four shapes

```sql
-- _get : straight SELECT over the included columns
SELECT COL1, COL2, …
FROM   <schema>.<table>

-- _post : INSERT bound to :col placeholders
INSERT INTO <schema>.<table> (COL1, COL2, …)
VALUES                       (:COL1, :COL2, …)

-- _put  : UPDATE non-key columns, WHERE on key with :NAME_ORIGINAL
UPDATE <schema>.<table>
SET    NON_KEY1 = :NON_KEY1, NON_KEY2 = :NON_KEY2, …
WHERE  KEY1 = :KEY1_ORIGINAL
   AND KEY2 = :KEY2_ORIGINAL

-- _delete : DELETE keyed on :NAME (the dialog binds the row's current values)
DELETE FROM <schema>.<table>
WHERE  KEY1 = :KEY1
   AND KEY2 = :KEY2
```

### Why `:NAME_ORIGINAL` on UPDATE?

A dialog's Save sends two snapshots of every key column: the current value (`:key1`) and the value the row had when the dialog opened (`:key1_ORIGINAL`). The UPDATE matches on the *original* so the row is found even when the operator edited the key itself. The CRUD Wizard wires this convention for you — if you hand-write a `_put` later, mirror it.

---

## Step 7 — Save

The **Save** button:

1. Appends the ticked queries to the connector's queries list.
2. Saves the connector file.
3. Triggers a hot reload — the new queries are callable immediately.

The four new queries appear in the **Tables** tab grouped under their shared base name, with the four CRUD slot badges showing which were emitted.

---

## Validation — what blocks Save

| Error | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| *Pick a table.* | No table selected. | Pick one. |
| *Name the table.* | The **base name** field is empty (auto-derived from the table name; clear it to override). | Type a base name — letters, digits, underscores. |
| *Include at least one column.* | Every column was unticked. | Tick at least one. |
| *The read (\_get) query is required.* | SELECT was unticked. | Tick it back. |
| *Pick at least one key column for UPDATE / DELETE.* | UPDATE or DELETE is ticked but no column has KEY on. | Mark the key column(s). |
| *A query named "X" already exists.* | The base name produces a `<base>_get` (or `_put` / `_post` / `_delete`) that collides with an existing query on this connector. | Pick a different base, or delete the old one first. |

---

## What you've just built

For a `customers` table with `customer_id` as the key, the wizard generated four queries:

| Name | Type | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `customers_get` | `table` (read) | The grid + form's read. |
| `customers_put` | `table` (write) | The dialog's Save (UPDATE). |
| `customers_post` | `table` (write) | The dialog's Save (INSERT). |
| `customers_delete` | `table` (write) | The grid's Delete action. |

They land in the **Tables** tab as one row labelled `customers` with the four GET / PUT / POS / DEL badges all green. The next step is to **build a screen on top** — covered in the upcoming Screens section.

---

## When to use the wizard vs hand-write

| Use the wizard | Hand-write (`Add query` in the Queries view) |
|---|---|
| The table exists in the DB. | The query is a custom report, an aggregate, or a stored procedure call. |
| You want the four standard CRUD shapes. | You need a `JOIN`, a `GROUP BY`, a `RECURSIVE` CTE. |
| You're starting from scratch and the columns are the source of truth. | You want a query that doesn't map 1-1 to a table. |

The wizard is the right tool for **80% of operational tables**. The other 20% — analytics, reports, multi-table joins — go through [Create a custom query](./create-custom.md).

---

- [Create a custom query](./create-custom.md) — when the wizard doesn't fit.
- [Clone a query or a connector](./clone.md) — start from an existing query instead of from scratch.
- [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md) — give the `:placeholder` params labels, defaults and bind values from screens.

## Liberty Next — Create a custom query
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/queries/create-custom/

Write a standalone query by hand in Liberty Next — the Queries section, the three-stage editor, the writable checkbox, the declared parameters, the SQL editor with autocompletion, tokens, SELECT wizard and Run.

When the wizard doesn't fit — analytics, reports, multi-table joins, stored-procedure calls, anything that doesn't map 1-1 to a single table — write the query by hand in the **Queries** view.

This page walks the editor form field by field.

---

## Where it lives

**Liberty Next → Data → Connectors → pick a connector → stage card Queries → ＋ Add query**.

The page prompts for a name, creates an empty query and opens its editor beside the list. The editor draws the query as three stage cards — **What it is** (label, description), **Statement** (SQL, writable) and **Parameters** — and shows the fields of the picked one.

---

## The editor form

---

## Field by field

### `name`

Shown in the editor's header, not editable there. The name is set when you click *＋ Add query* and is the permission key for the query — `sql:<connector>:<name>`. Rename via the **Rename** button of the header (cross-file — every screen / menu / dictionary reference is updated in one pass; refuses to run on unsaved local edits).

Naming rules:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Letters, digits, underscores. | TOML key, URL segment and permission string in one go. |
| Starts with a letter or underscore. | Same. |

Naming conventions that scale well:

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| `<entity>_<action>` | `customer_balance`, `invoice_send` |
| `<verb>_<noun>` | `get_top_clients`, `mark_paid` |
| `report_<topic>` | `report_monthly_revenue`, `report_overdue_invoices` |

### `writable`

A checkbox under the SQL, in the **Statement** stage.

| State | Allowed |
|---|---|
| **Off** (default) | `SELECT` and CTE-only statements. |
| **On** | `INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE` / `CALL` / `MERGE` / DDL — anything that mutates the database. |

Leave it off for read queries — the safety gate refuses non-SELECT execution otherwise. The CRUD Wizard already sets it for `_put` / `_post` / `_delete`; on a hand-written query you flip it yourself when needed.

### `sql`

The **Statement** stage holds the SQL editor. It accepts a single statement (the common case) or a per-dialect map (**+ per-dialect variants**) — see [Per-dialect SQL variants](./per-dialect-sql.md).

What the editor offers:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Syntax highlighting** | Keywords coloured. |
| **Autocompletion** | Tables after `FROM` / `JOIN` / `INTO` / `UPDATE`, columns after `<table>.`, read from the connector's pool. Ctrl+Space opens the list. |
| **Token** | Inserts a value the server fills at execution: `{{LOGIN}}`, `{{SYSDATE}}`, `{{SYSTIME}}`, `{{SYSTIMESTAMP}}`, `{{JDEDATE}}`, `{{JDETIME}}`, `{{PID}}`, `{{JOBN}}` — see [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md#tokens). The end of the menu, **Pool schemas**, inserts a schema token of the pool, so the same SQL runs against another environment's schema. |
| **Wizard** | Opens the SELECT builder: pick a table, its columns, the WHERE and ORDER BY clauses. |
| **Run** | Tries the statement on the connector's pool and shows the rows. Offered on a read statement only (SELECT, WITH). |
| **`:name` placeholders** | Any `:identifier` in the SQL is a bind parameter — declare it in the **Parameters** stage. |

A few rules from how the engine binds:

- Use `:name` for parameters, never literal string interpolation. The engine binds them through the SQLAlchemy driver — `'%' || :search || '%'` is the LIKE pattern you want, not `'%' + search + '%'`.
- Reserved suffix `_ORIGINAL` is used by the dialog Save for UPDATE WHERE matching (see [Create from a database table](./create-from-database.md#why-name_original-on-update) for the convention).
- A single statement per query. For chained statements, use a `CALL` to a stored procedure or split into multiple Liberty queries.

### `params`

The **Parameters** stage lists the declared parameters — one line per `:placeholder`, opened to edit it (**add** declares another one). Each entry carries:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The placeholder name (without the colon). Matched case-insensitively. |
| **Label** | What the form input shows above the field. Falls back to the name when empty. |
| **Default** | Pre-filled value. Blank means the caller can omit it (the engine binds SQL `NULL`). |
| **Help**, **Example** | What to put in it, in a sentence, and an example value — shown under the field where the parameter is filled, and given to the AI assistant. |
| **Choices** | The only values allowed, when there are a few: the field becomes a dropdown. |
| **Required** | A call without a value (and without a default) is refused before the query runs. |

Adding rows here doesn't change the SQL — it just tells screens and the AI assistant how to render an input for each placeholder. Skip this block when the query has no `:placeholders`; the engine accepts undeclared params at runtime (a column dialog can bind any `:column_name` it sees).

For binding values from other screens / sources (a row click, a parent filter, a chained action), see [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md).

### `label` (What it is)

Short name shown in dropdowns elsewhere — the screen designer, the menu target picker, the action editor. Defaults to the query name.

### `description` (What it is)

Longer text. Shows in the lists under the query's name, and as a tooltip when the operator hovers the query in the screen designer's read-query picker.

---

## Top-bar actions

The buttons of the query editor's header:

| Action | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **← back** | Closes the editor; the list takes the whole width again (no save). | Unsaved edits stay pending — *Save* in the page header writes them. |
| **Find usages** | Lists where the query is used (screens, charts, dashboards, dictionary…). | |
| **Rename** | Cross-file rename. | Refuses on unsaved local edits; updates every reference. |
| **Change type** | Moves the query to Tables, Sequences or Lookups. | See [the four kinds of queries](./overview.md#kinds). |
| **Move** | Moves the query to another SQL connector and rewrites the references. | |
| **Clone** | Per-query duplicate — prompts for the name of the copy. | Default suggestion `<name>_copy`. See [Clone a query or a connector](./clone.md). |
| **Delete** | Removes the query from the connector. | A confirm modal first. |

---

## Save and reload

The page-level **Save** at the top of the Connectors page commits the connector file and triggers a hot reload. The new query is callable immediately at `/api/sql/<connector>/<name>` (with the bound params as query-string values for GET, JSON body for writable POST).

---

## Verifying the query works

**Run**, above the SQL editor, tries a read statement on the connector's pool and shows the rows — the quickest check while writing. Beyond it:

| Path | When |
|---|---|
| Use it from a screen. | When the next step is building the screen anyway. |
| Hit the REST endpoint directly. | For a quick smoke test — `GET /api/sql/<connector>/<query>?from_date=2026-01-01&to_date=2026-01-31`. |
| Ask the AI assistant. | "Show me the result of `monthly_revenue` for last month" — when the connector is open to the assistant, it runs the read query and returns the rows. |

The REST path is the fastest debug — error messages come back verbatim, and you can pass params via URL.

---

## When to use this vs the wizard

| Use the wizard | Use the custom editor |
|---|---|
| The table exists in the DB and you want the standard CRUD shapes. | The query joins multiple tables. |
| You want consistent `:NAME_ORIGINAL` wiring on UPDATE. | The query is a `GROUP BY` aggregate. |
| You want a `_delete` keyed on the primary key. | The query returns a derived column the table doesn't have. |
| | The query is a stored-procedure call. |
| | The query is a write that's not a simple UPDATE / INSERT / DELETE (a `MERGE`, a `TRUNCATE`). |

- [Clone a query or a connector](./clone.md) — start from an existing query instead of from scratch.
- [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md) — give the `:placeholder` params labels, defaults and bound sources.
- [Per-dialect SQL variants](./per-dialect-sql.md) — ship one query with different SQL on Postgres vs Oracle.

## Liberty Next — Clone a query or a connector
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/queries/clone/

Duplicate one query inside a connector, duplicate every CRUD query of a table, or clone a whole application (connector + dictionary + screens + menu + dashboards + charts).

Liberty's Connectors page has **three** clone affordances, each with a different scope. They look similar — Clone buttons next to each other — but they touch different files and ask for different inputs. Pick the right one or you'll be writing more than you meant to.

| Affordance | Scope | Touches |
|---|---|---|
| **Per-query Clone** | One single query. | The connector file only. |
| **Duplicate table** | The four CRUD queries of one table. | The connector file only. |
| **Clone app** | The whole connector + everything scoped under it. | Connector file + dictionary + screens + menu + dashboards + charts. |

Each is covered below with when to use it.

---

## At a glance

---

## Per-query Clone

**Clone** is one of the buttons in the header of the query editor (Queries, Sequences and Lookups sections), with Find usages, Rename, Change type, Move and Delete. Clicking it:

1. Opens the *Clone* dialog — *Name of the new copy:*, `<original>_copy` proposed.
2. Deep-copies the query — name only differs; SQL, params, `writable`, `label`, `description`, per-dialect SQL map, every nested field is JSON-cloned and independent.
3. Appends the clone to the connector's queries list.
4. Selects the clone so you can immediately edit it.

The page then has unsaved changes: **Save**, in the page header, writes them.

### When to use it

| Pattern | Why clone |
|---|---|
| You want a variant of an existing query — same shape, different filter. | The clone preserves params and per-dialect SQL; you only edit the WHERE clause. |
| You need a `_v2` of a query while the old one stays. | Lets a screen keep using the old query while a new screen wires the new one. |
| You're experimenting. | Clone, mangle the copy, keep the original safe. |

### What changes — and what doesn't

| Stays the same | Changes |
|---|---|
| SQL, params, writable, label, description, per-dialect map. | Only the `name`. |
| | Cross-file references to the original — they still point at the original. The clone is a brand-new query nobody references yet. |

If you want references **moved** to the clone, that's a Rename, not a Clone (and Rename is destructive — it deletes the old name once the references are repointed).

---

## Duplicate table

In the **Tables** section, each row carries a *Clone* icon (the copy icon to the right of the CRUD slot badges); an opened table has the same icon among its actions. Clicking it:

1. Asks for the name of the copy (`<base>_copy` proposed).
2. Deep-copies **every CRUD slot** of the table — `<base>_get` → `<copy>_get`, `<base>_put` → `<copy>_put`, etc. Only the slots that exist are cloned (a read-only table with just `_get` clones one query).
3. Appends the clones to the queries list.
4. Selects the new base name in the Tables list.

### When to use it

| Pattern | Why |
|---|---|
| Two screens that share a table shape but need different filters or column lists. | Duplicate, edit the `_get` SELECT clause on the copy. The two screens stay independent. |
| Sandbox version of a production table. | Duplicate to `<base>_sandbox`, point at a sandbox schema, screens keep the original. |
| Multi-tenant per-tenant variant. | Duplicate per tenant, swap the schema name in each. (For a single tenant identifier passed at runtime, use `:placeholder` params on one shared query instead — see [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md).) |

The duplicate is a one-shot copy — future edits to the original don't propagate. For "one definition, many invocations" use **per-dialect SQL** (the same connector pool, different DBs) or **shared params** (one query, different bound values).

---

## Clone app — the whole application

The biggest of the three. Reached from:

- The **Clone** button in the header of the selected connector (with Find usages, Rename and Delete), or
- The same Clone button for any connector — the modal lets you pick which one to clone from.

The modal asks for three values:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Source connector** | Which connector to copy from. Defaults to the one you selected. |
| **New name** | The new connector key (lowercase, starts with a letter — same identifier rules as elsewhere). |
| **Pool** | Which pool the new connector should run on. Must already exist in *Liberty Next → Administer → Pools*. |

Clicking **Clone** triggers a cross-file copy through a dedicated endpoint. Liberty:

1. Copies the **connector** entry to the new key, with the new pool wired in.
2. Copies the connector's **dictionary overlay** (the `[connectors.<source>]` block in dictionary).
3. Copies the **screens** for that connector.
4. Copies the **menu** for that connector.
5. Copies the **dashboards** and **charts** scoped under the connector.
6. Reloads the framework so the new app appears in the top switcher immediately.

The status banner reports the number of entries copied; warnings (e.g. matching menu app key not renamed) ride alongside.

### When to use it

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| Parallel deployment for testing. | Clone `nomasx1` to `nomasx1b`, point at a fresh DB pool, run regression tests against the clone. |
| Per-customer instance. | Clone the base app per tenant; each gets its own pool, dictionary overlay and menu. |
| Major version of an app. | Clone `crm` to `crm_v2`, do destructive refactors on `crm_v2`, keep the old one running until cutover. |

### Constraints

| Constraint | Why |
|---|---|
| The new pool must already exist. | The clone doesn't create databases — wire the pool first via *Liberty Next → Administer → Pools*. |
| The source connector must not have unsaved edits. | The clone reads from disk; unsaved local edits would be missed. The button is disabled in the dirty state with an explanatory tooltip. |
| The new name must not collide. | The framework rejects duplicate connector keys; the modal validates before submit. |

---

## Side-by-side

| You want… | Use |
|---|---|
| A copy of one query (different filter, variant SQL). | **Per-query Clone**. |
| A copy of every CRUD slot of one table. | **Duplicate table**. |
| A copy of every query + dictionary entries + screens + menu + dashboards + charts. | **Clone app**. |
| A new query with the same name pointing somewhere else. | Don't clone — **Rename** the existing one and create a new one. |
| The same query running against a different database. | Don't clone — switch the connector's **pool** in *Liberty Next → Administer → Pools*, or use a **per-dialect SQL map**. |

---

- [Parameter binding](./parameter-binding.md) — once you've cloned, the cloned query may need different bound values from the original.
- [Per-dialect SQL variants](./per-dialect-sql.md) — for "same query, different SQL" without cloning.
- [Sequences and lookups](./sequences-and-lookups.md) — to add a sequence or lookup to the cloned app.
