## Liberty Next — Menus — overview
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/overview/

The Menus page, the flat-items-linked-by-parent model, the seven leaf kinds (screen / query / endpoint / dashboard / page / job / url), and how a menu plus show_in_switcher turns a connector into an app.

A **menu** in Liberty is what the user sees in the left navigation panel when they open one of your apps. It groups screens, endpoints, dashboards and routes into a tree of folders and leaves.

Three things are worth knowing up front:

| Fact | Implication |
|---|---|
| There is **no separate "app" object** in Liberty. | An "app" is just a **connector that has a menu attached** *and* whose `show_in_switcher` flag is on. Both conditions are required for the application picker of the sidebar to list it. |
| Menus are stored as a **flat list of items** linked by `parent`. | The tree is assembled by the backend — easier to hand-edit, round-trips cleanly through TOML, drag operations only ever mutate one list. |
| Every menu key is a connector name (`[menus.<connector>]`). | The connector named `crm` carries the menu under `[menus.crm]`; the screen `customers` on `crm` is reached from a `screen` leaf with `target = "customers"`. |

The page that manages menus is **Liberty Next → Screens → Menus**.

---

## In the application \{#sidebar\}

At the bottom of the sidebar, **Open on hover** folds the menu to its icons: it opens over the page while the mouse is on it and folds back once a page is picked, leaving the whole width to the screens. **Keep open** brings back the fixed menu. The choice is kept in the browser.

The menu is as wide as you make it: drag its right edge (from 180 to 460 pixels, kept in this browser); a double click on the edge brings back the default width. An entry's label takes up to two lines, its full text staying in the tooltip. On a tablet held upright the menu is the icon rail, opened over the page by its button; on a phone it is a drawer — see [Phone and tablet](../../mobile.md).

## The Menus page at a glance

Three regions:

| Region | What it carries |
|---|---|
| **Header and connector bar** | **＋ Folder** and **＋ Item** add an entry at the top level; **Discard**, **Save** and **Reload config** act on the whole page. Below, one chip per app (a connector that has a menu): a click loads its tree. **+ Add scope** gives an existing connector a menu. |
| **Tree (left)** | The app's name and its number of entries, a filter, then the tree. Each row shows a grip, the icon of what it opens (folder, screen, dashboard, job, query, endpoint, page), the label and the id. A click selects the row; on hover, the id gives way to *Move up / down*, *Indent / Outdent*, *Add child item*, *Delete*. Rows are dragged above, below or into a folder. |
| **Picked entry (right)** | Its label, id and kind, with **Clone**, **Find usages** and **Find dependencies**; then the form of the entry in three tabs: **General** (id, label, icon, type, connector, target), **Advanced** (parent, params, roles, override) and **Translations**. With nothing picked, the panel reads *Pick an item in the tree.* |

---

## What a menu carries

The schema's top-level shape:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `label` | The app's display name. Falls back to the connector name. Shown in the application picker. |
| `items` | A flat list of menu items, linked by their `parent` field. |

Each item:

| Field | Required | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | Unique inside this menu. Referenced by children's `parent`. |
| `parent` | no | Pick a folder, or leave blank for a top-level item. |
| `label` | yes | The sidebar text. |
| `l` | no | Per-language label overrides — `l.fr`, `l.de`, etc. |
| `icon` | no | One of the icon names the sidebar draws (`shield`, `users`, `barchart`, …) — see [Translations and icons](./translations-and-icons.md). |
| `type` | no | Blank = folder. Otherwise one of `screen`, `query`, `endpoint`, `dashboard`, `page`, `job`, `url` (see [Item types](./item-types.md)). |
| `connector` | no | Connector hosting the target. Blank = the app's own connector (the menu key). |
| `target` | conditional | Required on every leaf; ignored on folders. |
| `params` | no | Fixed parameters passed to the target when the item opens. |
| `roles` | no | Restrict to these roles. Empty = visible whenever the user can run the target. |

---

## Folder vs leaf

The `type` field decides:

| Setting | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `type` blank | The item is a **folder** — groups children. No `target`, no `connector`, no `params`. A folder is hidden when none of its descendants are visible (the runtime collapses empty folders). |
| `type` set | The item is a **leaf** — points at a thing the user can open. Must have a `target`. |

Folders can nest indefinitely. Leaves can't have children — they're terminal nodes.

---

## The seven leaf kinds

| `type` | Opens | `target` is | `connector` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`screen`** | A designed screen. | The screen's id (`customers`), picked from the application's screens. | Usually blank — the screen's own connector runs it. |
| **`query`** | The same grid view, picked from the raw queries — a query with no designed screen opens as a plain table. | A SELECT query name. | The connector that owns the query. Blank = the app's. |
| **`endpoint`** | The HttpRunner — fires an API connector endpoint. | An endpoint name. | The API connector. Blank = the app's. |
| **`dashboard`** | A dashboard (charts + KPIs). | A dashboard id (from `[dashboards.*]`). | Must NOT be set (dashboards live in their own flat namespace). |
| **`page`** | A registered frontend route (a custom feature area, e.g. `/nomaflow`), or a page an application ships (`/app/<app>/<page>`). | The route path. | Must NOT be set (the target is a route, not a connector resource). |
| **`job`** | The page of a Nomaflow job: its files and parameters, Run, the live log. | The job id. | Must NOT be set. |
| **`url`** | An external address, in a new browser tab. | The address (`https://…`, a path of this server, or `#URL.NAME#/…`). | Must NOT be set. |

The schema validator enforces:

- A leaf needs a `target` — saving fails without one.
- A `dashboard`, `page`, `job` or `url` leaf with a `connector` is rejected (misconfiguration); a `url` must start with `http://`, `https://`, `/` or `#URL.`.
- A folder with `target` / `connector` / `params` is rejected (those fields only make sense on leaves).

---

## Save and reload

The *Save* button validates the whole `MenusFile` (unique ids, parents exist, no cycles), writes `menus.toml` and triggers a hot reload. New menus apply immediately — no process restart.

The validation is strict on three things:

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| Every `parent` reference must point at an existing item. | A dangling parent would orphan the subtree. |
| No cycles (a parent chain that loops). | An infinite-loop guard. |
| No duplicate `id` within the same menu. | Children reference parents by id; duplicates break the link. |

Cross-menu duplicates are fine — `[menus.crm.security]` and `[menus.nomasx1.security]` coexist without conflict.

---

## How a connector becomes an app

**A connector is listed in the application picker of the sidebar only when both conditions are true:**

1. A menu exists — `[menus.<connector>]` is set up in *Liberty Next → Screens → Menus*.
2. **Show in the application list** on the connector — set in *Liberty Next → Data → Connectors → \ → Settings* (on by default).

Miss either one and the connector exists but is not listed. The picker itself appears only when there is more than one application. Setting up the menu first and **then** ticking `show_in_switcher` is the usual order.

Note: the Connectors page's own *Apps* / *Data sources* grouping is based on menu existence alone — connectors with a menu but `show_in_switcher = false` still show under *Apps* there. That grouping is an internal Settings-UI affordance; the user-facing picker is what **Show In Switcher** gates.

The next page covers the wiring from both sides.

---

## Permission pruning

When the user opens the app, `GET /api/menus` returns the tree **filtered to what the user can run**:

- A leaf is kept when the user may run what it opens (`sql:<connector>:<target>` for `screen` / `query`, `api:<connector>:<target>` for `endpoint`), or when a role sets the leaf, its folder or the whole application to **Read** or **Read and change** (a job: **Read and change**) — see [Permissions and roles](./permissions-and-roles.md).
- A `menu:` or `dashboard:` deny removes it.
- A folder with no surviving children is collapsed away.
- Items with a `roles` filter are kept only when the user's roles intersect the list.

A user sees only the parts of the menu they can actually use — no greyed-out items, no clicks on dead-end links.

---

|---|---|

| Pick the right leaf type (screen / endpoint / dashboard / route). | [Item types](./item-types.md). |

| Add icons + per-language labels. | [Translations and icons](./translations-and-icons.md). |

## Liberty Next — Make a connector an app
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/make-connector-an-app/

A connector becomes an 'app' visible in the application picker when it has a menu attached and show_in_switcher is on. Plus how the optional home field decides the landing page.

Liberty has **no separate Apps configuration**. The thing users call "an app" — what shows up in the application picker, what carries a menu in the left navigation — is just a **connector with a menu attached** and the `show_in_switcher` flag on.

This page walks the wiring from both sides: the connector flag + the menu key.

---

## The three pieces

| Piece | Where it lives | Required for an app? |
|---|---|---|
| **`show_in_switcher`** | On the connector (Liberty Next → Data → Connectors → stage **Settings**). | Yes — when off, the connector exists but doesn't appear in the application picker. |
| **`[menus.<connector>]`** | The menu file (Liberty Next → Screens → Menus). | Yes — without a menu, the connector is treated as a *data source*, not an app. |
| **`home`** | On the connector (Liberty Next → Data → Connectors → stage **Settings**). | Optional — sets the landing menu item when the user picks this app in the picker. |

Two separate effects, decided by different flags:

| Effect | Triggered by |
|---|---|
| The connector chip moves from *Data sources* to *Apps* on the Connectors page. | Menu existence alone — `[menus.<connector>]` is set up. |
| A tile for the app appears in the application picker (the user-facing app picker). | Both menu existence **and** `show_in_switcher = true`. |

Set up the menu first; flip `show_in_switcher` on second. Miss the second step and the connector still classifies as an "app" on the Connectors page but doesn't show up for end users in the switcher.

---

## Where each flag is set

---

## Step 1 — On the connector

Open **Liberty Next → Data → Connectors** and pick the connector in the list — connectors with a menu are under **Apps**, the others under **Data sources**. Its **Settings** stage opens first. The fields relevant to "this is an app" (labelled **Show in the application list**, **Home page** and **Home page per role** in the form):

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **`show_in_switcher`** | Default `true`. When on, the connector shows in the application picker (provided it has a menu). When off, the connector is reachable only by URL — useful for hidden / admin connectors. |
| **`home`** | Dropdown sourced from this connector's menu items. Picks the landing menu item when the user picks the app in the picker. Blank → the first visible top-level item. |
| **`home_by_role`** | A start page per role: one line per role, each with a menu item picked from the lists. A user lands on the item of their first role listed here, else on `home` — the auditors on the audit synthesis, the administrators on the settings screens. |

Save the connector page — the change applies immediately (hot reload).

---

## Step 2 — On the menu

Open **Liberty Next → Screens → Menus**. If the connector doesn't have a menu yet, the **+ Add scope** button opens a modal listing every connector **without** a menu — pick yours. The modal:

- Creates a new `[menus.<connector>]` entry with no items.
- Selects the new app chip.
- Reveals the empty tree.

If the connector already has a menu, its chip is in the scope bar — click it.

Add items via **＋ Folder** / **＋ Item** at the top of the tree pane. See [Build the tree](./build-the-tree.md) for the editor walkthrough.

---

## What changes after the wiring

Before:

- The connector shows up under **Data sources** on the Connectors page.
- It isn't listed in the application picker.
- Screens that point at its queries are reachable only by URL.

After:

- The connector shows up under **Apps** on the Connectors page.
- It is listed in the application picker (shown in the sidebar when there is more than one application).
- Picking it takes the user to the `home` item (or the first visible top-level item).
- The left navigation shows the menu tree.

The Connectors page reads the menus file to decide the grouping — there's no separate "this is an app" flag beyond *"has a menu + is in the switcher"*.

---

## Cloning an app

The Connectors page has a **Clone** action (covered in [Queries → Clone a query or a connector](../queries/clone.md#clone-app--the-whole-application)) that copies the connector + its dictionary overlay + its screens + its menu + its dashboards + its charts under a new connector key. The cloned connector inherits `show_in_switcher`; its menu is wired automatically — the cloned app appears in the application picker as soon as the clone completes.

This is the right move when:

- You need a parallel deployment (`nomasx1` → `nomasx1b` for regression testing).
- You're standing up a per-tenant instance.
- You're forking an app for a major refactor while keeping the original running.

---

## Hiding an app temporarily

Two ways to take an app out of the picker without deleting it:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| Turn off `show_in_switcher` on the connector. | The app vanishes from the switcher. Its screens are still reachable by URL; users with the URL keep working. |
| Delete the `[menus.<connector>]` entry. | The connector returns to *Data sources*. Screens still resolve, but the user has no nav to find them. |

The first is the right choice for maintenance windows — fully reversible in one click. The second is for genuinely retiring the app's UI.

---

## Multi-app installs

A typical Liberty install carries several apps:

| Connector | Role |
|---|---|
| `crm` | Customer-facing CRM. |
| `nomasx1` | Security review. |
| `nomajde` | JDE master data. |
| `nomaflow` | Job scheduler (its own product). |
| `default` | The framework's own pool — usually no menu, just a data source for shared queries. |

Each gets its own `[menus.<name>]` block, its own chip on the Menus page, its own entry in the application picker. They share the same framework process, the same authentication, the same dictionary (with per-connector overlays).

A user signing in sees only the apps they have permission for — `GET /api/menus` returns an empty tree for an app where the user can't run anything (and the app is left out of the picker).

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Connector has `show_in_switcher = true` but no menu. | The connector shows in the Connectors page's *Data sources* group; the application picker doesn't list it. | Add a menu in *Liberty Next → Screens → Menus*. |
| Connector has a menu but `show_in_switcher = false`. | The menu exists but the switcher hides the tile. | Either turn `show_in_switcher` on, or accept that users will reach the app by URL only. |
| `home` points at a menu item that no longer exists. | Picking the app lands on the first visible top-level item, ignoring the stale `home`. | Re-pick a valid item — the dropdown lists the live menu items. |
| Adding `[menus.<X>]` where `<X>` isn't a connector. | The page rejects the entry on save — the menu key must match a known connector. | Create the connector first, then attach the menu. |
| Cloning an app but the new pool doesn't exist. | The clone modal refuses to submit. | Create the pool in *Liberty Next → Administer → Pools* before cloning. |

---

- [Item types](./item-types.md) — pick between `query`, `endpoint`, `dashboard`, `page`.
- [Queries → Clone a query or a connector](../queries/clone.md) — the whole-app clone flow.

## Liberty Next — Build the tree
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/build-the-tree/

The tree editor — add folders and items, drag to reorder, indent/outdent to reparent, clone, rename, find usages. Every action's exact button and behaviour.

Once a connector has a menu attached (see [Make a connector an app](./make-connector-an-app.md)), the tree editor on the right is where you compose the navigation: folders that group, leaves that open screens / endpoints / dashboards / routes.

The model is a **flat list of items linked by `parent`** — but the editor lets you work with it as a tree. Drag operations mutate the underlying flat order; the tree on screen always reflects what's saved.

---

## The toolbar

In the page header:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **＋ Folder** | Adds a folder at the top level. The folder is the only item kind without a `type`. |
| **＋ Item** | Adds a leaf at the top level — set its type and target in the panel on the right. To add under a folder, use the row's **＋** (*Add child item*). |
| **Discard** / **Save** | Revert or write the whole menu. |
| **Reload config** | Re-reads the configuration files. |

On the panel of the picked entry, next to its kind:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Clone** | Duplicates the entry (subtree included). Prompts for a new id. |
| **Find usages** | Lists every place this menu entry is referenced (e.g. another connector's `home` field). Helps before a rename / delete. |
| **Find dependencies** | Lists what the entry relies on — its connector and its target (a screen, a query, an endpoint, a dashboard or a job) — and what they rely on in turn. |

---

## The tree rows

Each row carries:

| Element | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Indent | Visual depth — each level is 16 pixels in. |
| Chevron | ▾ for an expanded folder, ▸ for collapsed; a double click on the folder's row toggles it too. |
| Icon | The kind of the entry: an open or closed folder, a screen, a dashboard, a job, a query, an endpoint, a page. The item's own `icon` is the one the application's sidebar draws. |
| Label | The `label` field. |
| Id | Monospace, muted, after the label. Fades out on hover to make room for the actions. |
| Per-row actions (hover) | *Move up* (↑), *Move down* (↓), *Indent* (→), *Outdent* (←), *Add child item* (＋), *Delete* (🗑). |

Click anywhere on the row to **select** the item — the Inspector on the right loads its full form.

---

## Drag and drop \{#drag\}

A row is dragged onto another: **above** it, **below** it, or **into** it when it is a folder — with everything under it. A line or a highlight shows where it will land. Dragging is off while the tree is filtered.

Each row carries the icon of what it opens — folder, screen, dashboard, job, query, endpoint, page. The tree and the picked entry are two panels side by side; the entry's own actions — **Clone**, **Find usages**, **Find dependencies** — are on its panel, and **Folder**, **Item**, **Discard** and **Save** are in the page header.

---

## The per-row actions

The icons that appear on hover, left to right:

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| **↑ Move up** | Swap with the previous sibling. Disabled when the item is the first child of its parent. Moves the whole subtree together — child links follow. |
| **↓ Move down** | Swap with the next sibling. Disabled at the end. |
| **→ Indent** | Reparent the item under the previous sibling. The previous sibling becomes the new parent. Disabled when there's no previous sibling. |
| **← Outdent** | Move the item up one level — its grand-parent becomes the new parent. Disabled when the item is already at the top level. |
| **＋ Add child item** | Adds an item as a child of this row. |
| **🗑 Delete** | Removes the item — with its whole subtree, after a confirmation, when it has children. |

The icons are intentionally compact and only show on hover — the tree stays scannable in steady state.

---

## Building a tree from scratch

A typical flow for a new app's menu:

### Step 1 — Add the top-level folders

Click **＋ Folder** to add a folder. The default `id` is something like `folder_1`; the Inspector lets you rename it.

| Top-level pattern | Examples |
|---|---|
| One folder per domain. | `security`, `pipeline`, `reports`, `admin`. |
| One folder per workflow phase. | `setup`, `daily-ops`, `month-end`, `audit`. |
| One folder per audience. | `for-managers`, `for-operators`, `for-analysts`. |

Pick the convention that maps to how your users think — not how the data is shaped.

### Step 2 — Add the leaves under each folder

On the folder's row, click **＋** (*Add child item*). The new item appears under the folder. Set its `type`, `connector`, `target` in the Inspector — see [Item types](./item-types.md).

### Step 3 — Reorder

Use ↑ / ↓ on each row to put items in the order the user should see. The order in the tree = the order in the rendered sidebar.

### Step 4 — Nest where needed

Use → (Indent) to push an item under the previous sibling — useful when a folder grows long and you need a sub-folder. Use ← (Outdent) to pull it back out.

### Step 5 — Save

The page-level **Save** first checks the menus: an entry that opens nothing, two entries with the same id, an entry under a folder that does not exist. Each one is listed above the tree — *crm › Menu entry "Late orders" opens nothing: pick what it opens* — with **Open**, which selects the entry in its tree (folders unfolded, application switched when needed), and nothing is sent. Then the server validates the whole menu (no cycles…) and writes `menus.toml`; a refusal is listed the same way — see [A refused save](../../configuration/settings-ui.md#refused). The hot reload picks up the changes; the user's next page load shows the new tree.

---

## The application line \{#application\}

The line above the tree names the application — its name, else its id — with the number of its entries. A click on it shows the application's own settings beside the tree:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Application name** | The name shown for the application in the list at the top of the menu. Blank shows its id. |

---

## The Inspector form

Click a row → the panel on the right loads the form of the entry, in three tabs — **General**, **Advanced** and **Translations**. Each field carries one short sentence of help, the longer explanation behind **more**. The fields adapt to what the entry opens:

| Field | Tab | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Id** | General | A short name for the entry, unique in its application. Renaming here updates every child's folder reference automatically. Cross-file references (e.g. another connector's home pointing at this item) need a manual fix — use *Find usages* first. |
| **Label** | General | The sidebar text. |
| **Icon** | General | One of the [sidebar icons](./translations-and-icons.md#icons). |
| **What it opens** | General | *Screen (designed view)*, *Query (raw table view)*, *Endpoint (API call)*, *Dashboard (widget grid)*, *Page (frontend route)*, *Job (run it, follow its log)*, *Link (an address, opened in a new tab)* — see [Item types](./item-types.md). Blank = folder. Switching from leaf to folder clears what it opens and its fixed values. |
| **Application** | General | For a query or endpoint: the application that holds it. Blank = this one. |
| **Opens** | General | Picked among the valid targets for what it opens and its application. |
| **Folder** | Advanced | The folder the entry sits in, picked among the folders; blank for the top of the menu. The tree's indent / outdent actions change it too. |
| **Fixed values** | Advanced | Values given to what is opened — a filter already filled in. One line per value: its name, picked among the filters of the screen it opens or the parameters of the query it opens (or typed), and the value. A line left without a name is not saved. |
| **Only for the roles** | Advanced | Shows the entry to these roles only. See [Permissions and roles](./permissions-and-roles.md). |
| **Keep on upgrade** | Advanced | An upgrade of the application leaves this entry as saved here. |
| **Translations** | Translations | The label in the other languages. See [Translations and icons](./translations-and-icons.md). |

Edits are **live in memory** — the tree row updates as you type. Page-level *Save* is what writes to disk.

---

## Renaming an item

Renaming an **Id** is more involved than other fields because every reference must update:

1. **Children**: the children's **Folder** updates automatically.
2. **Cross-file**: a connector's `home` field, or another menu's item that references this one, doesn't update. Use **Find usages** (on the entry's panel) before renaming to see every place that references the item.

For a heavy rename, the safe pattern is **Find usages → Clone → fix references → delete the old one** — the new id can take over while every reference is updated.

---

## Cloning an item

**Clone**, on the panel of the picked entry, duplicates it:

- The whole subtree is cloned (a folder with children clones every descendant).
- The new ids are prompted from a modal — the default is the old id with a suffix.
- Cross-file references are **not** rewritten — the clones are brand-new items nobody references yet.

Useful when:

- You're building a variant of a section (e.g. `reports` for managers, `reports_admin` for admins).
- The same shape applies to two apps and you copy-pasted the tree.
- You want a sandbox version to experiment with.

---

## Deleting an item

The row's 🗑 icon removes the item. When it has children, a confirmation asks first, and confirming removes the whole subtree.

There's no soft delete — the item disappears immediately from memory. The page-level *Save* is what persists. Until you Save, you can **Discard** to revert.

For cross-file references (a `home` field pointing at the deleted item), the connector's `home` becomes invalid — the app falls back to the first visible top-level item on next load. Use *Find usages* before deleting heavy items.

---

## Filtering long trees

A search box above the tree narrows the visible items by id / label substring. Useful when a menu grows past 30-40 entries.

The filter is case-insensitive and matches anywhere in the id or label. Folders whose children match are kept (with the matching descendants visible).

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Two items with the same id in the same menu. | **Save** lists *has the same id as another entry* and sends nothing. | Pick a unique id. |
| An entry under a folder that doesn't exist. | **Save** lists *sits under a folder that does not exist*. | Pick a folder from the dropdown — only existing folders are listed. |
| Parent cycle (A → B → A). | Save validation fails ("parent cycle"). | The tree editor's indent/outdent never creates a cycle; only direct TOML edits do. |
| A leaf that opens nothing. | **Save** lists *opens nothing: pick what it opens*. | Set **Opens** in the Inspector. |
| Folder with **Opens** set. | Save validation fails ("folder cannot carry target"). | Either remove the target or set a non-folder type. |
| Dashboard or page leaf with an **Application**. | Save validation fails. | These two leaf types don't carry a connector; leave the field blank. |
| Renaming an item without checking *Find usages*. | Another connector's `home` or another menu's reference breaks silently. | Always check Find usages before renaming. |

---

- [Item types](./item-types.md) — what `query` / `endpoint` / `dashboard` / `page` open and the fields they take.
- [Permissions and roles](./permissions-and-roles.md) — the `roles` filter and how the menu prunes for each user.
- [Translations and icons](./translations-and-icons.md) — `l.fr`, `l.de`, icon picking.

## Liberty Next — Item types
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/item-types/

The seven leaf kinds — screen / query / endpoint / dashboard / page / job / url — what each opens, the target field's shape, the connector rule, and when to reach for each.

A menu item is either a **folder** (no `type`) or a **leaf** that opens something. The leaf's `type` decides what that something is and what the `target` / `connector` fields mean.

Seven leaf kinds:

| `type` | Opens | `target` is | `connector` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`screen`** | A designed screen. | The screen's id, picked from the application's screens. | Usually blank — the screen's own connector runs it. |
| **`query`** | The same grid view, picked from the raw queries. | A SELECT query name. | The connector that owns the query. Blank = the app's own connector. |
| **`endpoint`** | The HttpRunner — fires one API connector endpoint. | An endpoint name. | The API connector. Blank = the app's. |
| **`dashboard`** | A dashboard (charts + KPIs). | `<app>.<id>` of the dashboard. | Must NOT be set (the app is in the target). |
| **`page`** | A registered frontend route — a custom feature area like `/nomaflow`. | The route path. | Must NOT be set. |
| **`url`** | An external address, in a new browser tab. | The address: `https://…`, a path of this server, or `#URL.NAME#/…` — see [External addresses](../settings-app.md#external-urls). | Must NOT be set. |
| **`job`** | The page of a Nomaflow job: its files and parameters, Run, the live log, the previous runs. | The job id. | Must NOT be set. |

This page walks each in detail with concrete examples.

---

## At a glance

---

## `screen` and `query` — open a screen

The most common leaf kinds. They open a grid, but not from the same target:

- **`screen`** opens a designed screen. The target is the **screen's id** (`customers`), within the menu's application: the screen opens with its own columns, filters, views and record form — even when another screen reads the same query. The Inspector's *Target* list offers the application's screens, each with its label and id.
- **`query`** opens a query's rows. The target is the **query name** (`customers_get`): the list offers each table's read query (`<table>_get`, labelled with the table) and the standalone queries. When a screen is designed on that query, its column settings apply; otherwise the rows show in a plain grid.

### Fields

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **`type`** | `screen` or `query`. |
| **`target`** | `screen`: the screen id — `customers`, `security_users`. `query`: the query name — `customers_get`. The dropdown lists the valid targets for the chosen type and connector. |
| **`connector`** | `query`: the connector that owns the query; blank = the menu's app (most common case). `screen`: usually blank — the screen's own connector runs its queries. |
| **`params`** (**Fixed values**, Advanced tab) | Optional. Fixed values for the filters of the screen or the `:placeholder` parameters of the query — e.g. a *My open tickets* leaf with `OWNER` = `#LOGIN_USER#` and `STATUS` = `OPEN`. The names are picked among the screen's filters or the query's parameters. |

### Who sees the leaf

A `screen` leaf shows to whoever may run the screen's read query on the screen's connector (`sql:<connector>:<read query>`); a `query` leaf, to whoever may run the query itself. The entry's `roles` narrow it further — see [Permissions and roles](./permissions-and-roles.md).

### Example

```toml
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "pipeline.customers"
parent = "pipeline"
label = "Customers"
l.fr = "Clients"
icon = "users"
type = "screen"
target = "customers"
```

Opens the screen `customers` of the `crm` application.

```toml
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "my_open_tickets"
label = "My open tickets"
icon = "ticket"
type = "query"
target = "tickets_get"
params = { OWNER = "#LOGIN_USER#", STATUS = "OPEN" }
```

Opens the rows of `tickets_get`, with the screen designed on that query, bound to the user's own open tickets. The `#LOGIN_USER#` token resolves from the JWT — see [Parameter binding](../queries/parameter-binding.md).

---

## `endpoint` — fire an API endpoint

The second leaf kind: open the HttpRunner with one API connector endpoint pre-selected. The user gets a form prompting for the endpoint's parameters and a *Run* button.

### Fields

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **`type`** | `endpoint`. |
| **`target`** | An endpoint name declared on the API connector. The dropdown lists every endpoint on the picked connector. |
| **`connector`** | The API connector. Blank = the menu's app (works when the app is itself an API connector). |
| **`params`** (**Fixed values**) | Optional. Pre-fill the form fields. |

### When to use

- Custom integrations the user triggers manually (sync from an external system, refresh a cache).
- Operations that aren't naturally a screen — webhook tests, ad-hoc POST.
- Tools and diagnostic endpoints.

### Example

```toml
[[menus.nomaubl.items]]
id = "ppf.sync_directory"
parent = "ppf"
label = "Sync PPF directory"
icon = "refresh-cw"
type = "endpoint"
connector = "ppf"
target = "sync_directory"
```

Opens the HttpRunner for the `ppf` API connector's `sync_directory` endpoint. The user fills any required form fields and clicks *Run*.

---

## `dashboard` — open a dashboard

A dashboard is a page of charts and KPIs declared in `[dashboards.*]`. The menu item points at the dashboard's id.

### Fields

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **`type`** | `dashboard`. |
| **`target`** | `<app>.<id>` — the dashboard `[dashboards.<app>.<id>]`, for example `crm.pipeline`. The dropdown lists every dashboard. |
| **`connector`** | **Must not be set** — the app is part of the target; the validator rejects a stray `connector`. |
| **`params`** (**Fixed values**) | Optional. Pre-fill the dashboard's filters. |

### When to use

- Executive overviews (revenue by region, pipeline by stage).
- Operational dashboards (jobs status, system health).
- Anything that's a layout of charts rather than a single table.

### Example

```toml
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "pipeline.deals_dashboard"
parent = "pipeline"
label = "Deals dashboard"
icon = "chart-bar"
type = "dashboard"
target = "crm.deals_overview"
```

Opens the dashboard `deals_overview` of the `crm` app — note no `connector` field.

---

## `page` — open a registered frontend route

The escape hatch. A `page` leaf navigates to a hand-written React route — a custom feature area the framework doesn't compose from queries / screens / dashboards. The classic example is the Nomaflow product, which has its own routes (`/nomaflow`, `/nomaflow/jobs/:id`, `/nomaflow/runs/:runId`) for the scheduler UI.

### Fields

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **`type`** | `page`. |
| **`target`** | The route path — `/nomaflow`, `/runs/dashboard`, etc. Routes must be **registered** in the frontend (the menu doesn't create them; it just points at them). |
| **Tests pages** | `/liberty/tests` and `/liberty/test-results` put the [Tests](../tests.md) and [Test results](../../../monitoring/test-results.md) pages in an application's menu; the entries show to the holders of `tests:view`. |
| **`connector`** | **Must not be set**. The target is a route, not a connector resource. |
| **`params`** (**Fixed values**) | Optional. The runtime appends them as query-string parameters on the route. |

### The Data Explorer \{#explorer\}

`/explorer` opens the [Data Explorer](../../explorer/overview.md) on the application's first model; the entry shows to whoever may use one of the application's models. `/explorer/<app>/<model>` opens it on one model — `/explorer/crm/sales` — and the model picker still lets the user switch; the entry asks for `explorer:<app>:<model>`.

A saved and shared analysis or dashboard of the Explorer is put in a menu from the Explorer itself, with **Add to a menu** (application, folder, label) — see [Add to a menu](../../explorer/saved-and-dashboards.md#menu). The entry it creates is a `page` leaf whose target is:

| Target | Opens |
|---|---|
| `/explorer/<app>/<model>/a/<id>` | The saved analysis `<id>`, its result at once. |
| `/explorer/<app>/<model>/d/<id>` | The Explorer dashboard `<id>`. |

Like a link to the model, it shows to whoever may use the model (`explorer:<app>:<model>`).

### A page an application ships \{#app-page\}

`/app/<app>/<page>` opens a page an application ships with its plugins — a structure to browse, a guided flow, anything that is neither a grid nor a form. The entry needs the permission `page:<app>:<page>`. See [Plugins → Pages an application ships](../../apps/plugins.md#pages).

### When to use

- A bundled product (Nomaflow, Nomasx-1's specialised dashboards).
- A custom React component for something queries / screens can't express (live-streaming logs, complex interactive visualisations).
- A third-party component embedded into Liberty.

The `page` type is rare in user-built apps — most teams build with queries / screens / dashboards. Reach for `page` when one of the other three genuinely can't express the surface you need.

### Example

```toml
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "ops"
label = "Operations"
icon = "settings"

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "ops.nomaflow"
parent = "ops"
label = "Job scheduler"
icon = "calendar"
type = "page"
target = "/nomaflow"
```

A *Job scheduler* leaf in the `crm` app's Operations folder, pointing at the Nomaflow product's main route.

---

## `job` — run a Nomaflow job \{#job\}

A `job` leaf opens the page of a Nomaflow job for users who do not administer Nomaflow: a file picker per load step that needs a file, the parameters the job declares for its users, **Run**, the log followed live and the previous runs.

### Fields

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **`type`** | `job` — *Job (run it, follow its log)* in the type list. |
| **`target`** | The job id. The dropdown lists every job with the first line of its description. |
| **`connector`** | Must NOT be set. |
| **`params`** (**Fixed values**) | Optional: `{ preset = "Licences" }` runs the job with one of its presets — one job, several menu entries. |

The item is shown to who may run the job: the entry or its folder in **Read and change** in the role, or the permission `job:<id>` (rule type **Job** in a role's *Beyond the menus*); `!job:<id>` hides it. See [Run a job from an application's menu](../../../nomaflow/jobs/run-from-menu.md).

### Example

```toml title="menus.toml"
[[menus.sales.items]]
id = "import_sales"
parent = "import"
label = "Sales file (one month)"
type = "job"
target = "sales-load-month"
```

---

## Folders — group leaves

A folder is the only item kind **without** a `type`. It carries no `target`, no `connector`, no `params` — just `id`, `label`, `icon` and `l` (translations).

### Validation

The schema's validator rejects a folder with any of:

- `target` set — folders don't have targets.
- `connector` set — folders don't open anything.
- `params` non-empty — same.

### Behaviour

Folders are **collapsed away when empty**. If every child of a folder is hidden (e.g. because the user lacks permission on each), the folder itself disappears from the rendered menu. The user never sees an empty folder.

### Nesting

Folders can nest indefinitely. A typical Liberty app uses 2-3 levels:

```
Pipeline (folder)
├── Customers (query)
├── Deals (query)
├── Activities (query)
└── Reports (folder)
    ├── Daily summary (dashboard)
    └── Monthly revenue (query)
```

Deeper than 3 levels usually means the app is over-grouped — flatten when you can.

---

## Cross-cutting rules

### The `connector` field defaults to the app

For `query` and `endpoint` leaves, leaving `connector` blank means "the app's own connector" — i.e. the connector named by the menu key (`[menus.crm]` → `connector = "crm"`).

Set `connector` explicitly when:

- The query lives on a **different** connector — `crm` app showing a leaf that reads from `reporting`.
- You're reading shared data (a `default` connector for framework-wide queries).

For `dashboard` and `page`, the field is **always blank** — the validator enforces it.

### `params` carries fixed values

`params` is a flat map of key → value passed to the target at open time:

```toml
params = { STATUS = "OPEN", REGION = "EU" }
```

For `screen` and `query` leaves, the values bind to the query's `:placeholder` parameters. For `endpoint`, they pre-fill the HttpRunner's form. For `page`, they become query-string parameters. A `screen`, `query` or `endpoint` leaf passes them in its address when it opens — the page fills its inputs from them, as it does for a link that opens it on a record —, and so does a [Links widget](../../dashboards.md#text-links) that points at the entry.

The two reserved tokens — `#LOGIN_USER#` and `#SYSDATE#` — work here too: a *My data* leaf with `params = { OWNER = "#LOGIN_USER#" }` lands the user on a view scoped to their own rows.

### Switching `type` resets the fields

In the Inspector, changing `type` from `query` to `dashboard` clears `connector` (since `dashboard` rejects it). Switching from leaf to folder clears `target`, `connector`, `params`. The form prevents invalid combinations from reaching the save.

---

## Picking the right type

| You want to open… | Use |
|---|---|
| A list of rows with optional filter / add / edit. | `screen`. |
| A pre-filtered list (e.g. *My open tickets*). | `screen` with `params`. |
| A query that has no designed screen yet. | `query`. |
| A custom write or read-only API call. | `endpoint`. |
| A page of charts and KPIs. | `dashboard`. |
| A hand-written React feature (Nomaflow-style), or a page an application ships. | `page`. |
| A Nomaflow job users run themselves (file, parameters, log). | `job`. |
| Another application, in a new browser tab. | `url`. |

When in doubt, start with `screen` — most user-facing pages are lists. Promote to `dashboard` when the layout is multiple charts; reach for `endpoint` only for API operations that don't fit a screen; reserve `page` for custom React.

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `query` leaf with a `target` that's not a query name. | Clicking the leaf opens a default TableView with no columns. | Pick a real query from the dropdown. |
| `endpoint` leaf on a SQL connector. | Save validation may pass, but at runtime the connector doesn't expose endpoints. | Point at an API connector. |
| `dashboard` with `connector`. | Save validation fails. | Drop the `connector` field. |
| `page` with `connector`. | Save validation fails. | Drop the `connector` field. |
| `params` referencing a placeholder the target query doesn't have. | The bind is silently ignored. | Open the target query, declare the param. |
| `page` pointing at a route that isn't registered. | Clicking the leaf shows a 404 page. | Verify the route exists in the frontend bundle; mistypes are the usual cause. |

---

## Liberty Next — Permissions and roles
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/permissions-and-roles/

The roles filter on a menu item, the underlying sql / api permission inherited from the target, how empty folders collapse, and how the menu prunes per user.

The menu the user sees is **not** the menu you saved — it's the menu **filtered to what the user is allowed to use**. Liberty prunes the tree at fetch time so users never click on items they can't open.

Two filters apply:

| Filter | When it kicks in |
|---|---|
| **Implicit permission** | Every leaf inherits the permission of its **target** — `sql:<connector>:<target>` for a `query`, `api:<connector>:<target>` for an `endpoint`. Users without the permission don't see the leaf. |
| **Explicit roles** | The leaf's `roles` field is an additional gate — when set, the user must have at least one of the listed roles. |

After both filters run, folders with no surviving children are collapsed away.

---

## At a glance

---

## The implicit permission

Every leaf is gated by the permission of its target:

| `type` | Required permission |
|---|---|
| `screen`, `query` | `sql:<connector>:<target>` (the query's permission). |
| `endpoint` | `api:<connector>:<target>` (the endpoint's permission). |
| `dashboard` | The permission of at least one of its data widgets, or `dashboard:<id>` — see [below](#gating). |
| `page` | The page's own: `explorer:<app>:<model>` for the Data Explorer, `page:<app>:<page>` for a page an application ships, `nomaflow:view` for the Nomaflow pages, `tests:view` for the Tests pages, none for the others. |

A role that sets the entry, its folder or the whole application to **Read** (`menu:<app>:<id>`) or **Read and change** (`edit:<app>:<id>`) also shows the leaf: the server gives it what the screen needs, its target's permission included. A `menu:` deny always hides it. The role editor writes these strings from its menu tree — see [Roles and permissions](../secure/roles-and-permissions.md#access).

A user with `sql:crm:customers_get` sees the menu leaf that opens the Customers screen. A user without it doesn't — the leaf vanishes from the rendered menu.

This is the **same permission** the screen / endpoint already checks. The menu doesn't introduce a second permission; it just hides links the user couldn't follow anyway. Result: no greyed-out items, no clicks that take the user to a *403 forbidden* page.

---

## The explicit `roles` filter

The `roles` field on a menu item is a list of role names. When set:

- The user must have **at least one** of the listed roles.
- The check is in addition to the implicit permission — both must hold.

| `roles` value | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty (default) | Visibility determined by the implicit permission alone. |
| `["manager"]` | Visible only to users with the `manager` role. |
| `["manager", "admin"]` | Visible to users with either `manager` or `admin`. |

### Use cases

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| Hide an item that's open to read but only meaningful for a subset of users. | A *Reports* leaf where every user has read on the underlying query, but only managers actually use it. |
| Surface different sections to different audiences in the same app. | An `admin` folder visible only when `roles = ["admin"]` matches. |
| Stage a rollout. | Tag a new section `roles = ["beta-testers"]`; flip to empty when launching to everyone. |

The `roles` field is **not** an alternative to the permission — both must hold: the user needs one of the listed roles and the right to open the leaf.

---

## Folder collapse

A folder with **no visible children** disappears from the rendered menu. This means:

- A folder that wraps three leaves, all gated by `roles = ["admin"]`, vanishes entirely for a non-admin user — they don't see an empty *Admin* folder.
- A folder whose children are all gated by SQL permissions the user lacks similarly vanishes.

This happens at every level — a nested folder structure prunes from the leaves up. The user sees a minimal, useful tree.

The runtime walks the tree once per request, applying the filters and collapsing empties in one pass.

---

## A worked example

A menu with mixed visibility:

```toml
[menus.crm]
label = "CRM"

# Top-level — always visible
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "pipeline"
label = "Pipeline"
icon = "briefcase"

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "pipeline.customers"
parent = "pipeline"
label = "Customers"
type = "query"
target = "customers_get"
# implicit: sql:crm:customers_get

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "pipeline.deals"
parent = "pipeline"
label = "Deals"
type = "query"
target = "deals_get"
# implicit: sql:crm:deals_get

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "reports"
label = "Reports"
icon = "chart-bar"

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "reports.monthly"
parent = "reports"
label = "Monthly revenue"
type = "query"
target = "monthly_revenue_get"
roles = ["manager", "admin"]

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "reports.cohort"
parent = "reports"
label = "Cohort analysis"
type = "query"
target = "cohort_get"
roles = ["analyst", "admin"]

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "admin"
label = "Admin"
icon = "shield"

[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "admin.config"
parent = "admin"
label = "Config"
type = "query"
target = "config_get"
roles = ["admin"]
```

What different users see:

| User | Roles | Has `sql:crm:*` | Visible menu |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Alice** (user) | `["user"]` | `customers_get`, `deals_get` only | Pipeline → Customers, Deals. *(no Reports, no Admin)* |
| **Bob** (manager) | `["manager"]` | every `sql:crm:*` | Pipeline → Customers, Deals · Reports → Monthly revenue. *(no Cohort: not analyst; no Admin)* |
| **Carol** (admin) | `["admin"]` | every `sql:crm:*` | Pipeline → Customers, Deals · Reports → Monthly revenue, Cohort · Admin → Config. |
| **Dave** (manager + analyst) | `["manager", "analyst"]` | every `sql:crm:*` | Pipeline → Customers, Deals · Reports → Monthly revenue, Cohort. *(no Admin)* |
| **Eve** (no permission) | `["guest"]` | none | Empty tree — the app is left out of the picker. |

Note how the *Reports* folder doesn't appear for Alice (her roles don't intersect any child); the *Admin* folder doesn't appear for Alice / Bob / Dave; the app is left out of Eve's application picker.

---

## Permission shapes

Liberty's permission strings follow a simple pattern:

| String | Grants |
|---|---|
| `sql:<connector>:<query>` | Run that specific SQL query. |
| `sql:<connector>:*` | Run every query on that connector. |
| `sql:*` | Run every query on every connector. |
| `api:<connector>:<endpoint>` | Call that specific API endpoint. |
| `api:<connector>:*` | Call every endpoint on that connector. |
| `menu:<app>:<id>` | That menu folder or entry in read: shown, with what its screens read. A `!menu:…` deny hides it. |
| `edit:<app>:<id>` | On top of `menu:`, read and change: what its screens write and run, its jobs included. |
| `menu:<app>:*`, `edit:<app>:*` | The whole application, in read or in read and change; a choice on a folder or an entry wins over it. |
| `*` | Everything. |

A superuser is a flag on the user, not a permission: it passes every check.

For menu pruning, the relevant permissions are `menu:` (the folder or entry granted) and `sql:` / `api:` (matching the leaf's `target`). A role granting `menu:crm:*` or `sql:crm:*` opens every `screen` and `query` leaf on the `crm` app.

The usual way to grant an application is the **menu grant**, set in the role editor: a folder, or the whole application, in **Read** or in **Read and change**. The server works out the `sql:` / `api:` permissions the screens under it need — read query, dropdown lists, record-form tabs, and for change the writes, the actions' targets and the jobs —, so a role stays a few lines and follows its folders when screens are added. `sql:<c>:*` remains possible for a role that should run every query of a connector, menus or not; the `roles` filter on individual items handles the exceptions.

---

## How the pruning runs

`GET /api/menus` fires when the user opens the app. The runtime:

1. Loads the user's roles + permissions from the JWT.
2. Walks the tree depth-first.
3. For each **leaf**:
   - Check the implicit permission. If the user lacks it, the leaf is dropped.
   - Check the `roles` filter. If the list is non-empty and the user has none of them, the leaf is dropped.
4. For each **folder**: drop it if no descendants survived.
5. Return the pruned tree.

The pruning is **per-request** — it picks up permission changes the moment the user re-authenticates. No restart needed.

---

## Dashboards, pages and links \{#gating\}

An entry is shown for what the user may open through it:

| Leaf type | Shown when |
|---|---|
| `screen` | The user holds the `sql:` permission of the screen's read query. |
| `query`, `endpoint` | The user holds `sql:<connector>:<target>` / `api:<connector>:<target>`. |
| `dashboard` | The user can read at least one of its data widgets, or holds `dashboard:<id>`. A dashboard of texts and links only is shown to everyone. |
| `page` | Data Explorer, or an analysis or dashboard of it: the user may use the model (`explorer:<app>:<model>`). A page an application ships (`/app/<app>/<page>`): `page:<app>:<page>`. Nomaflow pages: `nomaflow:view`. Tests pages: `tests:view`. Any other page: everyone. |
| `job` | The user may run the job: the entry or its folder in **Read and change**, or `job:<id>`. **Read** alone does not show it. |
| `url` | Everyone. |

On every type but `job`, the entry or its folder in **Read** shows the entry; on every type, a `menu:` deny hides it, and the `roles` filter applies first.

**Which applications a user sees.** An application that has a menu and is shown in the switcher is listed for a user only when at least one of its entries is theirs through a permission. The entries open to everyone — an external address, an open page, a dashboard of texts — do not list an application by themselves. A superuser, or a role holding `*`, sees every application.

To check a role, open it in **Liberty Next → Administer → Access**: the eye of each entry and the count of each application (`sales · 4 of 6 shown`) follow this rule. The AI assistant names the applications by the same rule.

---

## Common pitfalls

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `roles = ["Manager"]` (capitalised). | Users with the lowercase `manager` role don't see the item. | Roles are case-sensitive. Use the exact spelling from the roles config. |
| Granting `sql:crm:*` to a role but the screen still doesn't appear. | The user's session was issued before the grant. | Sign out / sign back in to refresh the JWT. |
| `roles = []` (explicit empty list). | Equivalent to leaving the field blank — implicit permission alone. | If you meant "only admins", use `roles = ["admin"]`. |
| Folder visible despite all leaves being hidden. | The pruning ran on stale data (rare race condition during a hot reload). | Refresh the page. |
| A user does not see a dashboard entry. | The role reads none of the dashboard's data widgets. | Set the entry or its folder to **Read**, or grant `dashboard:<id>`. |
| A user does not see a job entry. | The entry or its folder is in **Read**: running a job needs **Read and change**. | Set the entry or its folder to **Read and change**, or grant `job:<id>`. |
| A user does not see an application in the switcher. | Its only entries open to that user need no permission (links, open pages). | Grant a permission on one of its screens, dashboards or Data Explorer models. |
| Menu shows nothing for a brand-new user. | The user's role grants no folder or entry of this app, and no `sql:` / `api:` permission on it. | Set a folder, or the whole application, to **Read** in the role. |

---

## Liberty Next — Translations and icons
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/menus/translations-and-icons/

Menu labels per language with the l map (l.fr, l.de…), how the language is chosen, and the icon names the Liberty Next sidebar can draw.

Two fields of every menu item shape what the user reads in the sidebar: `l`, the label per language, and `icon`.

---

## At a glance

---

## Translations — the `l` map \{#translations\}

`label` is the default label; `l` adds one label per language:

```toml
[[menus.crm.items]]
id = "security"
label = "Security"
l = { fr = "Sécurité", de = "Sicherheit" }
icon = "shield"
```

On the picked entry's panel (**Liberty Next → Screens → Menus**), the **Translations** tab lists one row per language — a language picked from the list, then the label, and a cross to remove the row; **+ add** adds one; the languages offered are `en`, `fr`, `de`, `es`, `it`, `pt`, `nl`, `pl`, `ja`, `zh`, `ar`. An empty row is removed on save.

### Which language \{#language\}

For each request, the language is, in order:

1. the `X-Liberty-Lang` header — the web application sends the language chosen in its interface;
2. otherwise the first language of the browser's `Accept-Language`, without its region (`fr-CA` → `fr`);
3. otherwise the default language of **Liberty Next → Administer → App**.

When `l` has no entry for that language, `label` is used. Use lowercase codes (`fr`, not `FR`).

Translate folders too: their label is what the user sees first. The screens' titles and column labels are translated in the dictionary and the screens, not here — see [Dictionary](../../dictionary.md).

---

## Icons \{#icons\}

`icon` names one of the icons the sidebar draws. Names are matched ignoring case and punctuation (`Shield`, `shield`, `trending-up` all work):

| Name | Name | Name | Name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `activity` | `filebarchart` | `mail` | `sparkles` |
| `alert` | `filetext` | `network` | `table` |
| `barchart` | `filter` | `package` | `tag` |
| `bell` | `folder` | `palette` | `trendingup` |
| `book` | `gitcompare` | `play` | `upload` |
| `briefcase` | `globe` | `receipt` | `user` |
| `building` | `grid` | `refreshcw` | `usercheck` |
| `calendar` | `history` | `rocket` | `users` |
| `clock` | `key` | `search` | `wand` |
| `code` | `layers` | `settings` | `workflow` |
| `compass` | `layoutdashboard` | `shield` | `wrench` |
| `database` | `link` | `shieldalert` |  |
| `file` | `lock` | `shieldcheck` |  |

Any other name draws no icon, without error. The **Icon** field of the **General** tab is typed as text (*Lucide icon name*): type one of these names.

Common choices: `shield` for security, `users` / `user` for people, `key` for roles, `database` / `table` for data, `barchart` / `trendingup` for reports, `settings` for administration, `folder` for plain folders.

---

## Liberty Next — i18n
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/apps/i18n/

Languages in Liberty Next — the interface in English and French, the per-language labels (l) of dictionary entries, enum values, menu items, screens, actions, dialog tabs, prompts, dashboards and starter questions, and how the language of each request is chosen.

Two layers carry text in Liberty Next:

| Layer | Content | Languages |
|---|---|---|
| **The interface** | Buttons, Settings, Nomaflow pages, messages. | English and French, shipped with the framework. |
| **The configuration** | Labels of data items, list values, menu items, screens, actions, dialog tabs, prompts, dashboards, starter questions. | One default label plus one translation per language, set in Settings. |

---

## The interface language \{#interface\}

Each user picks **EN** or **FR** in the bar at the top of the window. The choice is kept in the browser and applies at once: menus, column headers and list labels are reloaded in the new language.

Every request the application sends carries that language (`X-Liberty-Lang` header). A request without it — a direct API call — uses the first language of its `Accept-Language` header, without the region (`fr-CA` → `fr`), then the configuration's default language.

---

## Translating the configuration \{#configuration\}

Translatable elements have a default **label** and a **Translations** list — one line per language code (`fr`, `de`, `es`…), stored as `l`:

| Element | Where it is translated |
|---|---|
| **Dictionary entry** — the label of a data item, hence of every column that uses it | Liberty Next → Data → Dictionary → Entries, **Translations** tab. |
| **Enum value** | Liberty Next → Data → Dictionary → Enums, on each value. |
| **Menu item and folder** | Liberty Next → Screens → Menus, **Translations** tab of the picked entry. |
| **Screen** — its label (the tab, the list of screens) and its description (the page's heading) | Screen Designer, stage *What it is*: **Label translations** under the label, **Description translations** under the description. |
| **Action** — a row-menu entry, a toolbar or tab button, a step of a chain | The action's **Translations** tab — see [Actions and lifecycle](../build/screens/actions-and-lifecycle.md#translations). |
| **Dialog tab** | Screen Designer, stage *Record form* → **Tab settings** → **Title in the other languages** — see [Dialog builder](../build/screens/dialog-builder.md#tab-settings). |
| **Action prompt title** | The action's **prompt_l**. |
| **Dashboard** — its title and description, a card's texts, a link, a filter's label | Liberty Next → Insight → Dashboards: the *In the other languages* block under each field — see [Dashboards](../dashboards.md#languages). |
| **Starter questions** of the assistant | Liberty Next → Logic → AI, **Language** picker — see [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md#settings-ai). |

```toml
[entries.CUSTOMER_STATUS]
label = "Customer status"
l = { fr = "Statut client", de = "Kundenstatus" }
```

The server answers each text already in the request's language (`fr-FR` falls back on `fr`). When no translation matches, the default label is used. Language codes are written in lower case.

Column headers come from the dictionary: a column without its own label takes the translated label of its entry. A label typed directly on a screen column is not translated — leave it empty to inherit from the dictionary. See [Dictionary](../dictionary.md).

---

## Good practices

- **Translate in the dictionary** rather than on each screen: one entry feeds every column of every screen.
- **Write the default labels in the language most users read**, and add the others as translations.
- **Translate the menu folders too**: they are the first thing a user reads.

---

## What's next

- [Dictionary](../dictionary.md) — labels, formats and rules of data items.
- [Menus → Translations and icons](../build/menus/translations-and-icons.md) — menu labels per language.
- [Apps](./overview.md) — what belongs to an app.

## Liberty Next — Services
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/framework/build/services/

Logic → Services in Liberty Next: a service is a sequence of steps — queries, endpoint calls, plugin functions, conditions, loops — drawn as a flow and edited beside it; Run tries it with inputs and shows the answer and the steps that ran, Expose turns it into an API endpoint that a screen, a job, the assistant or an outside caller uses like any other.

A **service** composes several steps into one call: read a row, check it, call an endpoint, branch on the answer, write, answer. It is built by drawing — no code — and used two ways: a screen calls it from a button, or it is **exposed as an API endpoint** that a job, the assistant or an outside system calls like any other.

Access: **Liberty Next → Logic → Services**, for superusers. A screen calls a service with `call_action`; see [Actions and lifecycle](./screens/actions-and-lifecycle.md) for the actions of a screen.

---

## At a glance

---

## The list \{#list\}

Each line gives the service's identifier, its label, its number of steps and inputs and, once it is exposed, the endpoints it serves (`POST /api/http/<connector>/<endpoint>`). A click on the line opens its designer. On a line: **Run**, **Expose**, **Find usages**, **Find dependencies**, **Rename**, **Clone**, **Delete**.

- **New service** asks for its name — *Its name:*, *Close the period* —, makes its identifier from it (*Its technical id will be close_the_period.*) and opens the designer of the new, empty service.
- **Rename** and **Clone** ask for the new identifier; a rename also rewrites the screens that call the service.
- **Delete** asks for a confirmation: a screen that still calls the service then fails the integrity check — **Find usages** first.

---

## The flow \{#flow\}

The designer opens over the whole window, titled *Service ·* with the service's label, then its identifier in small, on the **Flow** view; **List** gives the same service as a form — label, description, inputs, then the steps one per line, with **Add action**. **Save** writes the service and reloads the configuration; **Cancel** with unsaved changes asks whether to save them, discard them or keep editing.

The flow reads left to right: **Start**, which shows the inputs; one card per step; **Answer**, which shows what the service returns. A **condition** forks into its **True** and **False** lanes; a **loop** or a **group** frames its own steps. The layout follows the structure of the service: nothing is placed by hand. A long flow continues on the next row, and the zoom (− / % / +) is kept on the device.

- **A click on a card** edits that step in the side panel, under the path *service › step*: its **Type**, its target — **Connector** and **Query** for a query (the pencil opens the query), the endpoint, the function or the service otherwise —, its **Id** and **Label**, **Stop on error**, **Keep the result**, and its **Values passed** — see [Values passed](#values). The bin of the card deletes the step.
- **The + on a link** opens the list of step kinds and adds the chosen one at that place.
- **With nothing picked**, the panel edits *The service*: **Label**, **Description**, **Inputs** and **Questions asked first** — see [Inputs and questions](#inputs).

| Step | Does |
|---|---|
| **Query** | Runs a query of a connector. |
| **Endpoint** | Calls an API endpoint. When the endpoint says where its rows are, the next steps read them by column name: `<step>.first_row.<COLUMN>`, `<step>.rows`. |
| **Function** | Calls a function of an application's plugin, picked in a list grouped by application and module — the same picker as a job's [Python step](../../nomaflow/steps.md#python). |
| **Service** | Calls another service. |
| **Condition** | Forks on a test. |
| **For each** | Repeats its steps for each row. |
| **Message**, **Notification** | Tells the user, or sends a notification rule — see [below](#notification). |
| **Answer** | Says what the service returns. |

### Inputs and questions \{#inputs\}

**Inputs** — **Add input** — are what the service receives from what calls it. Each input is a card:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Name** | What the steps read it by (`COMPANY`, read as `INPUT.COMPANY`). |
| **Label** | The name shown where the service is called (*Company*). |
| **Default value** | Used when the caller gives none: a value, or a built-in — the signed-in user, today… (`#LOGIN_USER#`, `#SYSDATE#`, `#NOW#`, `#CURRENT_TIME#`, `#LANGUAGE#`). |
| **What it is for** | A sentence on the input (*The company whose period is closed*). |

**Questions asked first** — **add** — are the fields the user fills in before the service runs, the same list of fields as the questions of a screen's button: a **Name** the steps read the answer by, a **Dictionary item** or a **Label**, a **Format**, **Required**, a **Default value**…

### Values passed \{#values\}

Under **Values passed**, each parameter of the step's target — the query, the endpoint, the function, the service called — receives a value, either **Fixed** (written there) or **Taken from**, picked in a list:

- the service's inputs (*Input · Company*) and the answers to its questions (*Answer · …*);
- what an earlier query, endpoint or function step returned: *first row of "Find the customer"*, completed by a column, or *every row of "…"*; when that step reads the query of a screen, each column of its first row is offered by itself (*EMAIL — first row of "Find the customer"*);
- the record, and the built-ins: the signed-in user, today.

A value picked replaces what the field held. Picking an earlier step's result ticks **Keep the result** on that step by itself. **+ a value to use when that one is empty** gives a fallback when the source is empty at run time. In the saved service, an input reads `INPUT.<name>` and an earlier step's result `<step>.first_row.<COLUMN>` or `<step>.rows`.

### The Notification step \{#notification\}

A **Notification** step sends one of the rules of [Logic → Notifications](../../nomaflow/notifications.md) whose trigger is *A screen action*: the rule says who receives the message and through which channels, the step says when.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Notification rule** | The rules triggered *by an action*, by label. A disabled rule is listed as *(disabled)* and the step sends nothing until it is enabled; a rule that does not exist, or has another trigger, is said too — the step would send nothing. With no such rule yet, the field says to create one first. |
| **Values of the message** | The values of the current record are sent by themselves. Each line adds what the message needs besides — a **name in the message** (a `{name}` of its subject, body or link) and its value or source: what the user typed (`INPUT.<name>`), the result of an earlier step. |

---

## Run \{#run\}

**Run** tries the service as it is saved: one field per input (its default as a placeholder), then **Run** in the dialog gives the result — *Done in N ms*, the **Answer** it would give as an endpoint (what it returns, with its messages), and the **Steps that ran**. A service without input runs as it is; a failure shows the error of the step that failed.

:::warning[The steps really run]
A step that writes, writes. Run a service that changes data on a test environment, or with inputs made for it.
:::

---

## Expose as an endpoint \{#expose\}

**Expose** creates an API endpoint served by the service. A screen, an action, a job, the assistant or an outside caller then calls it like any endpoint.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **On the connector** | An API connector of the installation, or the Studio's own — `studio`, created on first use. |
| **Endpoint name** | The service's identifier by default. |
| **It changes data** | Tick it when a step writes: the assistant then asks before calling it. |

The service's inputs become the endpoint's parameters — the dialog lists them, *Its parameters: …*; an `INPUT.<name>` the steps read counts even when the service does not declare it. The connector proposed is the Studio's own when it exists, otherwise the first API connector of the installation. The dialog answers with the address and the permission: *Exposed: POST … — permission `api:<connector>:<endpoint>`*.

**The service runs with the endpoint's permission**: who may call the endpoint runs all its steps, which are not checked again one by one — a composed service is granted as a whole. The caller's row-level data scope still applies to every query. What the service returns is the answer; its messages come with it; a step that fails is the endpoint's error.

---

## Where a service is used \{#usage\}

**Find usages** lists the screens that call the service and the endpoints it serves; renaming it follows them. In the [Studio](../studio.md), a selected service lights the screens that call it. A service is carried in a [package](./packages.md) with the screens and endpoints that need it.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Give each step a name that says what it holds (`customer`, `open_orders`): the next steps read it by that name.
- Put the checks first and the writes last: a condition that stops early leaves nothing half done.
- Expose a service when the same sequence is needed by a screen **and** by a job or an outside system: one definition, one permission.
- Cover an exposed service with a [test](./tests.md) case.

---

## Related

- [Overview and Studio](../studio.md) · [API endpoints](./api-endpoints.md) · [Tests](./tests.md)
- [Actions and lifecycle](./screens/actions-and-lifecycle.md) — the actions of a screen.
