## Nomasx-1 — Oracle
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/database/oracle/

Nomasx-1 Database → Oracle page — the Oracle database of a connected application as it was collected: its figures (size, processors, users, options on, features used, partitioned segments), then its options, features, partitions and instances.

The **Oracle** database page shows the Oracle database of a connected application **as it was collected**: its figures on top — what it is, its size, its processors, its users, how many options are on, how many features were used, how many segments are partitioned — then one tab per list: **options**, **features**, **partitions** and **instances**.

It is the technical inventory behind [Licences → Oracle](../licenses/oracle.md): where a component reads *in use*, this page says which option is on, which feature was used and when, and who owns the partitioned segments.

Open it from **Database → Oracle**.

---

## At a glance

---

## The header \{#header\}

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Application** | The application whose Oracle database is shown, as `id · name`. Only the applications an Oracle database was collected for are offered. The page reopens on the last application and the last tab. |
| **Read again** | Reads the application again. |

The assistant is given the database name, its size, the options on and the features used.

---

## The figures \{#figures\}

| Figure | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Database** | The database name, its host below. |
| **Size (GB)** | The size collected. |
| **Processors** | The CPU count collected. |
| **Users (active / all)** | The active accounts of the database against all its accounts. |
| **Options on** | How many options are on. Orange when there is one. |
| **Features used** | How many features were used at least once. |
| **Partitioned segments** | How many tables and indexes are partitioned. Orange when one of them belongs to an owner that is not flagged technical. |

The line under the figures gives the product and its version, the collection date, the management packs the database allows and whether it runs Data Guard.

---

## The tabs \{#tabs\}

Each tab card gives the number of lines of its list. The grid has the usual search, sort, filters, grouping, columns and export.

### Options \{#tab-options\}

What the database has installed: *Option*, *On* (*yes* / *no*), *Licensed as* — the licence component the option needs, as set on [Settings → Licences → Oracle → Options](../settings/oracle/options.md). The options on come first.

### Features \{#tab-features\}

What was used, and when: *Feature*, *Detected usages*, *First used*, *Last used*, *Licensed as* (from [Settings → Licences → Oracle → Features](../settings/oracle/features.md)). The first and last dates tell whether a feature was used once long ago or is still used today.

### Partitions \{#tab-partitions\}

The segments that use Partitioning: *Owner*, *Technical owner* (*yes* when the owner is flagged technical on [Users properties](../settings/security/users-properties.md)), *Type*, *Segment*, *Created*, *Last change*. A segment held by a vendor schema reads apart from one created by the business.

### Instances \{#tab-instances\}

The databases collected for the application, one line each: *Database*, *Host*, *Product*, *Version*, *Instances* (more than one under Real Application Clusters), *Processors*, *Active users*, *Users*, *Packs*, *Data Guard*, *Size (GB)*, *Collected*.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Start from *Licences → Oracle*.** A component *in use, NOT subscribed* there is explained here: the option on, the feature with its last date, the partitioned segment with its owner.
- **A feature used once, years ago** is not the same story as one used last week: read *Last used* before any estimate.
- **Partitioned segments of technical owners** usually come with a vendor product; those of business owners were created on site.
- **Active against all users** shows the dormant accounts of the database itself, apart from those of the application.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Audit Trail
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/database/audit-trail/

Nomasx-1 database audit trail — every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE read from Oracle archive logs, grouped by schema, table, operation and day, each opening on a field-level before / after diff read from the stored statement; collection, purge and rebuild jobs.

The **Audit Trail** screen (*Audit - Query* in its header) lists the changes made in the database of a connected application, as Oracle's archive logs record them: one line per change — `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` — with the schema, the table, the time, the database user, the row and the *System Change Number*. Open it from **Database → Audit Trail**.

It complements *Activity log* (who wrote how many rows each day) with each change itself — the kind of trace SOX-style controls expect.

---

## At a glance

---

## Summary view \{#summary\}

The screen opens on **Summary** (next to *Table* and *Chart*): the changes are grouped by **Schema**, **Table Name**, **Operation** and **Transaction date** (by day), and each group says how many changes it holds, in brackets. The chevron of a group lists its changes; **Table** shows the flat list instead.

---

## Field-level diff — expandable rows \{#diff\}

The chevron of a change opens its **before / after** diff, field by field: the header line says how many fields the row has and how many changed (*92 fields · 2 changed*), and **Changed only** — ticked by default — hides the fields that did not change. The values are **read on demand from the stored DML statement** (`AUDIT_TRAIL_QUERY`): the diff is built when you open it, not stored twice. Consequences:

- The values table (`AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES`, the source of *Audit Lookup*) can be **purged** to reclaim space; the diff still rebuilds from the statement alone.
- `INSERT` shows the values written as *After*; `DELETE` shows them as *Before*; `UPDATE` shows both, the changed fields highlighted.

---

## Columns \{#columns\}

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Schema** | `AUD_SEG_OWNER` — database schema. | Where the table is. |
| **Table Name** | `AUD_SEG_NAME` — table name. | Object changed. |
| **Operation** | `AUD_OPERATION` — `INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE`. | What was done. |
| **Transaction date** | `AUD_DT_TRANSACTION` — timestamp. | When the change reached the database. |
| **Application ID** | `AUD_APPS_ID` — application identifier. | The connected application. |
| **Row ID** | `AUD_ROW_ID` — row identifier. | Which row of the table. |
| **Last SCN** | `AUD_SCN` — *System Change Number*. | Position of the change in the archive logs. |
| **Object Type** | `AUD_SEG_TYPE` — `TABLE`. | Kind of object. |
| **User** | `AUD_USERNAME` — database account. | Who made the change at database level. |

**Advanced filters** narrow the list on the application, the transaction date, the operation, the schema, the table and the user.

---

## Auditing scope — Audit Columns tab \{#scope\}

Each connected application decides **how much of each audited table** is indexed into the values table, on the *Audit Columns* tab of its settings ([Applications](../settings/global/applications.md)). Three cases per table:

| Rules on the table | Effect |
|---|---|
| **No row for the table** | Default — every column of the row is indexed into `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES`. |
| **One or more column rows** | Only the listed columns are indexed. The other columns still appear in the on-demand diff, they just cannot be searched in *Audit Lookup*. |
| **A single `*SQL*` row** | Journal only — the full DML statement is kept in `AUDIT_TRAIL_QUERY` and **nothing is indexed** into `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES`. Use it on the widest tables where per-column search is not needed. |

The full DML statement is always kept, whatever the rules. The tab is the lever to keep the values table's volume in check on wide tables (an `F0911` row would otherwise index tens of columns per change).

---

## Collection, purge and rebuild jobs \{#jobs\}

The changes are collected by Nomaflow jobs, run on the application:

| Job | What it does |
|---|---|
| **nomasx1-audit-trail-1** | Reads the archive logs (LogMiner) from the last SCN of the application and adds the new changes. |
| **nomasx1-audit-trail-precheck-1** | Read-only check that the audited database has every prerequisite; gives the SQL to fix what is missing. |
| **nomasx1-audit-trail-reset-scn-1** | Resets the last SCN of the application — by default the next run starts from the current SCN. |
| **nomasx1-audit-trail-purge-values-1** | Purges `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES` to reclaim space — everything for the application (optionally one table), or only the values of statements older than N days. The statements are kept. |
| **nomasx1-audit-trail-rebuild-values-1** | Rebuilds `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES` for a table and a period by reading the stored statements again — after a purge, or after widening the *Audit Columns* rules of a table. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Filter on *Operation = DELETE*** over the audit period — every deletion has to be justifiable.
- **Open the change before *Audit Lookup*.** For one record, the diff already shows every changed field; *Audit Lookup* searches the indexed values across changes ("every change that wrote this value in this column").
- **Filter on a *User*** to read the database activity of one account. Compare with the *Activity log* to tell a change made through the application from one made directly in the database.
- **A group whose count is above the usual range** for the same table is worth a question to the DBA team.
- **Trim wide tables with *Audit Columns*.** On an `F0911`-style table, list only the columns you would search on — the values table stays small and the diff still shows everything from the statement.
- **Schedule the purge of values** in line with your retention policy, and run *rebuild values* on a period when a value-level search is needed again.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Audit Lookup
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/database/audit-lookup/

Detailed audit lookup — for each audited mutation, the before / after value of every changed column.

The **Audit Lookup** screen is the detail view of the database-level audit. One line per `(Application, Row, Column, Audit type, Value)`. Each row pairs a column with its `BEFORE` and `AFTER` value at the time of the operation, joining the audit header with the audit values.

This is the screen auditors open to *see what changed inside the row* — not just *that the row changed*. Open it from **Database → Audit Lookup**: it reads nothing until the **Advanced filters** are set (application, transaction date, user, table name, column, value — each with its operator) and **Run** is clicked.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each column captured in an audited operation:

- **What changed.** *BEFORE* + *AFTER* on the same column makes the modification visible in one read.
- **Joined to the user and the operation.** The header context (date, table, user, operation) is repeated on each row — handy when filtering on a specific column or value.
- **Source of evidence.** A row here is *the* proof that an operation took place. Auditors paste it into the SOX finding.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `AUD_APPS_ID` — application identifier. Filterable. | The connected application. |
| **Row ID** | `AUD_ROW_ID` — internal row identifier. | Stable reference across audit entries. |
| **Transaction date** | `AUD_DT_TRANSACTION` — date. Filterable. | When the operation happened. |
| **User** | `AUD_USERNAME` — application or DB user. Filterable. | Who performed the operation. |
| **Table Name** | `AUD_SEG_NAME` — table name. Filterable. | Object that was changed. |
| **Type** | `AUD_TYPE` — `BEFORE` / `AFTER`. | Snapshot side. |
| **Column** | `AUD_NAME` — column name. Filterable. | Which column the value applies to. |
| **Value** | `AUD_VALUE` — raw value. Filterable. | The value snapshotted. |
| **Operation** | `AUD_OPERATION` — `INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE`. | What the underlying operation was. |
| **Schema** | `AUD_SEG_OWNER` — database schema. | Where the table lives. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Filter on a *Column* + *Value*** to ask *who changed this field to that value, and when*.
- **Group rows by *Row ID*** to read a full before/after for the same record — the most useful view for auditors.
- **Filter the grid on *Operation*** to scope the search to a specific kind of mutation. `DELETE` rows have no `AFTER` value — only `BEFORE`.
- **Cross-reference with the *Audit Trail* header** to confirm the row count of an operation matches the number of rows you can see at this level.

---

## Nomasx-1 — CSI
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/licenses/csi/

Customer Support Identifier — list of the Oracle support contracts the connected applications are entitled to.

The **CSI** screen lists every Oracle *Customer Support Identifier* declared in Nomasx-1. One line per contract. Each row carries the identifier, a friendly description, the contract validity dates and its current status.

The CSI is the contractual anchor: its lines — components alone and bundles —, the figures the customer declares and the users of other applications are what the [Licensing review](../licensing-review.md) reads, the way [How a contract is counted](../how-a-contract-is-counted.md) describes.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each CSI under management:

- **Inventory the support contracts.** Every active CSI must be associated with at least one application — otherwise it is a contract for an application that has nothing left.
- **Track validity windows.** *From* / *To* dates drive the renewal calendar.
- **Say whether it counts.** *Enabled (Y/N)* is ticked while the contract is in force. A contract that ended stays on the list with the box cleared.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **CSI Number** | `CSI_ID` — numeric contract identifier. | The Oracle reference. |
| **Description** | `CSI_DESCRIPTION` — text. | Friendly label. |
| **From Date** | `CSI_FROM_DATE` — date. | Start of the support coverage. |
| **To Date** | `CSI_TO_DATE` — date. | End of the current support window. |
| **Enabled (Y/N)** | `CSI_STATUS` — `Y` / `N`, a green or red dot. | Whether the contract is still in force. |

Audit columns (`CSI_AUDIT_USER`, `CSI_AUDIT_DATE`) are hidden but tracked on the row.

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to register a new CSI, or click a row to open it. The dialog has seven tabs. Only *Contract Support* shows on a new contract — the six grids appear once the CSI is saved. Each grid has **Add row** and **Bulk edit**, and a click on one of its rows opens its own form (**Edit · License - Bundles**…). The footer carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**.

### Tab 1 — Contract Support

The contract identity.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **CSI Number** | Numeric Oracle contract identifier. Read-only once the contract is saved. |
| **Description** | Friendly label for the contract. |
| **From Date** | Start of the support coverage (date picker). |
| **To Date** | End of the current support window. |
| **Enabled (Y/N)** | Ticked while the contract is in force, cleared once it ends. |

### Tab 2 — Applications

Grid linking the CSI to the applications it covers (*CSI Number*, *Application ID*, with the application's type and database, read-only: they come from [Applications](../settings/global/applications.md)). On a saved line, *CSI Number* and *Application ID* are read-only. Add one row per application with **Add row**: an entry here is what makes the contract count for that application in the [Licensing review](../licensing-review.md) and the [licence audit report](../reports/audit-licences.md). Hidden on **Add**.

### Tab 3 — Components

Grid listing the components licensed alone on the CSI: *Component ID*, *Metric ID* and *Quantity*, one row per component and metric. Each one is a line of the contract (see [How a contract is counted](../how-a-contract-is-counted.md#lines)). Hidden on **Add**.

### Tab 4 — Bundles \{#tab-bundles\}

The bundles of the contract: several modules sold as one line, where a user is counted once for all of them.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **CSI Number** | The contract, filled in; read-only on a saved row. |
| **Bundle** | Required. A short code of the bundle on this contract (`DIST`, `INV-SALES`…). |
| **Description** | The name the pages show (*Distribution suite*). |
| **Metric ID** | Picked from the metrics: usually *Application User*. |
| **Quantity** | What was subscribed. |
| **Components** | Read-only: how many modules the bundle holds, from the next tab. |

A bundle with no component is listed on [Subscribed licences](./subscribed-licences.md) and said empty; it covers nothing.

### Tab 5 — Bundle components \{#tab-bundle-components\}

The modules of each bundle, one row per bundle and module: *CSI Number*, **Bundle** (picked from the bundles of this contract) and **Component ID** (picked from the components, by name). Both are required.

### Tab 6 — Declared figures \{#tab-declared\}

What the customer declares for the contract, dated: the latest date is the one the [Licensing review](../licensing-review.md#lines-other) reads.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Declared on** | Required. The date of the declaration. |
| **Revenue declared (millions)** | Compared with the lines in *Enterprise $M*. |
| **Employees declared** | Compared with the lines in *Employee*. Empty: the employees collected from JD Edwards are used. |
| **Comment** | Where the figure comes from (annual report, HR count…). |

### Tab 7 — Users of other applications \{#tab-other-users\}

The users of an application whose users cannot be collected — a reporting portal, a tool that signs in to the same database —, one row per application. They are added to the count of a database licensed per Named User Plus (see [Named User Plus on a database](../how-a-contract-is-counted.md#named)).

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application** | Required. The name of the application. |
| **Users** | Required. How many people use it. |
| **Counted on** | The date of the count. |
| **Comment** | How they were counted. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Sort by *To Date* ascending** to surface the next renewals — the budget-planning view.
- **Confirm every active CSI maps to at least one application** in [Subscribed licences](./subscribed-licences.md). An orphan CSI is a contract paid for an application that no longer uses it.
- **Ended contracts remain visible** for audit traceability — clear *Enabled* rather than deleting the row.
- **The screen is writable** — only the licence administrator should edit it. Each change is captured in the audit columns and surfaces in the *Audit Trail* if the underlying table is being audited.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Subscribed licences
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/licenses/subscribed-licences/

Nomasx-1 Subscribed licences page — each licence contract with its bundles, its lines grouped by how they are counted (users, named users, revenue, employees, processors), what the customer declared, and what each way of counting means.

The **Subscribed licences** page shows what each licence contract covers, read the way the licence position reads it: the **bundles** of the contract (one seat for all their modules), its **lines of one module grouped by how they are counted**, the **figures the customer declared** for it, and, on the side, **what each way of counting means**. It is the *what we are entitled to* half of the licence equation, for every contract of any connected application; the other half, what is used and what it may cost, is on **Reviews → Licences**.

The page only reads. A contract, its lines, its bundles and its declared figures are entered on the [CSI](./csi.md) screen: **Change the contracts** opens it.

Open it from **Licences → Subscribed licences**.

---

## At a glance

---

## One block per contract \{#contract\}

Each contract is a block, in the order of its identifier. Its head gives the description and the contract number, a **not active** badge when the contract is not in force, its validity (*from → to*) and the applications it **covers** — those linked to it on the *Applications* tab of the contract (*no application yet* otherwise). A contract that covers no application counts for none of them.

Inside the block, three parts, each shown only when it holds something:

| Part | What it lists |
|---|---|
| **Bundles** | One card per bundle of the contract: its name and code, its quantity and metric, and the modules it groups (*no module in it yet* when it is empty). One seat counts for every module of the bundle. |
| **Lines of one module** | The contract's lines on a single module, one table per way of counting: *Module*, *Metric*, *Subscribed*. |
| **Declared by the customer** | The figures declared for the contract, dated: *On*, *Revenue (millions)*, *Employees*, *Comment*. *Nothing declared yet.* when the list is empty. |

The module names are shortened: the *JD Edwards EnterpriseOne* prefix is left out.

---

## How a line is counted \{#how-counted\}

A line is grouped by its metric. The side panel says the same thing on the page, with the sign-in period of the application and the core factor in force.

| Group | Metrics | What it is compared with |
|---|---|---|
| **Counted in users** | Application User, Named User Plus on an application module | Each enabled user is one seat, on the modules they used — or, without usage tracking, on those their security allows when they signed in within the application's period (90 days by default). A bundle is tried before the module alone, the smaller one that fits first. |
| **Counted in named users** | Named User Plus on a database, an option or a pack | Not seat by seat — JD Edwards signs in to the database with one account — but a count: the enabled JD Edwards users of the contract's applications, the open accounts of the database that are not Oracle's own, and the users declared for the other applications; never below the minimum per processor of the price list. An Enterprise option or pack follows its database. |
| **Counted on the revenue** | Enterprise $M | The line covers its modules for everybody; its quantity is a revenue in millions, compared with the revenue declared for the contract. |
| **Counted on the employees** | Employee | The line covers its modules for everybody; it is compared with the employees declared, else those collected from the application. |
| **Counted on the processors** | Processor | Compared with the cores of the database servers × the core factor of their chip (0.5 for Intel and AMD), a virtual machine counting every physical host of its cluster. The sizes are those stated in nomajde's [Server sizes](../../nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes.md#processor-licences), else the CPU count collected. |
| **Not compared** | Concurrent User, Expense Report, Stream… | The line covers its modules; nothing is compared. |

:::info[JDE-specific]
The usage behind *Counted in users* is Object Usage Tracking, and the employees collected come from JD Edwards EnterpriseOne. For another source, the lines are read the same way; the usage comes from what its connector collects.
:::

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Check the groups before reading the position.** A line in the wrong group is almost always a wrong metric on the contract line — fix it on the [CSI](./csi.md) screen.
- **Declare the revenue and the employees** of a contract that holds an *Enterprise $M* or an *Employee* line: without a declared figure, nothing can be compared.
- **Bundles first.** When the contract sells modules as a suite, enter the bundle with its modules: a user of two of them then takes one seat, not two.
- **Ask the assistant.** It is given the number of contracts and bundles shown on the page.

---

## Nomasx-1 — JD Edwards
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/licenses/jd-edwards/

Nomasx-1 Licences → JD Edwards page — the users a licence counts and, per module, who is allowed, who used it and who wrote transactions, with a drill to the objects allowed and the transactions of a module or a user.

The **JD Edwards** page shows, for one JD Edwards EnterpriseOne application, **the users a licence counts** and, **per module, who is allowed, who used it and who wrote transactions**. The figures sit on top; each list behind them is a tab with its own grid. Each module and each user opens the two detail screens — objects allowed and transactions — already filtered.

It is the place to see where the licence headcount comes from before reading the position on **Reviews → Licences**, and to compare it with what the contracts hold on [Subscribed licences](./subscribed-licences.md).

Open it from **Licences → JD Edwards**.

:::info[JDE-specific]
The page lists the applications of type JD Edwards. *Used* comes from Object Usage Tracking and *Wrote transactions* from the user and last-update columns of the JD Edwards tables. For another source, the same questions are answered through a [custom query](../settings/global/custom-queries.md).
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The header \{#header\}

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Application** | The JD Edwards application read, as `id · name`. The page reopens on the last application and the last tab. |
| **Read again** | Reads the application again (*reading…* while it runs). |

The assistant is given the enabled, counted and recently signed-in figures of the application shown.

---

## The figures \{#figures\}

| Figure | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Enabled users** | The users enabled in the application's security. |
| **Counted for licences** | The enabled users a licence counts: technical accounts and accounts linked to another user are left out — the line below gives how many of each (*technical · linked … left out*). Both flags are set on [Users properties](../settings/security/users-properties.md). |
| **Signed in (N days)** | Counted users who signed in within the application's period (*Signed in within (days) = a user* on [Applications](../settings/global/applications.md), 90 days when empty). |
| **Never signed in** | Counted users with no sign-in date. Orange when there is one. |
| **With transactions (90 days)** | Counted users who wrote a transaction in the last 90 days. |
| **Transactions, not a user** | Accounts that wrote transactions in the last 90 days and are no user of the application. Orange when there is one. |

---

## The tabs \{#tabs\}

Each tab card gives the number of lines of its list. The grid has the usual search, sort, filters, grouping, columns and export.

### Users \{#tab-users\}

The enabled users of the application.

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **User**, **Name** | The account and its name. |
| **Roles** | How many roles the user holds. |
| **Last sign-in**, **Last transaction**, **Created** | The dates known for the user. |
| **Technical**, **Generic**, **Linked to** | The flags of [Users properties](../settings/security/users-properties.md); *Linked to* names the user the account is linked to. |
| **Detail** | **objects allowed** and **transactions**: the two detail screens, filtered on the application and the user. |

### Modules \{#tab-modules\}

One line per licence module, the most allowed first. A program or a table belongs to a module through its system code ([System code](../settings/jde/system-code.md) and [Reclassification](../settings/jde/reclassification.md)).

| Column | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Module**, **Category** | The licence component and its family (the *JD Edwards EnterpriseOne* prefix left out). |
| **Allowed** | Enabled users whose security lets them run a program of the module. |
| **Used** | Users who ran a program of the module, as Object Usage Tracking recorded it. |
| **Wrote transactions** | Users who wrote in a table of the module in the last 90 days. |
| **Detail** | **objects allowed** and **transactions**: the two detail screens, filtered on the application and the module. |

### Not declared \{#tab-not-declared\}

Accounts that wrote transactions in the last 90 days and are no user of the application: *User*, *Last transaction*, *Tables* (how many tables it wrote in).

---

## The detail screens \{#details\}

The two screens are also in the menu, under the page: **Licences → JD Edwards - objects allowed** and **Licences → JD Edwards - transactions**. Opened from the menu, they wait for a filter; opened from a line of the page, they arrive filtered.

| Screen | Columns |
|---|---|
| **JD Edwards - objects allowed** | *Application ID*, *Component ID*, *User ID*, *Technical (Y/N)*, *Is Linked (Y/N)*, *Object* — every object the user's security allows, per module. |
| **JD Edwards - transactions** | *Application ID*, *Component ID*, *User ID*, *Object* (the table written), *Last transaction*. |

Both are read-only.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Read *Counted for licences*, not *Enabled users*.** The gap is the technical and linked accounts; flag them on [Users properties](../settings/security/users-properties.md) so that no licence is counted for them.
- **Allowed far above Used** on a module is security wider than the work: a candidate for a role review rather than for more licences.
- **Clear *Not declared* first.** An account that writes without being a user is either a deleted user whose jobs still run, or a technical account to declare.
- **Never signed in** users are the first accounts to disable before a count.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Oracle
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/licenses/oracle/

Nomasx-1 Licences → Oracle page — each Oracle database component of an application, found in use or not, against what the contracts subscribe: in use and covered, in use with no line, subscribed and not in use.

The **Oracle** licence page shows, for the Oracle database of a connected application, **each licensable component — the edition, its options and its management packs — found in use or not, against what the contracts subscribe**. Four figures sit on top; the grid lists every component checked, with what it reads: covered, in use with no line, subscribed and not in use.

The technical side of the same database — its options, features, partitions and instances as collected — is on [Database → Oracle](../database/oracle.md); the contract lines are on [Subscribed licences](./subscribed-licences.md).

Open it from **Licences → Oracle**.

---

## At a glance

---

## The header \{#header\}

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Application** | The application whose Oracle database is read, as `id · name`. Only the applications an Oracle database was collected for are offered. The page reopens on the last one. |
| **Read again** | Reads the application again. |

---

## The figures \{#figures\}

| Figure | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Components checked** | Every Oracle component the collection checked on the database. |
| **In use** | The components found in use. |
| **In use, not subscribed** | Found in use with no contract line for the application. Orange, with the reminder *to qualify before any estimate: an option can be on without being used by the application*. |
| **Subscribed, not in use** | A contract line exists and the component was not found in use. |

---

## Components \{#tab-components\}

One line per component, those in use first.

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Component** | The licensable item: *Oracle Enterprise Edition*, *Partitioning*, *Diagnostics Pack*, *Tuning Pack*, *Advanced Compression*… |
| **Category** | Its family in the price list: Oracle Database, Oracle Enterprise Edition Options, Database Enterprise Management, Oracle Others Products. |
| **In use** | *yes* when the collection found it in use on the database. |
| **Subscribed** | The quantity on the contracts that cover the application, added up. |
| **Metric** | The metric of those lines (Processor, Named User Plus…). |
| **Reading** | *in use, subscribed* · *in use, NOT subscribed* · *subscribed, not in use* — empty when the component is neither in use nor subscribed. |

*In use* is what the licence collection found: it asks the database itself, one detection query per component, at each run of **Jobs → Collect licences**.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Qualify every *in use, NOT subscribed* line** on [Database → Oracle](../database/oracle.md): the *Features* tab says when the feature was last used, the *Partitions* tab whether a partitioned segment belongs to a vendor schema or to the business.
- **A pack in use with no line** is often a management console that was opened once: check the dates before counting it.
- ***Subscribed, not in use*** lines are the first to discuss at renewal.
- **The figures are an assumption to discuss with Oracle**, never a certified position.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Oracle Data Integrator
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/licenses/odi/

Nomasx-1 Licences → Oracle Data Integrator page — a questionnaire on an on-premise installation (where the agents run, the cluster behind a virtual machine, the repository database and its edition, the users), each answer stored, and beside it the processors needed against subscribed, the estimated risk and the findings.

The **Oracle Data Integrator** page describes an on-premise installation of Data Integrator for a licence contract, and says beside it what its licences should be. Nothing of Data Integrator is read on the machines: the page **asks** — where an agent runs, the cluster behind a virtual machine, the repository database and its edition, the users — **stores each answer as it is given**, and reads the analysis again after each one: **processors needed against subscribed**, **Named User Plus against the minimum**, the **estimated risk** and the **findings**.

Open it from **Licences → Oracle Data Integrator**.

:::warning[An assumption]
The page says it on top: *an assumption built from your answers and Oracle's public rules, to discuss with Oracle — never a certified position. On premise only: in Oracle's cloud the licences are included.*
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The contract \{#contract\}

An installation belongs to a contract: **Contract** in the header picks it (`number · description`), and the page reopens on the last one — at first, on a contract that already has a line on Data Integrator or a machine stated. With no contract at all, the page says to create one under **Licences → [CSI](./csi.md)**. **Read again** reads the installation again.

---

## The questionnaire \{#questionnaire\}

Four numbered steps on the left. Every change is saved at once — a list when a value is picked, a number when the field is left — and the analysis on the right is read again.

### 1 · Where does an agent run? \{#step-agents\}

Oracle counts every processor where the transformations are executed: each machine with an agent, wherever it was installed. Add a machine from **a known server…** (the machines of nomajde's [Server sizes](../../nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes.md)) or type **its name**, then **Add**.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Cores** | The cores of the machine. |
| **Processor family** | Its chip, with the core factor of Oracle's *Processor Core Factor Table* (0.5 for Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC, 1 for IBM POWER6 and later…). |
| **Virtualisation** | *Physical machine*, *Hardware partition*, *VMware virtual machine*, *Other virtual machine*. |
| **Cluster** | For a virtual machine, the cluster it runs on. |

The cores, the family, the virtualisation and the cluster are those of [Server sizes](../../nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes.md#processor-licences): one table of machines, shared with the sizing of the platform. **Remove** takes the machine out of the installation; its row in Server sizes stays.

### 2 · The clusters behind the virtual machines \{#step-clusters\}

A virtual machine that is not a hardware partition counts **every** physical host of its cluster. For each cluster named in step 1, state its hosts with their cores and processor family; they are kept in Server sizes as *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)*. *No virtual machine names a cluster.* when none does.

### 3 · The databases \{#step-databases\}

The repository needs an Oracle database; Express Edition can do, within its limits. Add the repository machine, then pick its **Edition** — *Express Edition*, *Standard Edition 2*, *Enterprise Edition* or *Not Oracle* — and tick **JD Edwards uses it too** when the repository sits on the JD Edwards database.

### 4 · The users \{#step-users\}

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **How many people run or access the transformations?** | A number; *not known* while empty. It counts when the contract has a Named User Plus line. |
| **Size of the Express Edition repository (GB)** | Asked only when the repository is on Express Edition. |

An empty answer goes back to *not known*.

---

## What it means \{#analysis\}

The right-hand side is the server's reading of the answers.

| Block | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Figures** | *Processors needed* (red when above those subscribed), *Processors subscribed*, *Named User Plus needed* and *subscribed* (when the contract has a Named User Plus line), *Estimated risk* in euros, *Still to answer*. |
| **What it means** | The findings, the risks first, each with its level: **risk**, **to check**, **not known**, **fine**. |
| **What is counted** | Each machine (`name: cores → processors`) or whole cluster (`cluster name: cores on hosts → processors`). |
| **Subscribed on this contract** | The contract's lines on Data Integrator, with their quantity and metric — *no line for this product* otherwise. |

### How the processors are counted \{#processors\}

Each machine's cores × the core factor of its chip, added up per factor before the factor is applied, then rounded up once. A virtual machine on VMware or another hypervisor counts the whole cluster it names; a hardware partition counts only itself. Named User Plus needed is the users stated, never below the minimum per processor of the price list × the processors needed. What is beyond the subscription is priced at the public list price with three years of support.

### The findings \{#findings\}

| Level | Finding |
|---|---|
| risk | **Cluster counted whole** — its cores on its hosts give the processor licences, because of the machine that names it. |
| risk | **An agent on a JD Edwards server** — all the cores of that server count for Data Integrator. |
| risk | **No line for this product** — the processor licences an audit would claim, priced. |
| risk | **Processor licences missing** — needed, subscribed, missing, priced. |
| risk | **Named User Plus missing** — needed (users, minimum per processor), subscribed, missing, priced. |
| risk | **Repository beyond Express Edition** — more than 12 GB: it needs a licensed edition. |
| risk | **Database with no line** — a repository on Standard Edition 2 or Enterprise Edition, not used by JD Edwards, with no line for that edition. |
| not known | No machine stated · a machine with no cores · a virtual machine whose cluster hosts are not stated (its own cores are only a floor) · a cluster host with no cores · a question not answered · no repository · an edition not stated. |
| fine | Repository within the 12 GB of Express Edition · database also used by JD Edwards (check the contract allows this use) · database covered by a line. |

The same sentences, in the language of the reader, appear for the installation on **Reviews → Licences**, in its PDF and in the licence audit report; what it is short of is part of the estimated risk there.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **State every agent**, including the one installed on a JD Edwards server for convenience: it brings all the cores of that server into the count.
- **Name the cluster of each virtual machine and state its hosts.** Without them, the figure is only a floor and says so.
- **Answer until *Still to answer* reads 0**: a question left open is said *not known*, never read as fine.
- **Keep the page for the discussion with Oracle**, as an assumption at public list prices, never as a certified count.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Oracle Analytics Server

Nomasx-1 Licences → Oracle Analytics Server page — a questionnaire on an on-premise installation (its servers, the cluster behind a virtual machine, the repository and data warehouse databases, where the users are kept and how many), the users kept in WebLogic counted through a directory pool, and beside it the processors and Named User Plus needed against subscribed, the estimated risk and the findings.

The **Oracle Analytics Server** page describes an on-premise installation of Analytics Server (the former Business Intelligence) for a licence contract, and says beside it what its licences should be. Nothing of Analytics Server is read on the machines, except the users kept in WebLogic: the page **asks** — its servers, the cluster behind a virtual machine, the repository and data warehouse databases with their edition, where the users are kept and how many — **stores each answer as it is given**, and reads the analysis again after each one: **processors and Named User Plus needed against subscribed**, the **estimated risk** and the **findings**.

Open it from **Licences → Oracle Analytics Server**.

:::warning[An assumption]

The contract lines read as Analytics Server are those on *Analytics Server* and on *Business Intelligence Suite Foundation Edition* (and its *for Oracle Applications* version).

## The questionnaire \{#questionnaire\}

Four numbered steps on the left. Every change is saved at once — a list when a value is picked, a number when the field is left — and the analysis on the right is read again.

### 1 · Which servers run Analytics Server? \{#step-servers\}

Every machine where Analytics Server is installed or running. Add a machine from **a known server…** (the machines of nomajde's [Server sizes](../../nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes.md)) or type **its name**, then **Add**.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Cores** | The cores of the machine. |
| **Processor family** | Its chip, with the core factor of Oracle's *Processor Core Factor Table* (0.5 for Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC, 1 for IBM POWER6 and later…). |
| **Virtualisation** | *Physical machine*, *Hardware partition*, *VMware virtual machine*, *Other virtual machine*. |
| **Cluster** | For a virtual machine, the cluster it runs on. |

These values are those of [Server sizes](../../nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes.md#processor-licences): one table of machines, shared with the sizing of the platform. **Remove** takes the machine out of the installation; its row in Server sizes stays.

### 2 · The clusters behind the virtual machines \{#step-clusters\}

A virtual machine that is not a hardware partition counts **every** physical host of its cluster. For each cluster named in step 1, state its hosts with their cores and processor family; they are kept in Server sizes as *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)*. *No virtual machine names a cluster.* when none does.

### 3 · The databases \{#step-databases\}

The repository database, and every database Analytics Server reads (the data warehouse). Add each one under **Repository** or **Data warehouse**, pick its **Edition** — *Express Edition*, *Standard Edition 2*, *Enterprise Edition* or *Not Oracle* — and tick **JD Edwards uses it too** when it is the JD Edwards database.

### 4 · The users \{#step-users\}

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Where are the users kept?** | *In WebLogic*, *In a database* or *Single sign-on*. |
| **How many users does Analytics Server have?** | A number; *not known* while empty. |
| **Size of the Express Edition repository (GB)** | Asked only when the repository is on Express Edition. |

An empty answer goes back to *not known*.

---

## Count the users kept in WebLogic \{#weblogic\}

When the users are *In WebLogic*, the step offers **Count them in WebLogic**: WebLogic keeps its users in an embedded directory, which Nomasx-1 reads through a **directory pool** (Liberty → Pools, see [An LDAP directory](../../framework/connectors.md#pool-ldap)):

| Pool field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Host**, **Port** | The WebLogic administration server and its port, over `ldap://` (`ldap://<administration server>:<its port>`). |
| **Base DN** | `dc=<the domain's name>` |
| **Account** | `cn=Admin` |
| **Password** | The domain's *Embedded LDAP* credential (WebLogic console → the domain → Security → Embedded LDAP). |

Pick the pool and click **Count**. The users of the default realm are counted under `ou=people,ou=myrealm` of that base (a pool whose base already starts with `ou=` is read as it is). The figure becomes the answer to *How many users*, with its date and its pool: *N users counted on … (pool …)*. Typing a number by hand takes over, and the line goes away. *No directory pool exists yet.* when there is none to pick; a directory that cannot be read says why (wrong credential, base not found).

Users kept in a database or behind single sign-on stay a declared number.

---

The right-hand side is the server's reading of the answers.

| Block | What it shows |

| **Figures** | *Processors needed* (red when above those subscribed), *Processors subscribed*, *Named User Plus needed* and *subscribed* (when the contract has a Named User Plus line), *Estimated risk* in euros, *Still to answer*. |
| **What it means** | The findings, the risks first, each with its level: **risk**, **to check**, **not known**, **fine**. |
| **What is counted** | Each server (`name: cores → processors`) or whole cluster (`cluster name: cores on hosts → processors`). |
| **Subscribed on this contract** | The contract's lines on Analytics Server, with their quantity and metric — *no line for this product* otherwise. |

### How the licences are counted \{#processors\}

Each server's cores × the core factor of its chip, added up per factor before the factor is applied, then rounded up once; a virtual machine on VMware or another hypervisor counts the whole cluster it names. **Named User Plus needed** is the users stated, never below the minimum per processor of the price list × the processors needed. What is beyond the subscription is priced at the public list price with three years of support.

### The findings \{#findings\}

| Level | Finding |
|---|---|
| risk | **Cluster counted whole** — its cores on its hosts give the processor licences, because of the server that names it. |
| risk | **No line for this product** — the processor licences an audit would claim, priced. |
| risk | **Processor licences missing** — needed, subscribed, missing, priced. |
| risk | **Named User Plus missing** — needed (users, minimum per processor), subscribed, missing, priced. |
| risk | **Repository beyond Express Edition** — more than 12 GB: it needs a licensed edition. |
| risk | **Database with no line** — a repository or data warehouse on Standard Edition 2 or Enterprise Edition, not used by JD Edwards, with no line for that edition. |
| to check | **Data warehouse on Express Edition** — check its size and use stay within the edition's limits. |
| not known | No server stated · a server with no cores · a virtual machine whose cluster hosts are not stated (its own cores are only a floor) · a cluster host with no cores · where the users are kept or how many, not answered · no repository · an edition not stated. |
| fine | Repository within the 12 GB of Express Edition · database also used by JD Edwards (check the contract allows this use) · database covered by a line. |

The same sentences, in the language of the reader, appear for the installation on **Reviews → Licences**, in its PDF and in the licence audit report; what it is short of is part of the estimated risk there.

## Tips & best practices

- **Count the WebLogic users rather than typing them**: the figure keeps its date and its pool, and is counted again in one click before a discussion.
- **State the data warehouse databases too**: a warehouse on Enterprise Edition with no line is a licence of its own.
- **Name the cluster of each virtual machine and state its hosts.** Without them, the figure is only a floor and says so.
- **Keep the page for the discussion with Oracle**, as an assumption at public list prices, never as a certified count.
