## Nomasx-1 — JD Edwards Licence Audit
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/reports/audit-licences/

A one-click compliance and optimisation audit for a JD Edwards application — licence inventory, real usage, financial exposure and a remediation plan, rendered as a PDF or Markdown deliverable. Bilingual (French default, English available); the report opens on a headline KPI band and inline charts (active-users donut, components-by-usage bar, financial risk by component).

The **JD Edwards Licence Audit** is a generated report, not a grid. It runs against one connected application and assembles a full compliance-and-optimisation deliverable: what is subscribed, what is actually used, where the financial exposure sits, and how to close it. The output is a polished PDF — or Markdown — ready to hand to a steering committee.

It draws on the data Nomasx-1 already collects — Object Usage Tracking, role and permission assignments, the segregation-of-duties matrix and the per-application licence inventory — and turns it into a single narrative document.

:::info[JDE-specific]
This report targets a **JD Edwards EnterpriseOne** application and its Oracle technology foundation. The connected application is identified by its Nomasx-1 `apps_id`.
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The deliverable

A confidential, branded document of roughly thirty to forty pages — PDF for the steering committee, Markdown when you want to edit or embed it. The cover carries the title *Audit Licences JD Edwards – \{client\}*, the subtitle *Analyse de conformité et plan d'optimisation des licences Oracle*, and a **Client / Date / Author / Version** block; every page is footed *Confidentiel*.

The report is generated in **French by default** (the working language of the audit); switch the **Language** parameter to `English` for a fully English deliverable.

It is an **internal** compliance-and-optimisation document — the basis for your own decisions and for preparing a contract renewal, not a declaration to hand to the vendor.

---

## Headline KPIs and inline charts

The executive summary opens on a **KPI band** and a small set of inline SVG charts, so the message reads in seconds before the reader dives into the detail:

- **Stat band** — active users, never-used accounts, quantifiable financial risk (€) and unassigned roles.
- **Active-users donut** — used vs never-used across the audited population.
- **Components-by-usage bar** — the Oracle components in use ranked by consumption.
- **Financial-risk-by-component bar** — the euro-denominated exposure sized per component.

The charts render inline in both PDF and Markdown output — no external image assets, no dependency on a chart engine at render time.

---

## What the report contains

Nine sections, each built from the data Nomasx-1 has collected:

1. **Synthèse** — executive summary: context and objectives, the principal findings each with a risk level, the estimated financial exposure, and the key recommendations.
2. **Périmètre de l'audit** — audited components, what is out of scope, the JD Edwards environments table (production vs non-production), and the **technical architecture**: software versions, a server inventory, and the architecture diagram on a landscape page of its own (see [The architecture page](#architecture)).
3. **Méthodologie** — the tools and data used, the analysis rules (usage is measured from real consumption, not from authorisations), and a **data-sources** table that dates every input.
4. **Licences acquises** — the subscribed inventory: Oracle Database Enterprise Edition (NUP), the options and packs, the components detected in use, the *règle des minimas* and the NUP minimum computed from the processor count; then the JD Edwards Oracle Technology Foundation and the application modules.
5. **Utilisation et conformité** — the core of the report:
   - JD Edwards modules cross-referenced **OUT × transactions** — real consumption versus write activity — with a drill-down on low-usage modules (which user touched which object);
   - **authorisations versus real usage** per module (authorised users vs OUT vs transactions vs number of roles), which surfaces access far wider than actual use;
   - the **optimisation analysis** (see below);
   - the Oracle Technology Foundation user analysis (declared / active / disabled, technical accounts, role assignments) and the Oracle database user count.
6. **Risque financier** — the calculation method (Oracle public price list plus three years of support arrears), each identified risk costed line by line, a consolidated figure and the prioritised levers. The risks come from the same licence position as the [Licensing review](../licensing-review.md): the missing seats per module and the modules no line of the contract covers, read [the way a contract is counted](../how-a-contract-is-counted.md) — bundles, revenue, employee and processor lines included. The section opens on the same warning: an assumption at public list prices, never a certified position.
   - **§6.5 Oracle Data Integrator and Oracle Analytics Server** — each installation described for the application's contracts ([Oracle Data Integrator](../licenses/odi.md), [Oracle Analytics Server](../licenses/analytics-server.md)): the processor licences or Named User Plus it needs against what is subscribed, its estimated risk, and its findings in the report's language — the same sentences as their pages and the Licensing review. A contract line on one of these products is read by its own questionnaire, never compared with the database servers or the JD Edwards users. The section appears only when such an installation is described.
7. **Plan de remédiation** — concrete clean-up: deactivating never-used accounts, and rationalising roles and access (dropping unassigned roles, reviewing excessive role stacking, aligning access to real use).
8. **Recommandations et plan d'action** — every action ranked by priority, effort and financial impact, an indicative four-phase schedule, and the follow-up indicators to track afterwards.
9. **Annexes** — the detailed list of users to deactivate (with creation and last-update dates, and the validation cautions to apply before disabling) and a glossary.

---

## The architecture page \{#architecture\}

The *Périmètre de l'audit* section shows the application's architecture on a landscape page. The report takes the first picture it finds, in this order:

1. **A picture put there for the application** — the file `data/architecture/<apps_id>.svg` in the applications' folder of the installation. It always comes first.
2. **The platform as Nomajde read it** — on [Nomajde → Monitoring → Architecture](../../nomajde/monitoring/architecture.md#download), **Keep for the audit report** keeps the reading of a JD Edwards pool. The report draws the reading kept for the pool the application names on [Applications](../settings/global/applications.md), **in the report's language** and with the date of the reading. The reading is kept on the installation: the report draws it even where Server Manager cannot be reached from the machine that writes the report. An application that names no pool takes the reading when only one is kept.
3. **The installation's picture** — the file `data/architecture/default.svg`, for an installation that holds a single application.

Without any of them, the report has no architecture page.

---

## The optimisation analysis

Beyond pure compliance, the report mines the **detailed OUT extract** — one row per user × module × object — to size licences to real need rather than to the blanket "full use" grant:

- the distribution of modules-per-user (most users touch only a handful of modules);
- the most frequent module combinations, which cluster around a commercial / logistics core;
- two usage profiles — **Standard** (the core) and **Étendu** (the core plus at least one specialised module);
- a proposed split into **differentiated bundles** to take into a contract renewal.

This is what turns the audit from a compliance snapshot into a cost-optimisation lever — the section the renewal negotiation is built on.

---

## Running the report

The report lives under **Reports** in the Nomasx-1 menu: one card per report, with its description. **Run** on the **Audit Licences JD Edwards** card opens its parameters; fill them, choose a **Format**, then **Run & download**.

| Parameter | Required | Default | What it sets |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Application** | Yes | — | The application to audit. Picked **by name** from the registered applications (*Settings → Global → Applications*) — the run form resolves the name to the underlying `apps_id`. |
| **Target connector** | No | `nomasx1` | Dropdown of the SQL connectors on the install. |
| **Schema** | No | `public` | Dropdown of the schemas of the picked target connector. |
| **Language** | No | `Français` | Report language — `Français` or `English`. |
| **Audit date label** | No | current month + year | The label printed on the cover page (e.g. *Mai 2026*). |
| **Client name** | No | the application name | The client name on the cover page. |

Every dropdown resolves server-side against live catalogs — *Application* against the applications registry, *Target connector* against the configured SQL connectors and *Schema* against the schemas of the picked connector. Cascading defaults mean picking a connector re-lists its own schemas.

**Format** — `PDF` for the steering-committee deliverable, `markdown` when you want to edit or embed the content. The run streams the file straight back to the browser.

**Every month, by e-mail** — *Jobs → Licence audit report* renders the same PDF for one or several applications and mails it to the auditors' role; scheduled on the 1st of the month once enabled. See [Nomasx-1 jobs](../jobs.md#reports).

---

## Before you run

The audit reads the data Nomasx-1 has already collected for the application — it does not collect on the fly. For an accurate picture, make sure the latest collection has run first. The report draws on:

- **Object Usage Tracking** — the synthesis (distinct users per module), the detail (users / objects / dates) and the fine detail (one row per user × module × object) that drives the *Utilisation et conformité* and optimisation sections. On an application with no usage tracking data, a user who **signed in within the application's period** — *Signed in within (days) = a user* on [Applications](../settings/global/applications.md), 90 days when empty — is a real user: the summary says so, and only those who did not sign in within it are listed as never used.
- **Modules with transactions** — users who generated at least one write per module.
- **The JD Edwards user list** — declared, active and disabled users, with creation and last-usage dates.
- **Roles, user-role assignments and access rights per role**, plus the **JDE menus** (object → module mapping) that link usage to modules.
- **The database options and packs inventory** — Oracle components in use versus subscribed.
- **The contracts and pricing** — the lines, bundles and declared figures of each [CSI](../licenses/csi.md), and *Settings → Licenses → Pricing*, otherwise the financial figures drift from the real price book.
- **The technical accounts** — the *Technical* flag of [Users properties](../settings/security/users-properties.md); while the application has no user property at all, the naming rules of its [Technical accounts](../settings/global/applications.md#technical-accounts) tab. With no flag and no rule, no account is counted as technical.
- **The application's pool** — the server and the database the report names in its scope are read from the pool the application names, and the pool is printed; an application that names no pool keeps what its row holds.
- **The architecture reading** — when Nomajde is installed, **Keep for the audit report** on its Architecture page for the application's JD Edwards pool, so that the report draws the platform as it stands (see [The architecture page](#architecture)).

A run against an application with no collected usage still produces the document, but the usage and financial sections will read as empty rather than wrong.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Run it after a fresh collection.** The audit is a snapshot of the current tables — schedule it right after the nightly collection so the figures match reality.
- **Set the *Audit date label* and *Client name*** for an external-ready cover page; leave them empty for an internal draft.
- **Use *markdown* to iterate, *PDF* to deliver.** The Markdown output is the same content without the cover styling, handy for review before the final export.
- **Read it next to the source screens.** Every figure traces back to a screen — *Object Usage Tracking*, *Conflicts*, *Licenses* — so a reviewer can drill from the audit into the live data.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Security & SoD Assessment
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/reports/security-sox/

A one-click security-posture and segregation-of-duties review for a connected application — user lifecycle, privileged access, role and object-security hygiene, SoD conflicts and a remediation plan, rendered as a PDF or Markdown deliverable.

The **Security & Segregation of Duties Assessment** is a generated report, not a grid. It runs against one connected application and assembles a full security-posture deliverable: who can sign in, which accounts are dormant or privileged, how clean the role and object-security setup is, where segregation-of-duties (SoD) conflicts sit, and how to close them. The output is a polished PDF — or Markdown — ready to hand to a steering committee or an auditor.

It draws on the data Nomasx-1 already collects — the user registry, roles and assignments, the object-security grants (Security Workbench) and the segregation-of-duties matrix — and turns it into a single narrative document, driven by **Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX)** IT general-control expectations. It is framed as a general security-posture review, not a formal control attestation.

:::info[JDE-specific]
The **segregation-of-duties** sections build on the SoD conflict refresh (the *Security and SoD* collection, `nomasx1-collect-all`), which today evaluates **JD Edwards EnterpriseOne** `SECURITY_RIGHTS` rows. The user, role and object-security hygiene sections read the `security_*` tables directly and apply to any connected application; the SoD matrix and `*PUBLIC` / Security Workbench language is JDE-flavoured.
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The deliverable

A branded document of roughly twenty to thirty pages — PDF for the steering committee or the auditor, Markdown when you want to edit or embed it. The cover carries the title *Security & SoD Assessment – \{client\}* (in French, *Évaluation Sécurité & Séparation des tâches – \{client\}*), a security-review subtitle, and an **Application / Date / Prepared by: NOMANA-IT** block. The report is generated in **English by default**; switch the **Language** parameter to `Français` for a fully French deliverable.

---

## Headline KPIs and inline charts

The executive summary opens on a **KPI band** and a small set of inline SVG charts, sized to make the security story readable at a glance:

- **Stat band** — headline metrics: total users, dormant accounts, privileged accounts and total SoD violations.
- **Findings-by-severity donut** — how the report's findings distribute across `high` / `medium` / `low`.
- **Most-conflicted roles bar** — the roles that carry the most conflicts, ranked by user count and distinct SoD rules.
- **Conflicts-by-process bar** — the SoD violations grouped by the business process the matrix assigns them to (when the matrix carries a process dimension).
- **SoD trend line** — the total-violations curve across recent refreshes; prints a *not enough history* note when only one refresh exists.

The charts render inline in both PDF and Markdown output — no external image assets, no dependency on a chart engine at render time.

It is an **internal** security-and-compliance document — the basis for your own remediation decisions and for an access review, not an attestation to file with a regulator.

---

## What the report contains

Eight sections plus a glossary, each built from the data Nomasx-1 has collected:

1. **Executive summary** — a KPI band, the principal findings each with a severity (high / medium / low), a severity breakdown, the key indicators, and a one-line SoD trend versus the previous refresh.
2. **Scope & methodology** — the application scope (name, id, type, database), the method (how a conflict is defined), and a **data-freshness** table that dates every input.
3. **User access & lifecycle** — the declared population, then **dormant and never-used accounts** (an enabled account with no sign-in within the dormancy window), **generic / shared accounts**, and **technical / service accounts**.
4. **Privileged access review** — the privileged accounts, with the count of privileged accounts and of privileged SoD pairings.
5. **Role & object-security hygiene** — role metrics (roles-per-user distribution, the most-entitled users, orphan roles) and **object security** read from the Security Workbench grants.
6. **Segregation of duties** — the core of the report: matrix coverage, the violation summary, **self-conflicting roles** (fix the role), the most-conflicted roles, the **most common conflicting role combinations** (fix the assignments), and — when the matrix carries them — conflicts by risk and by process.
7. **SoD trend** — a multi-refresh trend table and trend line; it needs at least two refreshes, otherwise it prints a *not enough history* note.
8. **Findings & recommendations** — every finding and a matching **recommended actions** table.

A closing **glossary** defines the ten terms the report uses (SoD, conflict matrix, self-conflicting role, conflicting role combination, privileged / generic / technical account, `*PUBLIC`, dormant account, ITGC).

---

## How a conflict is read

A **conflict** is a single enabled user who can perform **both** sides of an incompatible activity pair declared in the SoD **matrix**. The report does not list user-by-user; it groups the conflicts into the unit you actually remediate:

- **Self-conflicting role** — one role grants both sides of a pair. That is a role-design defect: **fix the role**.
- **Conflicting role combination** — the conflict only appears because a user holds *two* roles. That is an assignment problem: **fix the assignment**.
- **Most-conflicted roles** — ranked by the number of users and distinct conflict rules they carry, so you know which role to clean up first.

Severity comes from the operator's own levels on the matrix — the **Risk Level** (the primary sort) and, as a fallback, the **Critical Level** on the risk dimension. The headline *total violations* is a count of **user × matrix-entry pairings** (how many users trip each rule), not a raw count of rules.

The matrix itself — processes, activities, objects, risks and the incompatible pairs — is maintained under **Settings → Segregation of duties**, and refreshed into the conflict tables by the collection job, `nomasx1-collect-all` (*Jobs → Collect security and SoD*). Run it before the report so the figures are current.

---

## Running the report

The report lives under **Reports** in the Nomasx-1 menu: one card per report, with its description. **Run** on the **Security & Segregation of Duties Assessment** card opens its parameters; fill them, choose a **Format**, then **Run & download**.

| Parameter | Required | Default | What it sets |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Application** | Yes | — | The application to assess. Picked **by name** from the registered applications (*Settings → Global → Applications*) — the run form resolves the name to the underlying `apps_id`. |
| **Target connector** | No | `nomasx1` | Dropdown of the SQL connectors on the install. |
| **Schema** | No | `public` | Dropdown of the schemas of the picked target connector. |
| **Language** | No | `English` | Report language — `English` or `Français`. |
| **Dormancy window (days)** | No | `90` | An enabled account with no sign-in within this many days counts as dormant. |
| **Report date label** | No | current month + year | The label printed on the cover page (e.g. *June 2026*). |
| **Client name** | No | the application name | The client name on the cover page. |

Every dropdown resolves server-side against live catalogs — *Application* against the applications registry, *Target connector* against the configured SQL connectors and *Schema* against the schemas of the picked connector. Cascading defaults mean picking a connector re-lists its own schemas.

**Format** — `PDF` for the steering-committee deliverable, `markdown` when you want to edit or embed the content. The run streams the file straight back to the browser.

**Every month, by e-mail** — *Jobs → Security & SoD report* renders the same PDF for one or several applications and mails it to the auditors' role; scheduled on the 1st of the month once enabled. See [Nomasx-1 jobs](../jobs.md#reports).

---

## Before you run

The audit reads the data Nomasx-1 has already collected for the application — it does not collect on the fly. For an accurate picture, make sure the latest collection and the SoD refresh have run first. The report draws on:

- **The user registry** — declared accounts, status and last sign-in, plus the curated flags (privileged / technical / generic / linked) maintained on each user.
- **Roles and assignments** — the role catalog and the user-role assignments.
- **Object security** — the Security Workbench grants (run / add / change / delete, direct or via `*ROLE`, and `*PUBLIC` grants).
- **The SoD conflict tables** — refreshed by `nomasx1-collect-all`, decorated by the matrix and its process / activity / object / risk dimensions.
- **The applications registry** — for the cover and scope. The database named comes from the pool the application names (the service name of an Oracle pool, the base of a directory), and the pool is printed; an application that names no pool keeps what its row holds.

A run against an application with no collected data still produces the document, but the affected sections read as empty rather than wrong.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Refresh SoD first.** Run *Jobs → Collect security and SoD* right before the report so the conflict counts and the trend match reality.
- **Start with the role-level findings.** Self-conflicting roles and the most-conflicted roles are the fastest wins — one fix clears conflicts for every user who holds the role.
- **Set the *Report date label* and *Client name*** for an external-ready cover page; leave them empty for an internal draft.
- **Use *markdown* to iterate, *PDF* to deliver.** The Markdown output is the same content without the cover styling, handy for review before the final export.
- **Read it next to the source screens.** Every figure traces back to a screen — *Users*, *Roles*, *Security Workbench*, *Segregation of duties* — so a reviewer can drill from the report into the live data.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Applications
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/global/applications/

Nomasx-1 registry of every connected application — identifier, type, the pool it is reached through, and its JD Edwards, LDAP, activity log, audit trail and technical-account settings.

The **Applications** screen is the central registry of every application Nomasx-1 connects to — JD Edwards EnterpriseOne, a directory, a database or any other connected application. One line per application. Each row holds the identifier displayed across the rest of the product, the type of the source system and the **pool** it is reached through; its tabs carry the JD Edwards, LDAP, activity log, audit trail and technical-account settings of the application.

It is the first screen to populate when bringing a new source system in. Open it from **Settings → Global → Applications**.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

Maintain the registry that every other screen references:

- **Declare each source system.** One row per application — ID, name, type (`JDE`, `DATABASE`, `LDAP`, `WEBLOGIC`, `CUSTOM`) and database technology (`ORACLE`, `MSSQL`, `DB2`, `POSTGRES`…).
- **Name its connection.** The *Pool* says where the collection reads the application: a database pool, or a directory pool for an LDAP application. The address, the account and the password belong to the pool, set once under **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools**.
- **Establish the application ID** that flows through every other screen — the link between user, role, conflict, licence and audit data.

---

## Columns

The default view shows *Application ID*, *Application Name*, *Application Type*, *Database type* and *Pool*. A column picked from a list shows twice: its code (*Application Type (ID)*) and its label (*Application Type*). **Columns** shows the others.

| Column | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application identifier referenced everywhere else in the product. |
| **Application Name** | Human-readable label. |
| **Application Type** | Kind of source system: `JDE` (JD Edwards), `DATABASE`, `LDAP`, `WEBLOGIC` or `CUSTOM` (Custom Application). Drives the collection steps that apply. |
| **Database type** | Database technology: `ORACLE`, `MSSQL`, `DB2`, `POSTGRES`, `MYSQL`, `MARIADB`, `LDAP`, `GENERIC`. |
| **Pool** | The pool the collection reads this application through, so one installation can reach several environments. Blank: the collection job's own pool. |
| **Host**, **Port**, **Database name**, **User**, **DB-Link**, **Direct connection**, **Country Code** | Hidden. Connection details kept on the row; they are not on the form. Only an LDAP application without a pool still reads its host, port, user and password from them (see [LDAP](#tab-ldap)). |

The JD Edwards and LDAP settings of each application are columns of the same grid as well (*JDE SY*, *JDE DTA*… *LDAP Context*…): they are described with the dialog's tabs below.

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to declare a new application, or click a row to open it. The dialog, **Edit · Settings - Applications**, opens on the **Application** tab and carries eight tabs. **Task Views**, **Activity Log**, **Audit Trail**, **Audit Columns** and **Technical accounts** only appear on an application that is already saved. The footer carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**.

### Tab 1 — Application

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Numeric identifier, entered when the application is created and read-only on a saved application. It stays stable across the product. |
| **Application Name** | Friendly label shown on every screen and export. |
| **Application Type** | Kind of source system, picked from a list (`JDE` — JD Edwards…). Drives which collection steps apply. |
| **Database type** | Database technology, picked from a list (`ORACLE` — Oracle…). |
| **Pool** | The application's connection, picked from the pools of the installation. A database pool for a JD Edwards or database application; a directory pool (type *LDAP directory*) for an LDAP application. Blank: the collection job's own pool. |
| **Signed in within (days) = a user** | For a JD Edwards application whose Object Usage Tracking has no data: a user who signed in within this number of days counts as a real user — the [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md) counts them on the modules their security allows, and the [licence audit report](../../reports/audit-licences.md) does not list them as never used. Empty: 90 days. |

The pool is the only connection setting of the application: its address, its account and its password are set on the pool, under **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools** — see [Pools](../../../framework/connectors.md#pools). The [reports](../../reports/audit-licences.md) also read from it the system they name (the server and the service name of an Oracle pool, the base of a directory) and print the pool.

### Tab 2 — JD Edwards

:::info[JDE-specific]
The schemas that locate the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne tables, each with its database link, then what the collection reads. The same settings are on their own screen, [JD Edwards](./jd-edwards.md).
:::

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **JDE DTA**, **JDE CTL**, **JDE SY**, **JDE SVM**, **JDE CO**, **JDE OL** | Schemas of the business data, control, system, server map, central objects and object librarian tables. |
| **F00950** | Schema of the security workbench table. |
| **JDE_UDO_SEC** | Schema of the user defined objects' security table (F00950W): its rows are added to the security collected. Blank: skipped. |
| **JDE_UDO_OL** | Schema of the user defined objects' librarian (F9860W, F9861W), read for the composite pages, the E1 pages and the inventory of user defined objects. Blank: those steps do nothing and say so. |
| **…_DBLINK** | Next to each schema: the database link to reach it, blank when the JDE tables are local. |
| **Thick LOB read (Y/N)** | Tick when the JDE tables are reached through a database link: the menus and the cross reference specifications (LOB columns) are then read by a short-lived thick-mode process. Leave cleared for a local install. |
| **Standard Menu (Y/N)**, **E1 Pages (Y/N)**, **E1 Composite (Y/N)** | Which menus the security build reads: the standard JDE menus, the E1 pages and the composite pages. A composite page gives what its tiles open, the forms shown in its panes and the task of a task tile — for a landing page, every task under its menu; an E1 page gives the applications and reports its code calls or names. |
| **Purge OUT (Y/N)** | Tick to let Nomasx-1 purge old Object Usage Tracking rows. |
| **OUT Retention Days** | Days of usage history kept by the purge. |

:::tip
Object Usage Tracking writes several thousand rows a day. Once Nomasx-1 has aggregated them, the purge keeps the JDE table small — tick **Purge OUT** and pick a retention that fits the audit needs. The usage Nomasx-1 has already collected is kept on its side.
:::

The schema values come from the JDE installation — the JDE administrator is the right person to ask.

The tab is saved with the application, **Thick LOB read** included — also on an application created without JD Edwards settings: filling the tab later and saving the application creates them.

### Tab 3 — Task Views

Grid of the JDE task views (the roots of the menu tree, such as *EnterpriseOne Menus*): **Task ID**, **Task Name** and **Collect Security (Y/N)**. Only the task views ticked here are walked by the security build — the rights of the *Menus* and *Rights* screens start from them. **Add row** declares another task view; on a saved line, *Task ID* is read-only.

### Tab 4 — LDAP \{#tab-ldap\}

LDAP / Active Directory scope of the application, read by the LDAP collection.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **LDAP Context** | Base DN the search starts from (for example `OU=Users,DC=acme,DC=local`). Blank: the base of the directory pool. |
| **LDAP Filter** | LDAP search filter restricting the entries read. |
| **LDAP Exclude** | Entries to leave out. |

The directory itself — its server, the account and the password the collection binds with — is the application's **Pool** (tab *Application*): a pool of type *LDAP directory*, created under **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools** (`ldap://`, or `ldaps://` for an encrypted connection; see [An LDAP directory](../../../framework/connectors.md#pool-ldap)). When **LDAP Context** is blank, the collection starts from the pool's base DN. An LDAP application that names no pool keeps reading the host, port, user and password stored on its row; naming a pool takes over.

Like the JD Edwards tab, the LDAP tab of an application created without it is saved when it is filled later. The same settings are on their own screen, [LDAP](./ldap.md).

### Tab 5 — Activity Log

Grid of the rules that decide **what the activity collection watches** to feed *Applications → Activity log*. One row per rule; **Add row** widens the scope, deleting a row narrows it.

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **ACL Type** | What the rule targets: `ROLE`, `SCHEMA`, `TABLE` or `USER`. |
| **ACL Application Type** | Where the name is read: `DATABASE` or `JDEDWARDS`. |
| **Name** | Name of the role, schema, table or user. |
| **ACL Rule** | `INCLUDE`, `EXCLUDE` or `AUDIT`. |

*ACL Type*, *ACL Application Type* and *Name* identify the rule: read-only on a saved line, where only *ACL Rule* changes.

### Tab 6 — Audit Trail

Grid holding **the connection Nomasx-1 uses to read the Oracle archive logs** of the application — one row — read by the collection that feeds *Database → Audit Trail* and *Audit Lookup*.

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **User ID** / **Password** | Database account allowed to read the archive log views. |
| **Host** / **Port** / **Database** | Where that database is (`1521` on a standard Oracle install). |
| **Last SCN** | *System Change Number* the next extraction resumes from. |
| **Last Timestamp** | Time of the last extraction. |

The line belongs to the application: its *Application ID* is read-only once saved.

### Tab 7 — Audit Columns

Grid that sets **how much of each audited table is indexed** into the values table `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES` for this application. One row per rule:

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Table** | Table name (for example `F0911`). |
| **Column (or *SQL* for journal-only)** | Column to index, or `*SQL*` for the journal-only mode. |

| Rule set on a table | Effect |
|---|---|
| **One or more named columns** | Only the listed columns are indexed. The others stay visible in the on-demand diff of *Audit Trail*, but cannot be searched in the values table. |
| **A single `*SQL*` row** | Journal only — the full DML statement stays in `AUDIT_TRAIL_QUERY`, nothing lands in `AUDIT_TRAIL_VALUES`. Use it on the widest tables where per-column search is not needed. |
| **No row for the table** | Default — every column is indexed. |

The tab keeps the values table's volume in check on wide tables. The full DML statement is always kept in `AUDIT_TRAIL_QUERY` — nothing is lost, whatever the rule set. Pair it with the *Rebuild values* job of the [Audit Trail](../../database/audit-trail.md) screen when you widen the rule set: re-parsing `AUDIT_TRAIL_QUERY` back-fills the newly listed columns for the historical rows.

---

### Tab 8 — Technical accounts \{#technical-accounts\}

How this application names its technical accounts — batch users, integration and service accounts, the accounts held by IT — so that the [licence audit](../../reports/audit-licences.md) sets them apart from the people. One rule per line; **Add row** adds one.

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Compared with** | What the rule is compared with: **Account name** (the account's name) or **User id**. |
| **Rule (\* = any text)** | The name or the id to match. `*` stands for any text (`BATCH*`, `*INTERFACE*`, `SVC_*`); any other character is read as written. Upper and lower case are not told apart. |

The report takes the *Technical* flag of [Users properties](../security/users-properties.md) first. While the application has no user property at all, it applies these rules. **With no flag and no rule, no account is counted as technical**: enter the rules once for each application, or set the flags.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Application IDs should be stable.** Once an application is referenced across roles, conflicts, licences and audit trail, renumbering the ID breaks the history.
- **Pick a meaningful name.** The application name surfaces on every export and report — short, recognisable labels make the deliverables easier to read.
- **One pool per environment.** Credentials are changed on the pool, once, for every application and job that uses it. A connection failing on credentials is the most common reason collections go stale.
- **For an LDAP application, create a directory pool** and pick it here: the pool also allows `ldaps://` for an encrypted connection.
- **Enter the technical-account rules before the first licence audit** — otherwise the batch and service accounts are counted with the people until the user properties are set.
- **For non-JDE sources** (`DATABASE`, `LDAP`, `WEBLOGIC`, `CUSTOM`), check the *Application Type* — the collection steps branch on it. The security of such an application is collected through its own queries: see [Custom Queries](./custom-queries.md).

---

## Nomasx-1 — Custom Queries
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/global/custom-queries/

Nomasx-1 custom queries — an application's own query for the Users, Roles, Assignments, Menus or Rights collection, run on its own pool instead of the built-in one; the way to collect the security of an application that is not JD Edwards.

The **Custom Queries** screen holds an application's own query for a security collection: *Users*, *Roles*, *Assignments*, *Menus* or *Rights*. When an application has a query for a collection, the collection runs it **instead of the built-in one**, on the pool the row names — or on the application's pool when it names none. One line per *(application, collection)* pair. Open it from **Settings → Global → Custom Queries**.

It is also **what lets an application that is not JD Edwards be collected**: the built-in queries read the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne security tables; any other connected application — a database, a custom application — gives its users, roles and rights through its own queries. An application that is not JD Edwards and has no query of its own for a collection is refused by that collection, which names it in the run's log.

---

## At a glance

---

## What a query replaces \{#collections\}

| Collection | What the query fills | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Users**, **Roles**, **Assignments** | The users, the roles and the user–role assignments of the application. | The query takes the place of the built-in one in the same collection: the rows it returns are loaded as a new snapshot, the previous one kept in the history. |
| **Menus**, **Rights** | The menus and the effective rights of the application — the final tables the *Applications* screens read. | The built-in collection builds them in several steps from JD Edwards staging tables. A query fills the final table directly: the application's rows are replaced by what it returns, and the built-in steps add nothing for that application. |

What follows from these tables runs on the application whoever filled them: **segregation of duties** reads its rights and its users, so the conflicts, the [Segregation of duties](../../sod-dashboard.md) dashboard and the security report cover it as well.

:::info[JDE-specific]
The licence collections — employees, transactions, Object Usage Tracking — read JD Edwards EnterpriseOne only; a custom query does not replace them.
:::

---

## Writing the query \{#query\}

The query must **return the columns of the target table**, aliased with their names (`USR_ID`, `USR_NAME`… for *Users*) — the easiest way to get them right is to start from what the built-in collection loads. Before it runs, Nomasx-1 fills in:

| In the text | Replaced by |
|---|---|
| `{apps_id}` | The application ID. |
| `{jde_sy}`, `{jde_dta}`, `{jde_ctl}`… and their `{jde_sy_dblink}`… | For a JD Edwards application: the schemas and database links of its [JD Edwards](./applications.md) tab. |
| `:ukid` | Bound to the snapshot number of the collection — write it where the target table expects its `…_UKID` column. Left out, nothing is bound. |

Any other brace is left as written — a JSON literal or a regular expression in the query is not touched. A trailing `;` is ignored.

---

## Columns

| Column | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application the query is for. It shows twice: its ID (*Application ID (ID)*) and its name. |
| **Collection** | The collection the query replaces: *Users*, *Roles*, *Assignments*, *Menus* or *Rights*. It shows twice: its code (*Collection (ID)*: `SECURITY_USERS`…) and its label. |
| **Pool (blank = the application's)** | The pool the query runs on. Blank: the application's pool, set on [Applications](./applications.md). |
| **User (Audit)** / **Date (Audit)** | Who saved the query last, and when. |

**Columns** also shows the query and the pool's code.

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to declare a query, or click a row to open it. The dialog — **New · Settings - Custom queries**, or **Edit · Settings - Custom queries** on a saved row — has three tabs: **Properties**, **Pool** and **Query**. The footer carries **Cancel** and **Save** — plus **Delete** and **Duplicate** on a saved row.

### Tab 1 — Properties

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | One of the declared applications. The query applies to this one only. |
| **Collection** | The collection replaced: *Users*, *Roles*, *Assignments*, *Menus* or *Rights*. |
| **User (Audit)** / **Date (Audit)** | Filled in by Nomasx-1 on save; read-only. |

*Application ID* and *Collection* name the line: they are entered when the line is created and read-only on a saved line — its pool and its query change, and the change is saved. To move a query to another application or collection, duplicate the line (**Duplicate**) and delete the old one.

### Tab 2 — Pool

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Pool (blank = the application's)** | A dropdown of the installation's pools. Pick one when the query reads another database than the application's — a data warehouse, a copy of the security tables; leave blank otherwise. The pool holds the account the query runs with. |

### Tab 3 — Query

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Query** | The `SELECT` to run instead of the built-in query of the collection picked on *Properties*. A blank query is ignored: the built-in one runs. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Run the query on its pool first** with the application ID filled in — the columns, their names and their types must match the target table.
- **One collection at a time.** Start with *Users*, check the [Users](../../security/users.md) screen after a collection, then add *Roles* and *Assignments*.
- **Mind *Menus* and *Rights*.** Their query fills the final table: the rows it returns are what the rights, the conflicts and the reports see for that application.
- **Delete the row to go back to the built-in query** — or empty the query.

---

## Nomasx-1 — JD Edwards
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/global/jd-edwards/

Nomasx-1 JD Edwards settings of each connected application — where the JDE E1 tables are read (schemas and database links), which menus build the security, the user defined objects libraries and the Object Usage Tracking purge.

The **JD Edwards** screen (*Settings - JD Edwards*) holds, for each connected JD Edwards EnterpriseOne application, where the collection reads the JDE tables and what it reads. One line per application. Open it from **Settings → Global → JD Edwards**.

The same fields are on the **JD Edwards** tab of [Applications](./applications.md); this screen shows every application side by side.

---

## At a glance

The **Application ID** field above the grid narrows it to one application; blank, it shows them all.

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

Click **Add row** to give an application its JD Edwards settings, or click a row to open them. The dialog, **Edit · JD Edwards Settings**, is one form in four columns, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application. Read-only once saved. |
| **JDE DTA** | Schema of the business data tables (F0101, F4211…). |
| **JDE CTL** | Schema of the control tables (F0005…). |
| **JDE SY** | Schema of the system tables (security F00950, users F0092…). |
| **JDE SVM** | Schema of the server map tables. |
| **JDE CO** | Schema of the central objects — the specifications read by the cross reference. |
| **JDE OL** | Schema of the Object Librarian (F9860, F9861) — the objects catalogue and the menus. |
| **F00950** | Schema of the security workbench table, when it is not the system one. |
| **JDE_UDO_SEC** | Schema of the user defined objects' security table (F00950W): its lines are collected as the [UDO security](../../applications/rights/udo-security.md), and the view lines of the composite and E1 pages feed the rights. Blank: skipped. |
| **JDE_UDO_OL** | Schema of the user defined objects' librarian (F9860W, F9861W), read for the composite pages, the E1 pages and the inventory of user defined objects. Blank: those steps do nothing and say so. |
| **…_DBLINK** | Next to each schema: the database link that reaches it. Blank when the JDE tables are in the database Nomasx-1 connects to. |
| **Thick LOB read (Y/N)** | Tick when the JDE tables are reached through a database link: the menus and the specifications (LOB columns) are then read by a short-lived thick-mode process. |
| **Standard Menu (Y/N)** | Read the standard JDE menus for the security build. |
| **E1 Pages (Y/N)** | Read the E1 pages: the applications and reports their code calls or names become access paths. |
| **E1 Composite (Y/N)** | Read the composite pages: what their tiles open, the forms in their panes, the task of a task tile — for a landing page, every task under its menu. |
| **Purge OUT (Y/N)** | Purge old Object Usage Tracking rows in JDE once Nomasx-1 has collected them. |
| **OUT Retention Days** | Days of usage history the purge keeps in JDE. |

:::info[JDE-specific]
The menus read decide the access paths behind *Menus*, *Rights*, the segregation of duties and the licence figures: switching **E1 Pages** or **E1 Composite** on or off changes them at the next security collection. The inventory of user defined objects (queries, grid formats, watchlists, form extensions, composite pages, orchestrations…) and the cross reference built from the central objects are read by Nomajde's screens, from what Nomasx-1 collects with these settings.
:::

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Ask the JDE administrator** for the schema names and the database links — they come from the JDE installation (path code, data sources).
- **Check the library first** on the [UDO libraries](./udo-libraries.md) screen: it lists every library that holds F00950W, F9860W and F9861W, and marks the one with the 9.2 layout to put in **JDE_UDO_SEC** and **JDE_UDO_OL**.
- **Fill JDE_UDO_OL** on any Tools 9.2 installation: much of what a customer changes is a user defined object, and composite pages give access paths the standard menus do not.
- **Tick Thick LOB read only with a database link**; a local install reads the LOB columns directly.
- **Keep the OUT retention longer than the collection interval**, so no usage row is purged before Nomasx-1 has read it.

---

## Nomasx-1 — UDO libraries
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/global/udo-libraries/

The Nomasx-1 UDO libraries screen: for each JD Edwards EnterpriseOne table of the user defined objects (F00950W, F9860W, F9861W), every library that holds it, the setting to fill (JDE UDO SEC or JDE UDO OL) and whether the table there has the 9.2 layout — the library to use is the one marked.

The **UDO libraries** screen (**Settings → Global → UDO libraries**) answers one question before the [JD Edwards settings](./jd-edwards.md) are filled: *which library goes in **JDE UDO SEC** and **JDE UDO OL**?*

The security collection reads the security of the user defined objects (F00950W) from the library set as **JDE UDO SEC**, and the user defined objects themselves (F9860W, F9861W) from the one set as **JDE UDO OL**. A JD Edwards database often holds these tables in several libraries — a system library kept from 9.1 next to the 9.2 one — and a wrong library makes the step fail, with an Oracle message such as `ORA-00904: "WSWOBNM"`. The screen reads the JD Edwards database and lists, for each of the three tables, every library that holds it.

:::info[JDE-specific]
The screen reads the dictionary of the JD Edwards database through the JD Edwards connector (Oracle), behind the pool's database link when it has one. It is read-only.
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## Columns

| Column | What it tells |
|---|---|
| **Setting to fill** | **JDE UDO SEC** for F00950W, **JDE UDO OL** for F9860W and F9861W. |
| **Table** | The table: F00950W (UDO security), F9860W and F9861W (the user defined objects and their location). |
| **Library** | A library that holds the table. |
| **9.2 layout** | Marked when the table in that library has the 9.2 layout. |

**The library to use is the one marked.** A line with no mark is an older copy of the table: setting it fails the collection step.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Open this screen before filling JDE_UDO_SEC and JDE_UDO_OL** in [JD Edwards](./jd-edwards.md), or when the security collection fails on a UDO step.
- **F9860W and F9861W go together**: both lines of **JDE UDO OL** should name the same library.
- **Collect again after correcting a library**: [UDO security](../../applications/rights/udo-security.md) and the access paths of the composite and E1 pages are read at the next security collection.

---

## Nomasx-1 — LDAP
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/global/ldap/

Nomasx-1 LDAP settings of each connected application — the Active Directory context, filter and exclusions read by the LDAP collection that feeds Security → LDAP.

The **LDAP** screen holds, for each connected application, which part of the LDAP / Active Directory directory the LDAP collection reads — the accounts compared with the application's users on the *Security → LDAP* screens. One line per application. Open it from **Settings → Global → LDAP**.

The same fields are on the **LDAP** tab of [Applications](./applications.md); this screen shows every application side by side. The directory server, the account and the password are not set here: they belong to the **directory pool** the application names on its *Application* tab — see [LDAP tab](./applications.md#tab-ldap). A blank **LDAP Context** means the base of that pool.

---

## At a glance

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

Click **Add row** to give an application its LDAP scope, or click a row to open it. The dialog is a single form with **Cancel** and **Save** — plus **Delete** and **Duplicate** on an existing row.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application. Read-only once saved. |
| **LDAP Context** | Base DN the search starts from (for example `OU=Users,DC=acme,DC=local`). |
| **LDAP Filter** | Standard LDAP filter restricting the entries read (for example `(objectClass=user)`). |
| **LDAP Exclude** | Entries to leave out of the collection. |

The grid also shows **User (Audit)** and **Date (Audit)**: who changed the row last, and when.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Start narrow.** A context on the users' organisational unit and a filter on user objects keep the collection fast and the comparison readable.
- **Leave service accounts out** with **LDAP Exclude** when they have no counterpart in the application.
- **Group the directory's departments** on [Department](../security/department.md): the grouping drives the LDAP Excel export.

---

## Nomasx-1 — SoD — Process
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/sod/process/

Catalog of business processes that group the activities monitored by the segregation-of-duties matrix.

The **Process** screen is the catalog of business processes used by every other SoD setting. One line per `(Application, Process)`. Each row carries a numeric identifier and a friendly name — for example `P2P` (*Procure to Pay*), `O2C` (*Order to Cash*), `R2R` (*Record to Report*).

It is the top of the SoD hierarchy: *Activities* attach to a process, *Risks* are defined inside a process, the *Matrix* groups risk-bearing activity pairs by process.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Declare the processes** that will host the SoD activities and risks.
- **Use stable identifiers** — *Process ID* is referenced by the *Activities*, *Risks*, *Matrix* and *Objects* tables. Renumbering breaks references.
- **One process per major business area** — keep the catalog short so it stays readable. Most companies live with five to eight.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `PROCESS_APPS_ID` — application. | Application the catalog applies to. |
| **Process ID** | `PROCESS_ID` — short identifier. | Reference used by every dependent SoD setting. |
| **Process** | `PROCESS_NAME` — friendly label. | Human-readable name. |

Audit columns (`PROCESS_AUDIT_USER`, `PROCESS_AUDIT_DATE`) are kept on the row.

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

**Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it, titled **Edit · Settings - Process (SOD)**, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**. **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid itself.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application, picked from the list. |
| **Process ID** | Short code of the process (`OTC001`, `PTP001`…), referenced by every other SoD setting. |
| **Process** | Name of the process. |

The keys — Application ID and Process ID — are read-only once the row is saved: to change one, delete the row and add it again.

---

## Import from Excel \{#import\}

Many rows at once are added or changed with **Import**, from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — the easiest way is to **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back.

1. Pick what happens to **Existing rows**: **Update or insert** (the default), **Insert only** or **Update only**.
2. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
3. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Key — the application (its ID). |
| **Process ID** | Key — short code of the process (`P2P01`, `O2C01`…). |
| **Process** | Name of the process. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Per-application catalog.** If two applications carry the same SoD perimeter, declare the process in each — Nomasx-1 does not share rows across applications.
- **Match the auditor's vocabulary.** Use the labels (`P2P`, `O2C`, `R2R`, `HR`, `IT`) the audit team already uses in their walkthroughs.
- **Keep the list stable across audit cycles** — comparing the SoD figures quarter over quarter only works if the process IDs don't change.

---

## Nomasx-1 — SoD — Activities
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/sod/activities/

Named activities within each business process — the atomic units the segregation-of-duties matrix combines.

The **Activities** screen lists the named activities within each business process. One line per `(Application, Process, Activity)`. An activity is the *atomic unit* of the SoD analysis — for example *Create vendor*, *Approve payment*, *Post journal entry*.

The *Matrix* combines pairs of activities to express incompatibilities. The *Objects* screen attaches each activity to the source-system programs that back it.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Define the atomic actions** the SoD model reasons about.
- **Stable identifiers across audit cycles** — *Activity ID* feeds the matrix and the conflict reports.
- **One row per granular action.** Keep the activities tight: *Create vendor* and *Modify vendor* are different activities, not one combined entry.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `ACT_APPS_ID` — application. | The application the activity applies to. |
| **Process ID** | `ACT_PROCESS_ID` — links to *Process*. | The business process the activity belongs to. |
| **Activity ID** | `ACT_ID` — short identifier. | Reference used by *Matrix*, *Objects* and the *Conflicts* views. |
| **Activity** | `ACT_NAME` — friendly label. | Human-readable name. |

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

**Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it, titled **Edit · Settings - Activities (SOD)**, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**. **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid itself.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application, picked from the list. |
| **Process ID** | The process, picked among those of the application. |
| **Activity ID** | Short code of the activity (`OTC02`…), referenced by the matrix and the objects. |
| **Activity** | Name of the activity. |

The keys — Application ID, Process ID and Activity ID — are read-only once the row is saved: to change one, delete the row and add it again.

---

## Import from Excel \{#import\}

Many rows at once are added or changed with **Import**, from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — the easiest way is to **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back.

1. Pick what happens to **Existing rows**: **Update or insert** (the default), **Insert only** or **Update only**.
2. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
3. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Key — the application (its ID). |
| **Process ID** | Key — the process the activity belongs to. |
| **Activity ID** | Key — short code of the activity. |
| **Activity** | Name of the activity. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Name from the business angle.** Use verbs (*Create*, *Modify*, *Approve*, *Post*) — easier to discuss with the business owners than technical names.
- **Keep activity names stable.** Renaming breaks the comparison between SoD reports across cycles.
- **Group activity definitions per process.** Activities that span two processes typically point to a misclassification of either the activity or the process.

## Nomasx-1 — SoD — Risks
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/sod/risks/

Named risks within each business process, with the severity level used to weight the segregation-of-duties findings.

The **Risks** screen catalogs the named risks declared within each process. One line per `(Application, Process, Risk)`. Each row carries a friendly name and a severity level — the multiplier the *Matrix* uses to weight the conflicts in the dashboards.

Risks are the *what could go wrong* — *Approve a payment to a vendor you created yourself*, *Adjust the receivable on a customer you maintain*. Activities are the verbs; risks are the sentences.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Name the risks** the audit framework expects.
- **Weight the impact.** *Risk level* (`High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or a numeric scale) is the multiplier the dashboards apply to the conflict count.
- **One row per risk policy.** Avoid combining several risks into one row — the matrix reasons one risk at a time.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `RISK_APPS_ID` — application. | Application the risk applies to. |
| **Process ID** | `RISK_PROCESS_ID` — links to *Process*. | The business process the risk belongs to. |
| **Risk ID** | `RISK_ID` — identifier. | Reference used by *Matrix* and the *Conflicts* views. |
| **Risk** | `RISK_NAME` — descriptive label. | Human-readable name of the risk. |
| **Critical Level** | `RISK_LEVEL` — severity. | `High` / `Medium` / `Low` (or numeric scale) — drives weighting. |

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

**Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it, titled **Edit · Settings - Risks (SOD)**, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**. **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid itself.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application, picked from the list. |
| **Process ID** | The process, picked among those of the application. |
| **Risk ID** | Code of the risk (`OTCR05`…), referenced by the matrix. |
| **Risk** | Description of the risk, on several lines. |
| **Critical Level** | Level of the risk (`H`, `C`…): high and critical risks count as *High risk* in the [review](../../sod-review.md#tabs). |

The keys — Application ID, Process ID and Risk ID — are read-only once the row is saved: to change one, delete the row and add it again.

---

## Import from Excel \{#import\}

Many rows at once are added or changed with **Import**, from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — the easiest way is to **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back.

1. Pick what happens to **Existing rows**: **Update or insert** (the default), **Insert only** or **Update only**.
2. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
3. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Key — the application (its ID). |
| **Process ID** | Key — the process the risk belongs to. |
| **Risk ID** | Key — short code of the risk. |
| **Risk** | What the conflict allows a user to do. |
| **Critical Level** | How serious the risk is. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Write the risk in sentence form.** *Create vendor + Approve payment* is clearer than *VEN-PAY*. Auditors read the sentence, the code is for filtering.
- **Pick a consistent severity scale.** Use `High` / `Medium` / `Low` everywhere, or a numeric scale everywhere. Mixed scales make the dashboards hard to interpret.
- **High-severity risks should be few.** Marking everything `High` empties the signal — the matrix loses its prioritisation value.

## Nomasx-1 — SoD — Matrix
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/sod/matrix/

Pairs of incompatible activities — the SoD matrix that defines which activity combinations trigger which risk.

The **Matrix** screen lists the pairs of activities that produce an SoD risk. One line per `(Application, Process, Activity 1, Activity 2)`. Each row maps the pair to a *Risk* and a *Risk level* — the **rules engine** behind every conflict the *Conflicts* views surface.

This is the most operationally important SoD setting: editing a row here changes what every conflict screen computes from the next refresh.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Encode the SoD rule book** — every pair declared here generates a row in *Conflicts → Details* whenever a user holds the two activities.
- **Tie each pair to a named risk.** The *Risk* column is what auditors read; the *Risk level* drives weighting.
- **Maintain symmetrically.** `(A, B)` and `(B, A)` mean the same thing — declare one and let the engine traverse both ways.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `MATRIX_APPS_ID` — application. | The application the rule applies to. |
| **Process ID** | `MATRIX_PROCESS_ID` — process. | The business process. |
| **Activity 1 ID** | `MATRIX_ACT1_ID` — links to *Activities*. | First incompatible action. |
| **Activity 2 ID** | `MATRIX_ACT2_ID` — links to *Activities*. | Second incompatible action. |
| **Risk ID** | `MATRIX_RISK_ID` — links to *Risks*. | The named risk the pair instantiates. |
| **Risk Level** | `MATRIX_RISK_LEVEL` — severity. | Multiplier applied to the conflicts produced. |

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

**Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it, titled **Edit · Settings - Matrix (SOD)**, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**. **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid itself.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application, picked from the list. |
| **Process ID** | The process, picked among those of the application. |
| **Activity 1 ID** · **Activity 2 ID** | The two incompatible activities, picked among those of the process. |
| **Risk ID** | The risk the pair carries, picked among the risks of the process. It can be changed on a saved rule. |
| **Risk Level** | Level of the rule. |

The keys — Application ID, Process ID and the two activities — are read-only once the row is saved: to change one, delete the row and add it again.

---

## Import from Excel \{#import\}

Many rows at once are added or changed with **Import**, from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — the easiest way is to **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back.

1. Pick what happens to **Existing rows**: **Update or insert** (the default), **Insert only** or **Update only**.
2. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
3. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Key — the application (its ID). |
| **Process ID** | Key — the process. |
| **Activity 1 ID** | Key — first activity of the pair. |
| **Activity 2 ID** | Key — second activity of the pair. |
| **Risk ID** | The risk the pair raises. |
| **Risk Level** | Level of the pair. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **[What to fix](../../security-analysis.md#consistency) lists the rules that cannot work** — a risk or an activity missing.
- **Adding a row** generates new conflicts at the next SoD refresh — coordinate with the security administrator and HR.
- **Removing a row** clears existing conflicts at the next refresh. Document the rationale: an auditor reviewing the SoD framework will ask why.
- **Risk level here should match the *Risks* catalog level** — keeping the two in sync avoids confusing dashboard rendering.
- **A pair of activities with low business interaction** should not be a rule — keep the matrix to the conflicts that actually happen in practice.

---

## Nomasx-1 — SoD — Objects
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/sod/objects/

Source-system programs attached to each SoD activity — the technical objects whose execution counts as performing the activity.

The **Objects** screen attaches source-system programs to SoD activities. One line per `(Application, Process, Activity, Row, Object)`. Each row says: *running this object counts as performing this activity*. An activity typically maps to several objects — interactive forms, batch programs, the same program with different versions.

This is the bridge between the abstract SoD model and the concrete programs the source system runs.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Tell Nomasx-1 what counts as "doing" an activity.** Each row pins an SoD activity to a concrete source-system object.
- **Multiple rows per activity is normal.** *Row* numbers them — the engine considers any of them as evidence the activity was performed.
- **Source for *Conflicts → Proven*.** Without an object mapping the activity has no observable footprint, so the proven analysis cannot work.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `OBJECT_APPS_ID` — application. | The application. |
| **Process ID** | `OBJECT_PROCESS_ID` — process. | The SoD process. |
| **Activity ID** | `OBJECT_ACT_ID` — activity. | The activity the object backs. |
| **Object ID** | `OBJECT_ROW_ID` — sequence. | Stable identifier among the objects of the same activity. |
| **Object Code** | `OBJECT_ID` — technical object. | Program code (e.g. JDE `P0401`). |
| **Object Name** | `OBJECT_NAME` — friendly label. | Human-readable name of the program. |

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit-dialog\}

**Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it, titled **Edit · Settings - Objects (SOD)**, with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**. **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid itself.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application, picked from the list. |
| **Process ID** | The process, picked among those of the application. |
| **Activity ID** | The activity, picked among those of the process. |
| **Object ID** | Number of the object within the activity. Left empty, it is given by itself: the next free number of the activity. |
| **Object Code** | The program — `P4210`, `P0411`… — as named in the source application. |
| **Object Name** | Name of the program. |

The keys — Application ID, Process ID, Activity ID and Object ID — are read-only once the row is saved: to change one, delete the row and add it again.

---

## Import from Excel \{#import\}

Many rows at once are added or changed with **Import**, from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — the easiest way is to **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back.

1. Pick what happens to **Existing rows**: **Update or insert** (the default), **Insert only** or **Update only**.
2. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
3. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | Key — the application (its ID). |
| **Process ID** | Key — the process. |
| **Activity ID** | Key — the activity the object performs. |
| **Object ID** | Key — row number of the object in the activity. |
| **Object Code** | The program (`P04012`, `R04570`…). |
| **Object Name** | Its name. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **[What to fix](../../security-analysis.md#consistency) lists the objects JD Edwards does not have** — an object mistyped here never matches.
- **Map every program that touches the activity** — the *Proven* view depends on a complete mapping. Missing rows produce false negatives on the conflict analysis.
- **Re-check the mapping after a source-system patch** — new versions of a program (or a new alternative entry point) need to be added here.
- **Per-activity mappings should not overlap.** The same object on two different activities makes the model ambiguous.

## Nomasx-1 — Users properties
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/security/users-properties/

Per-user flags — technical, generic, linked, privileged — that drive licence calculations and audit filtering.

The **Users properties** screen carries the per-user flags Nomasx-1 uses to interpret usage data. One line per `(Application, User)`. Each row is the place to mark an account as *technical*, *generic*, *linked* to another login, *privileged*, or attached to a previous account.

These flags are read by *OUT — Users / Roles*, the *Licenses* reports and several account-hygiene views — they let the analysis distinguish a real human from a batch service account or a shared login.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

Tag each user account so downstream views can filter intelligently:

- **Technical accounts** — batch / service users. Excluded from headcount-based licence calculations.
- **Generic accounts** — shared logins. *Generic count* lets you state how many real people are behind it.
- **Privileged accounts** — flagged for special audit attention.
- **Linked / Previous accounts** — duplicate or successor relationships. *Linked User* and *Previous User* hold the reference to the primary login.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Application ID** | `USRP_APPS_ID` — application. | The application. |
| **User ID** | `USRP_ID` — user identifier. | The account being tagged. |
| **Technical (Y/N)** | `USRP_TECHNICAL` — `Y` / `N`. | Marks the account as a service / batch user. |
| **Generic (Y/N)** | `USRP_GENERIC` — `Y` / `N`. | Marks the account as shared by several people. |
| **Generic count** | `USRP_GENERIC_COUNT` — number. | How many real people share the generic account. |
| **Privileged (Y/N)** | `USRP_PRIVILEGED` — `Y` / `N`. | Marks the account as carrying elevated privileges. |
| **Is Linked (Y/N)** | `USRP_IS_LINKED` — `Y` / `N`. | Whether the account is declared as duplicate of another. |
| **Linked User ID** | `USRP_ID_LINKED` — login. | If linked, the primary login it points to. |
| **Is renamed (Y/N)** | `USRP_IS_PREVIOUS` — `Y` / `N`. | Whether the account is the successor of a previously used login. |
| **Previous User ID** | `USRP_ID_PREVIOUS` — login. | If marked, the previous login. |

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to flag an account, or click a row to open it; **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid and **Import** loads them from Excel. The form has two columns, each flag paired with its detail.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Application ID** | The application. Read-only on a saved line. |
| **User ID** | Picked from the application's users. Read-only on a saved line. |
| **Privileged (Y/N)** | Tick when the account carries elevated privileges. |
| **Technical (Y/N)** | Tick when the account is a service / batch user. |
| **Generic (Y/N)** | Tick when the account is a shared login. |
| **Generic count** | With *Generic*: number of real people behind the login. |
| **Is Linked (Y/N)** | Tick when the account is a duplicate of another login. |
| **Linked User ID** | With *Is Linked*: the primary login the account belongs to. |
| **Is renamed (Y/N)** | Tick when the account is the successor of a previous login. |
| **Previous User ID** | With *Is renamed*: the previous login. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Tag technical and generic accounts early.** Every untagged technical user pollutes the licence headcount.
- **Use *Linked* for duplicate pairs the *Duplicate users* screen surfaced as known-good.** Declared once, removed from the audit noise.
- **Privileged should be sparing.** Setting `Privileged = Y` is a deliberate audit signal — limit it to accounts that truly carry elevated rights.

## Nomasx-1 — Department
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/security/department/

Nomasx-1 Settings → Security → Department: the editable list of group / AD department pairs that groups the directory's departments for Users by applications, its Excel export and the read-only LDAP Settings view.

The **Department** screen (**Settings → Security → Department**) is where the `(Group, Department)` pairs are maintained: one line per pair, the group rolling one or several AD departments into one functional bucket. *Users by applications* and its Excel export only show the departments listed here, grouped as declared here.

It is intentionally simple — just the two text columns. The read-only [Security → LDAP → Settings](../../security/ldap/settings.md) screen shows the result: for each application, the AD departments found in the directory with the group they belong to here — an empty group means a department still to declare.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Master list of *(Group, Department)* pairs.** The only place where the grouping of AD departments is edited; *Security → LDAP → Settings* and *Users by applications* read it.
- **Keep the pairs aligned with the AD department attribute** so the *Users by applications* matrix matches correctly.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Group** | `LDAPD_GROUP` — text. | High-level functional bucket. |
| **Department** | `LDAPD_DEPARTEMENT` — text. | AD department value. Must match the `department` attribute on the LDAP entries. |

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to declare a new pair, or click a row to open it; **Bulk edit** changes several rows in the grid and **Import** loads them from Excel. The form holds the two fields.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Group** | Free text. The functional bucket that ties departments together. |
| **Department** | Free text. Must match the `department` attribute on an LDAP entry, character for character. |

Both fields can be changed on a saved line: saving moves the department to another group, or corrects its spelling.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Check *Security → LDAP → Settings* after a directory collection** — a department shown there with an empty group has no pair here yet, so it stays out of *Users by applications* and its export.
- **Validate the spelling against AD** — a mistyped department disappears from the LDAP join silently.
- **Remove pairs that are no longer in use** to keep the groups readable.
