## Nomasx-1 — System Code
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/jde/system-code/

Mapping of every JDE System Code to its functional module and to the licence component it falls under.

The **System Code** screen maps every JDE System Code (`SY`) to its functional module and to the licence component Nomasx-1 uses for usage / compliance reporting. One line per `SY`. This is the table behind the *Component* column of every OUT view.

Maintaining this mapping correctly is what makes the licence compliance analysis truthful.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Map JDE System Codes to functional modules.** The basis for the *Module* breakdown across the application.
- **Tie each `SY` to a licence component.** This is the only place where Nomasx-1 knows that a `P0411` (SY = 04) consumes the *Financials* licence.
- **Carry the E1 component label.** When Oracle ships its own component naming in JDE EnterpriseOne, the mapping keeps both perspectives readable.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | `SYC_ID` — JDE System Code. | The code (e.g. `04`, `42`, `08`). |
| **Description** | `SYC_DESCRIPTION` — text. | Friendly module description. |
| **Module E1** | `SYC_MODULE` — high-level grouping. | Functional area used in non-licence views. |
| **E1 Component** | `SYC_COMPONENT_E1` — JDE E1 component. | The component Oracle names inside JD Edwards EnterpriseOne. |
| **Component ID (ID)** · **Component ID** | `SYC_CPT_ID` — links to *Pricing → Components*. | The licence component of the code, by number and name. Empty: the code is not tied to a licence yet — it is listed all the same. |

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit\}

The grid is writable. **Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it; **Bulk edit** changes the rows in place, in the grid. The form, **Edit · Settings - System Code (JDE)** (**New · Settings - System Code (JDE)** on a new row), carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**; a new row has **Cancel** and **Save** only.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Code** | The system code. Read-only on a saved row. |
| **Description** | Friendly description of the module. |
| **Module E1** | Functional area. |
| **E1 Component** | The component as Oracle names it in JD Edwards EnterpriseOne. |
| **Component ID** | Picked from the licence components, by name. The module the [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md) counts the code's objects in. |

### Import from Excel \{#import\}

**Import** loads rows from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back. **Existing rows** says what to do with a row whose key is already there: **Update or insert** (the default: rows found are updated, the others added), **Insert only** or **Update only**.

1. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
2. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Code** | Key — the two-character JDE system code. |
| **Description** | Name of the module. |
| **Module E1** | Functional area. |
| **E1 Component** | Component as Oracle names it. |
| **Component ID** | Licence component the code counts against (from *Pricing → Components*). |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Bring this mapping in line with your contractual catalog**, not the bundled Oracle defaults. A licence renegotiation often introduces new component names — update them here.
- **Every new SY introduced by a JDE upgrade** must be classified here; otherwise it appears unmapped in the OUT views.
- **Audit changes** through the hidden `SYC_AUDIT_USER` / `SYC_AUDIT_DATE` columns — useful when explaining why a component count moved.

## Nomasx-1 — Reclassification
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/jde/reclassification/

Override of the JDE object → SY mapping when the default classification is wrong or missing.

The **Reclassification** screen overrides the default System Code that Nomasx-1 would otherwise apply to a JDE object. One line per object. Useful when the default SY of a program does not match its actual licence relevance — typically when a program is *technically* in `H9` but *commercially* in `Financials`.

Each row says: *for this object, use this `SY` instead of the default one*. The change propagates to every OUT view and licence report that resolves through *System Code*.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Override the SY** when JDE's own classification does not reflect the contractual reality.
- **Keep the override list short.** Every entry is an exception — too many overrides make the licence model hard to defend in audit.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Object** | `JDES_OBJECT` — technical object. | The program being reclassified. |
| **Description** | `JDES_DESCRIPTION` — friendly label. | What the program does. |
| **System Code** | `JDES_SY` — System Code. | The SY Nomasx-1 should use instead of the JDE default. |

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add row** to move a new object to another system code, or click a row to open it. **Import** loads a list from an Excel or `.csv` file. The dialog, **Edit · Settings - Reclassification (JDE)**, is a single form with **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Object** | JDE object name (e.g. `P0411Z1`). Read-only on a saved line: to reclassify another object, add a line. |
| **Description** | Friendly label of what the program does. |
| **System Code** | Picked from the list of system codes. The value Nomasx-1 uses instead of the object's own. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Document the rationale** of each override — a one-line description that a future auditor can read.
- **Re-validate the list after an Oracle upgrade.** JDE sometimes moves an object between system codes, retroactively making an override redundant.
- **Avoid systemic overrides** — if more than a handful of objects from the same module need reclassification, consider revisiting the mapping in *System Code* instead.

## Nomasx-1 — Prerequisite
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/jde/prerequisite/

Inter-component prerequisites — when buying component X requires having component Y.

The **Prerequisite** screen captures the contractual prerequisites between JDE licence components. One line per `(Component, Prerequisite)`. Each row says: *to use the component, the prerequisite component must also be licensed*.

It is the catalog of dependencies Nomasx-1 applies when computing the compliance: if you have rights to a component but not to its prerequisite, the matrix surfaces the missing prerequisite as a separate compliance gap.

## At a glance

## Goal of the view

| **Component** | `PRQ_COMPONENT` — component requiring the prerequisite. | The dependent component. |
| **Prerequisite** | `PRQ_PREREQ` — required component. | The component that must also be licensed. |

## Tips & best practices

- **Keep the rules in sync with Oracle's price book and supplemental terms** — both can introduce new prerequisites at renewal time.

## Nomasx-1 — Restrictions
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/jde/restrictions/

Mutually-exclusive components — when buying component X excludes the right to use component Y.

The **Restrictions** screen captures the mutual-exclusion rules between JDE licence components. One line per `(Component, Restriction)`. Each row says: *if the company subscribes to the component, it cannot also use the restricted component without re-licensing.*

This is the symmetric counterpart of *Prerequisite*: where prerequisites add requirements, restrictions remove options. Nomasx-1 surfaces a restriction breach as a compliance gap the same way it surfaces an over-consumption.

## Tips & best practices

### Import from Excel \{#import\}

**Import** loads rows from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back. **Existing rows** says what to do with a row whose key is already there: **Update or insert** (the default: rows found are updated, the others added), **Insert only** or **Update only**.

1. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
2. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Component ID** | Key — the licence component. |
| **Price List** | Oracle price list (JD Edwards, Technology…). |
| **Category** | Group of components. |
| **Component** | Name of the component. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Add a new component once and reference it widely.** Avoid creating per-application duplicates — the model is global.
- **Keep the *Price list* aligned with Oracle's price book** so that the catalog reads like the contracts.
- **Audit changes through `CPT_AUDIT_USER` / `CPT_AUDIT_DATE`** — useful when a column suddenly displays a different label.

---

## Nomasx-1 — Components included
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/pricing/components-included/

Nomasx-1 licence settings: the components a licence component includes — a contract line on it, alone or in a bundle, covers them too (Oracle Technology Foundation covers JD Edwards Core Tools and Infrastructure and Oracle Standard Edition 2).

The **Components included** screen lists what a licence component includes. A contract line on the component — alone or in a bundle — covers the components it includes too: the [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md) seats their users on that line instead of counting them on *a module no line covers*.

The screen is delivered with the case Oracle's price list states: **Oracle Technology Foundation for JD Edwards EnterpriseOne** includes **JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Core Tools and Infrastructure** and **Oracle Standard Edition 2**.

Access: **Settings → Licenses → Pricing → Components included**.

---

## At a glance

---

## How it is read \{#reading\}

- A line on a component covers itself **and** everything it includes; what an included component includes is followed too.
- The users of an included module take a seat on the line of the component that includes it. Beyond its quantity, they are **missing seats** on that module — no longer a module no line covers.
- On the *Usage* tab of the Licensing review, such a line says what it includes (*Application User · includes Core Tools and Infrastructure, Oracle Standard Edition 2*).

See [How a contract is counted](../../how-a-contract-is-counted.md#includes).

---

## Columns

| Column | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Component (ID)** · **Component** | The component a contract line names, by number and name. |
| **Includes (ID)** · **Includes** | A component it includes, by number and name. |

One row per component and component included.

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit\}

The grid is writable. **Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it; **Bulk edit** changes the rows in place. The form carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**; a new row has **Cancel** and **Save** only. The screen has no import.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Component** | Required. Picked from the licence components, by name: the one a contract line names. |
| **Includes** | Required. Picked from the licence components, by name: what that line covers too. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Only state what the price list says.** A component included by mistake hides the users of a module that is really missing from the contract.
- **Read the Licensing review again after a change.** The page reads the settings each time it opens.

## Nomasx-1 — Metrics
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/pricing/metrics/

Catalog of licensing metrics — Application User, Named User Plus, Processor, Employee, etc.

The **Metrics** screen is the short list of licensing metrics Nomasx-1 supports. One line per metric. Each row carries the metric identifier (referenced by the lines of the [contracts](../../licenses/csi.md) and by [Pricing](./pricing.md)) and its Oracle name.

The metric defines *how* a component is counted — by named user, by processor, by employee, by application user…. Changing a metric on a contract changes how compliance is computed.

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Declare the licensing metrics** the contracts use. Each metric is referenced by the lines of the contracts and by *Pricing*.
- **Short by design.** Most contracts use a handful: *Application User*, *Named User Plus*, *Processor*, *Employee*, *Enterprise $M*.

The form, **Edit · Settings - Licenses Metrics** (**New · Settings - Licenses Metrics** on a new row), carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**; a new row has **Cancel** and **Save** only.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **Metric ID** | The number of the metric. Read-only on a saved row. |
| **Metric** | The Oracle name of the metric. |

The [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md) counts a line after its metric number: 10 *Application User* and 40 *Named User Plus* in people (a count on a technology product), 20 *Processor*, 30 *Employee*, 80 *Enterprise $M*; any other metric is not counted (see [How a contract is counted](../../how-a-contract-is-counted.md#lines)). A metric added here is therefore listed, never compared.

## Tips & best practices

- **Keep the catalog minimal.** A handful of metrics is enough — invent more only when a contract actually requires it.
- **Always describe the metric** with the Oracle official label so the auditor can match it against the contract.

## Nomasx-1 — Pricing
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomasx1/settings/pricing/pricing/

Unit list price, minimum and support fee per component × metric — the price book the Nomasx-1 Licensing review uses to estimate the cost of missing seats, modules not covered and Named User Plus beyond the subscription.

The **Pricing** screen is the price book Nomasx-1 uses to estimate the financial risk. One line per `(Component, Metric)`. Each row carries the unit list price, the minimum quantity Oracle imposes on the metric, and the annual support fee.

The [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md#risk) prices each missing seat and each user of a module no line covers at the *Application User* price of the module plus three years of support, and the Named User Plus beyond a subscription at their own price; the *Minimum* gives the Named User Plus per processor (see [How a contract is counted](../../how-a-contract-is-counted.md#named)).

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

- **Price book input.** Per (Component × Metric), the unit list price and unit support fee.
- **Read by the [Licensing review](../../licensing-review.md#risk)** and the [licence audit report](../../reports/audit-licences.md): list price + 3 × support for each gap.
- **Audit traceability.** Changes to a row should be approved and audit-stamped.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **ID** | `PRC_ID` — internal identifier. | Number of the price line. |
| **Component ID (ID)** · **Component ID** | `PRC_CPT_ID` — the component, and its name. | The component being priced. |
| **Metric ID (ID)** · **Metric ID** | `PRC_MET_ID` — the metric, and its name. | The unit the price applies to. |
| **Price** | `PRC_PRICE` — list price. | Unit list price. |
| **Minimum** | `PRC_MINIMUM` — minimum quantity. | Oracle's minimum for the metric: the Named User Plus per processor (25 for the Enterprise Edition database). |
| **Support** | `PRC_SUPPORT` — yearly support fee. | Per-unit support cost — counted three years in the estimates. |

The *Price List*, *Category*, *Component* and *Metric* columns are hidden by default; **Columns** shows them.

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit\}

The grid is writable. **Add row** opens an empty form; a click on a row opens it; **Bulk edit** changes the rows in place, in the grid. The form, **Edit · Settings - Licences Pricing** (**New · Settings - Licences Pricing** on a new row), carries **Delete**, **Duplicate**, **Cancel** and **Save**; a new row has **Cancel** and **Save** only.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **ID** | Read-only. Left empty on a new line: the line takes the next number. |
| **Component ID** | Picked from the components, by name. Read-only on a saved row. |
| **Metric ID** | Picked from the metrics, by name. Read-only on a saved row. |
| **Price** | Unit list price. |
| **Minimum** | The minimum per processor, for a Named User Plus price. |
| **Support** | Yearly support fee per unit. |

### Import from Excel \{#import\}

**Import** loads rows from an Excel (`.xlsx`) or `.csv` file whose columns match the grid's — **Export** the grid, edit the file and import it back. **Existing rows** says what to do with a row whose key is already there: **Update or insert** (the default: rows found are updated, the others added), **Insert only** or **Update only**.

1. Drop the file in the dialog, then click **Check**: every row is checked against the screen's rules and the database, and each invalid row is listed with the reason.
2. **Save N valid rows** writes the valid rows; the invalid ones are left out.

The file carries these columns:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **ID** | Key — row number. |
| **Component ID** | Key — the licence component. |
| **Metric ID** | Key — the metric. |
| **Price** | Unit list price. |
| **Minimum** | Minimum quantity for the metric. |
| **Support** | Yearly support fee per unit. |

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Update the price book at renewal time** — Oracle ships a new technical price list every year. Keeping the numbers current is what makes the financial impact view trustworthy.
- **Remember the *Minimum*** — Oracle imposes a minimum (e.g. 25 NUP per processor on Database EE). The count of a database never goes below the minimum × its processors, whatever the number of users.
- **Cross-reference with [Subscribed licences](../../licenses/subscribed-licences.md)** to detect prices being applied to a metric the contract does not use.

## Nomajde — Platform synthesis
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/synthesis/

Platform synthesis in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform at a glance — six figures, one list of what the server, performance and database analyses flag, the most serious first, the architecture diagram, one tab per analysis, the platform's capacity and how its figures move, what could be improved in the architecture, and the Platform synthesis PDF. Read-only.

**Platform synthesis**, right under **Overview** in the Nomajde menu, puts the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform on one page: six figures, then **what needs attention** across the three analyses of the Monitoring folder — [Platform analysis](./monitoring/platform-analysis.md), [Performance](./monitoring/performance.md) and [Database audit](./monitoring/database-audit.md) — in one list, the most serious first, and the [architecture](./monitoring/architecture.md) as it is found. It is the page to open first when the question is "how is the platform doing?"; each tab leads to the full page behind it. Two more tabs look further: **Capacity** — the size of the platform and how its figures move — and **Improvements** — what could be improved in the architecture. **Get the report (PDF)** writes it all as a document to share.

Everything is read live the first time the page is opened; the page only reads. What it read is then kept while the browser session lasts: opening the page again draws it at once, and the header says when the oldest of its readings was made (*Read at 14:02*). **Read again** reads everything anew. The Monitoring pages — Platform synthesis, Architecture, Platform analysis, Performance and Database audit — share their readings: what one page has read, the others draw at once, and what one page reads again is fresh in the others. The readings are kept per user, in the browser's memory only: reloading the browser reads again. The history of the figures is what the *Platform snapshot* job keeps.

---

## At a glance

---

## The figures \{#figures\}

| Figure | What it counts |
|---|---|
| **Instances running** | The Server Manager instances running, out of all those it declares — amber when one is not running. |
| **Users online** | The users signed in to the web and AIS servers. |
| **Business function calls** | The calls the web servers have made to the enterprise servers since they started. |
| **Database size** | The size of the JD Edwards database, in GB. |
| **Not declared in Server Manager** | What the database side shows and Server Manager does not declare — a database server, a machine running kernels, another client of the database (see [Architecture](./monitoring/architecture.md#undeclared)). Amber when there is one. |
| **Points to review** | The lines of the **Attention** tab — red when one is to act on first, amber when there are only points to review, green when there is nothing. |

---

## The tabs \{#tabs\}

The page opens on the last tab chosen. Each tab names, in its description, how many points it has to review.

| Tab | Content |
|---|---|
| **Attention** | What the three analyses flag, in one list: **To act on first**, then **To review**. Each line names the analysis it comes from (*Servers*, *Performance*, *Database*), its area and the fact, worded as its own page words it. A fact flagged by two analyses on the same instance — zombie processes, for example — is given once. |
| **Architecture** | The [architecture diagram](./monitoring/architecture.md): the tiers, the hosts, the instances, the database and the lines drawn on evidence. A click on a card opens the full Architecture page. |
| **Servers** | What the [Platform analysis](./monitoring/platform-analysis.md) says: instances, processes, business functions, web and AIS nodes. |
| **Performance** | What the [Performance](./monitoring/performance.md) advice says: where the time goes. |
| **Database** | What the [Database audit](./monitoring/database-audit.md) says: size, space, activity. |
| **Capacity** | The size of the platform, and how its figures move — see [Capacity](#capacity). |
| **Improvements** | What could be improved in the architecture, each proposal with what it rests on and what to do — see [Improvements](#improvements). The tab's description counts the proposals *to plan*. |

The **Servers**, **Performance** and **Database** tabs list every line of their analysis — those to review and those that are fine — and **Open the full page** leads to the page with the figures, the details and the grids.

Every analysis is read on its own: one that fails or is slow does not hide the others. An analysis that did not answer is said in a warning (*Not read — Performance: …*) and the rest of the page is shown.

---

## Capacity \{#capacity\}

The **Capacity** tab says how large the platform is, how loaded it is, and how its figures moved. It reads in four blocks.

### The size of the platform

Read now: the **processors** of the database server with its cores, its **memory** and its load, the **database size**, and the batch volume — **batch jobs a day** on average over the days with jobs, **the busiest day**, **batch jobs in error** and **batch jobs waiting now**. The database server's figures are read from an Oracle, SQL Server or Db2 database (Db2 for i included), each from its own dictionary.

**Batch jobs per day** draws the jobs of the last 30 days, one bar per day, with the queues they went through. The batch figures come from JD Edwards' own job table (F986110, in the server map), which keeps its history: nothing has to be collected first. On SQL Server, the table is looked for in the databases the pool names. When the JD Edwards database is reached through a database link, the table is read through the link the pool names under the key `SVM` in its **Database links** (see [Connectors → Schema and DB-link tokens](../framework/connectors.md#schema-and-db-link-tokens)); when the pool names no `SVM` library, the table is looked for in the remote database's dictionary.

### The servers and their size

Every machine of the platform with what it carries (database, enterprise server, web server, AIS server…) and its processors, physical cores, memory and disk, as held by [Server sizes](./monitoring/server-sizes.md). Each figure is marked *stated*, *measured by the database* or *standard configuration*, and the heading counts how many machines rest on each. **State the sizes** opens Server sizes.

### The JD Edwards servers, in use now

As Server Manager measures them: the enterprise server's **processor** and **memory** in use, its **kernels running**, and the **Java heap** of the web and AIS instances against the maximum it may reach. Server Manager says what a server uses, not how large the machine is. **Open the full page** leads to [Platform analysis](./monitoring/platform-analysis.md).

### How the figures move

One small chart per figure kept by the snapshots — users online, sessions, business function response, timeouts, requests waiting, enterprise server processor and memory, kernels, Java heap, cache hits; the database's sessions, load, cache hits, blocked sessions and size; batch jobs of the day, in error and waiting, zombie processes, instances running — with its **lowest** and **highest** value. The heading says how many snapshots are kept and over which period.

The snapshots are written by the **Platform snapshot** job (hourly as shipped, off until it is turned on): one row per figure in the Nomajde database, kept 400 days by default. Without a snapshot the block says so; a trend needs at least two. **Open the job** opens it (see [Jobs](./jobs.md)).

---

## Improvements \{#improvements\}

The analyses flag what is wrong now. The **Improvements** tab reads the same material one level up — how the platform is built and how it is loaded — and words what a consultant would propose, drawn from the architecture, the figures read now and those the snapshots kept.

Each proposal gives **What it rests on** — the figures, to check — and **What to do**. They come in three groups, the most pressing first:

| Group | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Measured at its limit** | A Java heap near its maximum, an enterprise server's processor above 80 %, a database server whose load exceeds its processors — at the peak the snapshots kept, else as read now. |
| **To plan** | Everything on one machine, the database or the web tier sharing a machine, a single enterprise server for the users and the batch jobs, a single web instance, batch jobs that queue, a machine below Oracle's published minimum for what it carries, machines that act as enterprise servers and that Server Manager does not know. |
| **To know before a sizing** | No history of the figures yet (the peaks are not known), servers whose size is neither stated nor measured, a database that grows (with the yearly figure at the rate observed). |

### What was checked \{#checked\}

The block lists the fifteen checks with their outcome — **a proposal**, **nothing to propose**, or **not checked — not enough was read**: an absent proposal is never a silent one.

| Checks |
|---|
| Java heap of the web and AIS instances · Processor of the enterprise servers · Load of the database server · Batch jobs waiting · Machines against Oracle's minimum |
| Everything on one machine · The database on its own machine · Web and enterprise servers apart · More than one enterprise server · More than one web instance |
| More than one AIS instance · Servers Server Manager does not know · Growth of the database · History of the figures · Size of the servers |

---

## Get the report \{#report\}

**Get the report (PDF)**, at the top of the page, writes the Platform synthesis as a document for a reader who was not in front of the page, in the page's language: what needs attention, the architecture on a landscape page with each server's size and where each figure comes from, the capacity (the size of the platform, the batch jobs per day, how the figures moved) and what could be improved. The database sections take the words of the database read (*Data files*, *Transaction logs*, *Disk pools*, *Journals*…). A source that did not answer is named in the document.

The same document is on the **Reports** page (*JD Edwards platform synthesis*), with the language, the customer name written on the cover and **With the OCI estimate**: the [OCI target](./monitoring/oci-target.md) and its estimate are then added as a chapter, with their own choices (currency, licence, edition, high availability, recovery site, non-production platforms). The *Platform synthesis report* job sends it by mail every month (see [Jobs](./jobs.md)).

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry. It reads with the functions of the four Monitoring pages — `plugin:nomajde.architecture:*`, `plugin:nomajde.platform:*`, `plugin:nomajde.performance:*` and `plugin:nomajde.dbaudit:*` — and, for Capacity and Improvements, `plugin:nomajde.capacity:*`, `plugin:nomajde.sizing:*` and `plugin:nomajde.proposals:*`: a role that lacks one sees that tab not read. The PDF needs the right to run the application's reports. The predefined roles **Platform operator** and **Administrator** hold them all (see [Predefined roles](./overview.md#roles)).

It reads Server Manager through the `jde_server_manager` pool (see [Server Manager](./monitoring/server-manager.md#connection)) and the JD Edwards database.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Start with **Attention**: a red line is where users wait now; the amber ones are tuning.
- After a restart of the servers the counters start from zero: read the page again once the platform has worked for a while.
- To prepare a meeting or an audit, **Get the report** gives the whole synthesis as a PDF; the **Architecture** tab gives the picture and the Architecture page saves it as SVG.
- Turn on the *Platform snapshot* job early: **Capacity** and **Improvements** read peaks only once a week or more of snapshots is kept.
- State the server sizes before reading **Improvements**: a machine on the standard configuration is a proposal *to know before a sizing*, not a fact.
- The assistant knows what the page shows — the figures and the points to act on first: ask it *JD Edwards is slow: where should I look first?* (see [AI assistant](./ai-assistant.md)).

## Nomajde — Prepare for upgrade
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/upgrade/analysis/

The Prepare for upgrade page of Nomajde: load the object list Oracle publishes for a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne release or update, run the analysis of a path code, and follow on one page what has to be retrofitted, how complex it is, how many days it takes, in which order, who does it and how far it is — with the dependencies, the user defined objects to test again, the objects left in other path codes and Oracle's list.

**Prepare for upgrade**, right under **Platform synthesis** in the Nomajde menu, answers the first question of a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne upgrade or update: **what has to be retrofitted, and for how many days?** Nomajde reads the customer's objects of a path code, compares them with the list of objects Oracle changed in the target release, and gives each object a kind, a retrofit decision, a complexity and a number of days. Everything then sits on one page: the work and the progress in figures, where the work is (type, complexity, status, person), in which order to do it, and five tabs — **Overview**, **Objects**, **User defined objects**, **Other path codes**, **Oracle's list**. JD Edwards is only read; the analysis and the planning are kept in Nomajde's own database.

---

## At a glance

---

## The page \{#page\}

The heading names the path code, the list it is compared with and the date of the analysis. When several path codes were analysed, a list next to the buttons switches from one to the other.

| Button | Does |
|---|---|
| **Load Oracle's list** | Opens the [job that loads Oracle's object list](#load). |
| **Run the analysis** | Opens the [analysis job](#build), the path code and the list already filled in. |
| **Weekly report (PDF)** | Downloads the [weekly report](#weekly-report) of the path code shown, in the language of the page. |
| **Read again** | Reads the page again — after a run, or after a colleague changed the planning. |

The two job buttons show only to the users who may run their job; **Weekly report (PDF)** shows once an analysis exists. Before the first analysis, the page says so and points to the two steps.

### The figures \{#figures\}

Seven figures sit above the tabs; a click on one opens the list it counts.

| Figure | Counts |
|---|---|
| **to retrofit** | The objects Oracle's list makes the customer retrofit, out of all the customer's objects of the path code. |
| **days left** | The days of the objects still to do, out of the days of the whole work. |
| **% done** | The share of the days done, and the number of objects done. |
| **ready to start** | The objects not yet done whose dependencies are all done or dropped: nothing they wait for is left. |
| **no use recorded** | The applications and reports to retrofit that object usage tracking and the submitted jobs show unused, with the days they represent. A dash when no usage is known for the analysis. |
| **UDOs of yours to test** | The customer's user defined objects that sit on, show, open, run or read an object the upgrade touches. |
| **in other path codes only** | The customer's objects found in another path code but not in this one. |

A status **Done** counts as done; **Dropped** takes the object out of the work — its days show apart on the progress bar.

---

## Overview \{#overview\}

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **Progress** | The days done, left and dropped on one bar, with the number of objects of each. |
| **Where the work is** | The objects and days **By type of object**, **By complexity**, **By status**, **By person**. Each bar shows in green what is done; a click on a bar opens the **Objects** tab filtered on it. |
| **In which order** | The waves. An object waits for the objects it uses that are to retrofit too; wave 1 waits for nothing, wave 2 only for wave 1, and so on. Objects that wait for each other go together in the same wave. A click on a wave filters the objects. |
| **Start with** | The objects ready now, the ones the most other objects wait for first. |
| **No use recorded** | The applications and reports to retrofit with no use recorded, the largest first: to question before retrofitting them. |
| **User defined objects** | The customer's UDOs to test again, by type, and the number delivered by Oracle; a line opens the [User defined objects](#udos) tab. |

A line of **Start with** or **No use recorded** opens the [object window](#object).

The waves need the links between the customer's objects. When none is known, **In which order** says so: collect the cross reference in Nomasx-1, then run the analysis again.

---

## Objects \{#objects\}

The **Objects** tab is the working list, in the shared grid: search, filters, grouping, columns, saved views and export. The chips above it choose the objects shown:

| Chip | Keeps |
|---|---|
| **To retrofit** | The objects to retrofit (the default). |
| **Ready** | The objects ready to start. |
| **No use recorded** | The applications and reports to retrofit, still to do, with no use recorded. |
| **Not assigned** | The objects to retrofit, still to do, assigned to no one. |
| **All** | Every customer object of the path code, retrofit or not. |

A filter set from the overview shows as a chip of its own, with **✕** to clear it.

| Columns | Content |
|---|---|
| **Object**, **Description**, **Type**, **Kind** | The object as the Object Librarian knows it, and its [kind](#rules). |
| **Complexity**, **Days**, **Wave** | The result of the analysis and the wave of the object. |
| **Status**, **Assigned to**, **Module**, **Finish** | The planning. |
| **Waits for**, **Blocks**, **Uses**, **Used by** | The names of the objects it waits for, of those that wait for it, of those it uses and of those that use it. |
| **Oracle changed it**, **Last used**, **UDOs** | The date of the object — or of its original — in Oracle's list, its last known use, the number of user defined objects on it. |

**›**, at the start of a row, opens it on its dependencies: **Waits for**, **Wait for it**, **Uses** and **Used by**, each object with its type, its description and, when it is to retrofit, its status. A click on a name opens that object. The four lists are columns of the grid, so the export carries them.

### The object window \{#object\}

A click on a row opens the object in a window, over the list.

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | The type, the kind, who changed it last and when; for a copy, its original, [how it was found](#original) and the other objects it could be a copy of (*could also be*). |
| **To retrofit** / **No retrofit** | The complexity, the days, the wave, the date Oracle changed it. |
| **Last used** | The last use and the number of users — or *no use recorded*. |
| **Waits for**, **Wait for it**, **Uses**, **Used by** | Links: a click opens that object in the same window. |
| **User defined objects on it** | The UDOs on the object: name, type and, when not delivered by Oracle, the user who created it. |
| **Planning** | **Status** (To do, In progress, To test, Done, Dropped), **Assigned to**, **Start**, **Finish**, **Module**, **Complexity (yours)**, **Days (yours)**, **Copy of (your choice)** — for an object that is not a changed standard object nor an audit table —, **Note**. |

**Save** writes the planning; the page is then read again. The planning survives every new analysis. A complexity typed in **Complexity (yours)** replaces the computed one, days typed in **Days (yours)** replace the computed days, and an object named in **Copy of (your choice)** becomes the copy's original — all three are applied by the next analysis. A user without the right to change the planning sees the fields greyed, with a line that says so.

---

## User defined objects \{#udos\}

The **User defined objects** tab lists the UDOs — queries, grid formats, watchlists, personal forms, form extensions, E1 pages, composite pages, One View reports, CafeOne layouts, orchestrations, service requests, notifications… — that sit on, show, open, run or read an object the upgrade touches: one of the customer's objects of the analysis, or a standard object Oracle changes in the release.

| Chip | Keeps |
|---|---|
| **Yours** | The UDOs the customer created (the default). |
| **On your objects** | The UDOs on one of the customer's objects of the analysis, whoever created them. |
| **All** | Every UDO listed, those delivered by Oracle included. |

| Columns | Content |
|---|---|
| **Why** | **Updated by Oracle**, or **Your object** (custom, copied or modified). |
| **Object**, **Type**, **Form**, **Version** | Where the UDO sits. |
| **How** | Sits on it, shows it, opens it, runs it, reads it, writes it, names it in its code. |
| **UDO type**, **Name**, **UDO** | The UDO itself and its identifier. |
| **Created by**, **Owner**, **Status** | The user in the UDO's identifier — `JDE` for one Oracle delivers —, its owner, its status (**Shared** for a shared UDO). |
| **Oracle changed it** | The date of the object in Oracle's list. |

A click on a row opens the object it sits on, when that object is in the analysis. The list is the shared grid: search, filters and export to hand the test campaign over.

---

## Other path codes \{#other-path-codes\}

The **Other path codes** tab lists the customer's objects found in another path code but not in the one analysed: work that never reached it, to promote or to delete before the upgrade. Columns: **Object**, **Description**, **Type**, **Found in**, **Merge flag**, **What to do**.

---

## Oracle's list \{#oracle-list\}

The **Oracle's list** tab shows the objects Oracle changes, as loaded from its file. One chip per loaded list, with its number of objects; the list of the analysis is chosen first. Columns: **Object**, **Version**, **Description**, **System code**, **Changed on**, **Yours** — the kind of the object when it is in the customer's analysis — and **As written in the file**. A click on one of the customer's objects opens its window.

---

## Weekly upgrade report \{#weekly-report\}

**Weekly report (PDF)** downloads a document for the steering meeting — **not the list of the objects**, which the page already gives, but what moved and what comes next:

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| **Where the work stands** | Four figures — progress, objects done, days remaining, ready to start —, the objects to retrofit and their days, what is done and dropped; what moved since the last report kept; and a forecast: at the pace of the last four weeks, when the remaining days end. |
| **This week** | The objects finished and started over the last seven days, by the dates and statuses typed in the planning, then the objects in progress. |
| **What comes next** | The objects **late** (their finish date has passed), those **due** in the coming days, and those **ready to start** — the ones that unblock the most first; the objects still to do that nobody carries. |
| **Who carries what** | Per person, then per module: the objects, the days, what is done, the days remaining. |
| **The remaining work, week after week** | A chart of the days remaining and the days done, from the figures each report keeps. |
| **What could be left out** | The applications and reports to retrofit that no user ran, and the days they represent. |

Each list stops at twenty lines and counts the rest. The forecast and "what moved" need figures kept from one week to the next: the job [Weekly upgrade report](../jobs.md#report-upgrade) keeps them each time it runs, then mails the document to the developers every Monday. The cover can carry the customer's name when the job makes it.

---

## The two steps \{#steps\}

### 1. Load Oracle's object list \{#load\}

**Load Oracle's list** opens the job that takes the Excel file Oracle publishes for a release or an update — columns *Object*, *Version*, *Description*, *System Code*, *Date* — and stores it under the name given in **Name of the list (UN9)**. Loading a list again under the same name replaces it. The loaded lists show in the [Oracle's list](#oracle-list) tab.

Load two lists when the platform already runs an update: the target one (`UN9`) and the one in place (`UN2`).

### 2. Run the analysis \{#build\}

**Run the analysis** opens the job that reads JD Edwards and writes the result, with the path code and the list of the analysis already filled in.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Path code the upgrade starts from** | `PD920` | The path code whose objects are analysed. |
| **Object list to compare with (its name; blank = none)** | blank | The target list. Without one, no object is marked as changed by Oracle. |
| **Object list the customer already runs** | blank | Optional. With it, only what Oracle changed **after** that list counts. |
| **Central objects schema, when not the pool's (PD920)** | blank | The schema of the central objects when it differs from the one of the connection. |
| **JDE of nomasx1 to read: usage kept, cross reference, UDOs (blank: the only one)** | blank | The JD Edwards whose usage history, cross reference and user defined objects are read, when Nomasx-1 collects several. |

The run collects, for the path code: the objects added or changed by the customer in the Object Librarian, the original of each copy, what is really used (object usage tracking and the history of submitted jobs), and the cross reference between the customer's objects. It can be run again at any time: the planning typed on the page is kept.

The run also reads what Nomasx-1 collects for the same JD Edwards, when it does:

- **the links between the customer's objects** — event rules calling a business function, reading or writing a table or a view, opening another application's form, launching a report; a view's tables; a function's or a form's data structure. JD Edwards' own cross reference is often not built: without these links, **Waits for**, **Uses**, **Used by** and the waves stay empty;
- **the usage kept over time** — the latest use known by JD Edwards' tracking, by the submitted jobs and by the history Nomasx-1 keeps, which reaches further back than JD Edwards' purged table;
- **the user defined objects** that sit on, show, open, run or read an object the upgrade touches (see [User defined objects](#udos)).

These need the cross reference and its UDO step collected first in Nomasx-1; run the analysis again to take them.

#### A JD Edwards behind a database link \{#dblink\}

When Liberty reaches the JD Edwards libraries through a database link, the run follows the JD Edwards pool: each table is read with its library from the pool's **Schemas** and that library's link from its **Database links**, under the same key — `OL` for the Object Librarian, `SY` for the usage tables, `CO` for JD Edwards' own cross reference. A library with no link is read locally. The run's log says which library and which link it reads. See [Schema and DB-link tokens](../../framework/connectors.md#schema-and-db-link-tokens).

---

## How an object is judged \{#rules\}

| Kind | When | Retrofit |
|---|---|---|
| **Audit Trail** | An audit table of the database audit. | No — complexity `Configuration`, 0 day. |
| **Custom** | An object created by the customer, with no JD Edwards original. | No — `Retrofit not needed`. |
| **Copied** | A copy of a standard object: its original is found as [said below](#original). | Yes when Oracle changed **the original** in the list. |
| **Modified** | A standard object changed by the customer. | Yes when Oracle changed it in the list. |

An object Oracle did not change is `Not updated`: nothing to retrofit. For the others, the complexity and the days follow the object type:

| Object type | Complexity | Days |
|---|---|---|
| Applications, reports | `Hard` | 3 |
| Business functions | `Medium` | 1 |
| Everything else | `Easy` | 0.5 |

### How the original of a copy is found \{#original\}

A copy has to be retrofitted when Oracle changes its original, but nothing in JD Edwards says "this object is a copy of that one". The analysis looks for the original the ways a consultant does, the most reliable first, among the standard objects **of the same type**:

| Order | Found by | How |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Your choice** | The object named in **Copy of (your choice)** — in the [object window](#object), or in the column of the same name on the screen *Upgrade — objects to retrofit* (opened from the Data Explorer model *Upgrade analysis*), where a customer's list can be pasted into the grid. |
| 2 | **Its application id** | The application id the copy kept from its original. |
| 3 | **Its name** | The name without the customer's system code: `P554210` is `P4210`, `R5543500` is `R43500`. |
| 4 | **Its description** | The same description as exactly one standard object of its type — a description too short to mean anything is not used. |

Only an object the customer added can be a copy. The object window says how its original was found — *your choice*, *found by its application id*, *found by its name*, *found by its description* — and, when several objects were met, which others it could be (*could also be*). A choice typed or pasted is applied by the next run of the analysis.

---

## Summaries \{#summaries\}

The [Data Explorer](../data-explorer.md) model **Upgrade analysis** gives the totals, with four saved analyses: *Retrofit by complexity and object type*, *Days of retrofit by complexity and object type*, *Days of retrofit by assignee and module*, *The customer's objects by kind*. The Nomajde [Overview](../home.md) leads here from its *Prepare for upgrade* group.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry, with the permissions `page:nomajde:upgrade` and `plugin:nomajde.upgrade_view:*`. Saving the planning needs `sql:nomajde:jde_upg_object_put`; the two job buttons need the `job:` permission of their job, and the weekly report the right to run Nomajde's reports, which the **Developer** and **Administrator** roles hold. The connection used to read JD Edwards needs read access to the Object Librarian tables of the central objects.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Load the list **already in place** as well: without it every object Oracle ever touched counts, and the estimate is too high.
- Plan by wave: start with **Ready**, the objects of **Start with** first — the most other objects wait for them.
- Look at **No use recorded** before estimating: a modified report nobody has run for three years is a decision to take, not three days to plan. Set it to **Dropped** once decided.
- The days are a first estimate by object type; correct them in **Days (yours)** for the objects the team knows.
- Before the tests, export the **User defined objects** tab on **Yours**: each line is a screen to check again after the upgrade.
- Collect the cross reference in Nomasx-1 before running the analysis: the waves, **Waits for** and the UDOs depend on it.
- Export the **Objects** tab to share the plan: the dependencies travel as columns.
- Send the **Weekly report (PDF)** rather than the export to a steering meeting: it says what moved, what is late and when the work should end.
- When a copy's original is wrong or missing, name it in **Copy of (your choice)**: the next analysis uses it first. The objects found only by their description deserve a look.
- The AI assistant knows the procedure: ask it to *prepare an upgrade* and it runs the two jobs and reads the result with you. It also knows the tab, the filter and the object open on the page: *Which objects can be started now?* — see [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md).

## Nomajde — Data Explorer
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/data-explorer/

Free analysis of the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne security, development and upgrade data in the Nomajde Data Explorer: the Security, Development and Upgrade analysis models, their shipped analyses and dashboard, the models shipped by the JDE presets, and the data dictionary labels.

**Data Explorer**, right under **Overview** in the Nomajde menu, opens the explorer on the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne data: rows, measures, filters and a period picked from a list of fields, shown as a table, a pivot, a chart or a KPI, then saved, shared, gathered into a dashboard and exported. The figures are read live from JD Edwards, under the user's rights.

How the explorer works is described in the [Liberty Next documentation](../framework/explorer/analysis.md). This page lists what Nomajde ships.

---

## Security \{#security\}

The users (F0092) with their address book name, their role relationships (F95921) and roles (F00926), their security records (F00950) and UDO security (F00950W), their environments (F0093).

**Analyses**: *Users*, *Users by type*, *Users by language*, *Users with the most roles*, *Users per role*, *Security records by type*, *Secured objects per user or role*, *Environments per user*.

**Dashboard** *Security overview*: users by type, the roles with the most members, the users with the most roles, the security records by type.

---

## Development \{#development\}

The Object Librarian (F9860): the objects per type and per product code.

**Analyses**: *Objects by type*, *Objects by product code*.

---

## Upgrade analysis \{#upgrade\}

The objects of the [upgrade analysis](./upgrade/analysis.md): kind, retrofit, complexity, days, module, assignee, status, usage.

**Analyses**: *Retrofit by complexity and object type*, *Days of retrofit by complexity and object type*, *Days of retrofit by assignee and module*, *The customer's objects by kind*.

## Models shipped by the JDE presets \{#presets\}

Nomajde also ships **eighteen models on the JD Edwards modules** — those of the JD Edwards presets of the [Screen Assistant](../framework/build/screen-assistant.md), built from the Oracle E1 data models: the hub table with the tables joined to it.

| Area | Models |
|---|---|
| Address Book | Address Book — full entry (master, contacts, customer, supplier). |
| General Accounting | Account Ledger (F0911), Account Balances (F0902). |
| Accounts Payable | A/P Ledger (F0411), Payments (F0413). |
| Accounts Receivable | Customer Ledger (F03B11), Receipts (F03B13). |
| Inventory | Item (F4101). |
| Sales | Sales Order (F4201), Sales History (F42019 + F42119). |
| Procurement | Purchase Order (F4311, one row per order line), Receipts (F43121, one row per receipt or match), Receipt Routing (F43092, one row per routing step: dock, inspection, transfer, stock). |
| Manufacturing | Work Order (F4801), Production Cost (F3102). |
| Product Data Management | Bill of Material (F3002), Routing (F3003). |
| Product Costing | Item Cost Components (F30026). |

They appear in the model picker with the others, grouped by area (*JDE · Accounts Payable*, *JDE · Sales*…); the page header says *shipped by the preset “…”*. They are real models: in the Explorer builder (**Liberty Next → Insight → Explorer**) a superuser opens one and changes it like a model made by hand — its entities on the real columns of the tables, its hub, its relations. Their fields carry the labels of the JD Edwards data dictionary from the start (in English, the language of the data dictionary).

JD Edwards amounts are shown in real units: the data dictionary's decimals apply in the tables, the totals and the filters.

## Labels from the data dictionary \{#dictionary\}

A column without a dictionary entry shows its raw column name. A superuser sees on the explorer page how many columns are in that case, and **Create the entries from the data dictionary** fills them from the JD Edwards data dictionary (description, type, decimals, UDC lookup) in one click. The [dictionary refresh job](./jobs.md#dictionary) does the same for every model, or for one.

On the explorer page, the assistant offers to create what the user describes: *Create an analysis of the users per role*, *Create a dashboard with the analyses of this model*. It builds the analysis on the model, checks it by running it, and saves it — private unless the user asks to share it. See [AI assistant](../framework/ai-assistant.md#tools).

A model is offered to the holders of a role that grants it (**Data Explorer** in the role's *Beyond the menus* rules). The row-level scope of the user's roles applies inside every analysis.

## Nomajde — Cross Reference
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/cross-reference/

The Nomajde Cross Reference page: one search over the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne specifications — applications, reports, data items, business views, tables, data structures, business functions, user defined objects — to see what an object holds and where it is used, with its last use, its event rules and its UDOs.

**Cross Reference**, right under **Data Explorer** in the Nomajde menu, answers the two questions every JD Edwards change starts with: **what is in this object**, and **where is it used**. One search box finds an application, a report, a data item, a business view, a table, a data structure, a business function or a user defined object; the page then opens on what the object holds, and a click on **Where used** switches to the other question.

The page reads the cross reference collected from the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne specifications — forms, report sections, event rules, views, tables, data structures, business functions, user defined objects — and the object usage kept over time. It is read-only: nothing is written to JD Edwards.

---

## At a glance

---

## Search \{#search\}

Type part of a name, an identifier or a description; the examples under the search box start one in a click: `P01012`, `P4210`, `R42565`, `AN8`, `V0101E`, `F0101`, `F4211`, `D0100033`, `B4200310`, `F4211FSBeginDoc`, *address number*, *sales order*. The results are grouped by kind — **Applications**, **Reports**, **Data items**, **Business views**, **Tables**, **Data structures**, **Business functions**, **User defined objects** — each line with its description from the Object Librarian. A click opens the object on the right. The search starts about half a second after the last letter typed: a word typed at normal speed starts one search, not one per letter.

The closest match comes first: an identifier typed exactly, then — for the applications and the reports — the object whose title is exactly what was typed, before those whose title only starts with it. Typing *address book* opens on `P01012` *Address Book*, ahead of the twenty applications whose title begins with those words.

A user defined object is found by any part of its identifier, its name or its description; its line says its type and the application, form and version it sits on.

### List a whole kind \{#browse\}

The chips under the search box — **Everything**, **Applications**, **Reports**, **Views**, **Tables**, **Data structures**, **Functions**, **UDOs** — list every object of that kind in the left column, sorted by identifier, with the total: the first 300, then a line says how many there are. With a kind chosen, the search box becomes **Narrow the list…**: what is typed narrows that kind only — the identifiers that start with it, the titles that contain it. **Everything** returns to the search over all kinds. A UDO line shows its name, its identifier and its type.

---

## What is in it \{#content\}

| Object | Opens on |
|---|---|
| **Application** | Its forms as cards two lines high: the identifier and the title, then the business view and the counts of fields, grid columns, buttons and exits, UDOs — the whole of it on hover. At most three rows of cards show; more scroll inside their block, so the grid under them keeps its room. A form the application calls from outside is tagged **entry point**. A form's tabs: **Fields**, **Grid columns**, **Buttons and exits**, **Everything**, **Event rules**, **Interconnection** (the data items a caller hands it) and **UDOs** (the user defined objects that sit on it, the service requests that run it, the pages and links that open it). |
| **Report** | Its sections as cards, laid out as the forms (kind, business view, counts), and in a section its **Fields**, **Labels**, **Data selection**, **Data sequencing** — in their rank, ascending or descending —, **Everything** and **Event rules**. |
| **Business view** | The tables it reads (the primary one first), its columns, its **Joins** as cards, laid out as the forms — which two tables, the join type, the columns they are joined on. |
| **Table** | Who uses it, then its **Columns** (data item and SQL name, in order), its **Indexes** (primary, unique, their columns) and its **Triggers**. |
| **Data structure** | Its items in their order, and the business functions that take it. |
| **Business function object** | Its functions, each with its data structure and its module; **Where called** lists the objects whose event rules call a function, and where in each. |
| **User defined object** | What it is — type, system code, owner, status, who changed it and when — and the **objects it uses**, each line with **How** it uses it and **Where in the page**: see [User defined objects](#udo). The **Objects that carry it** list the pages, orchestrations or other UDOs that hold this one. |

A control the form gives no text to shows the data dictionary's title **in grey**: it is what JD Edwards displays. The texts of a form — its title, its labels, its column headings — are those of JD Edwards' base language, as the reports' texts are: a text that exists only as a translation is not shown, and the data dictionary's title stands in its place. The texts are taken when an application is read: to bring them up to date, read the applications again — the job `nomasx1-xref` with **What to read** = `all`, or **Refresh from JDE** on one application. The **Event rules** tab lists what the rules of a form, a section or a function do — the business functions they call, the tables and views they read and write with the operations, the forms they open, the reports they run.

Every list is a grid of its own: search, filters, grouping, columns and export.

:::info[Behind a database link]

When the JD Edwards database is reached through a database link, the data dictionary's titles (F9202) are read through the link the JD Edwards pool names under the key `DD` in its **Database links** — see [Schema and DB-link tokens](../framework/connectors.md#schema-and-db-link-tokens). No link for `DD`: the table is read locally.

:::

### User defined objects \{#udo\}

A user defined object opens on what it names, and each line leads on — to the application (on its form), the report, the table, the view, the data item or the other UDO.

| UDO type | What it uses |
|---|---|
| **Composite page** | The applications and reports its tiles open, the forms shown in its panes, the task of a task tile, the menu of a landing page, the watchlists, queries, personal forms and other pages it carries — each with where in the page. |
| **E1 page** | The applications and reports its code calls or names — for a page built with HTML and JavaScript as for a classic one. |
| **Orchestration** | Its steps — service requests, rules, cross references, white lists, other orchestrations, notifications — and its schedule. |
| **Service request** | The forms it runs (application, form, version), the tables and views its data requests read, the reports it launches, the orchestration a connector calls, the form a message links to. |
| **Notification** | Its orchestration, rule, watchlist and schedule, and the forms its links open. |
| **CafeOne layout**, **One View report** | The forms it shows, the forms its links open. |
| **Search**, **Process** | What it reads and the forms it opens; what a process depends on and the table it reads. |
| **Form extension** | The columns it adds: the data item and its table. |
| **Watchlist** | Its query. |
| **Query**, **Grid format**, **Personal form** | The application, form and version it sits on. |

A rule, a cross reference, a white list, a schedule and an image name no object, and the page says so; a logic extension is not read. When the content of a type has not been collected yet, the page says to run the UDO step of the cross-reference job.

In the other direction, a form's **UDOs** tab lists the UDOs that sit on it, the service requests that run it and the pages and links that show or open it; a table, a view and a data item have a **UDOs** tab too — the data requests and searches that read them, the form extensions that add them.

---

## Where is it used \{#where-used\}

**Where used**, on a line of a list, opens the data item, the view or the table on its usages.

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **Tabs** | One per kind of user: **Applications**, **Reports**, **Business views**, **Tables**, **Data structures**, **Event rules**, **UDOs** (the data requests, searches and form extensions that read or add the object) — and, for a table, its own **Columns**, **Indexes** and **Triggers**. |
| **Totals** | In how many applications, forms and places the object is used, and as what: a field, a grid column, a label. |
| **Only the customer's own objects (55 to 59)** | Keeps the objects of the customer's system codes. |
| **Only the applications of the upgrade analysis** | Keeps the objects the [upgrade analysis](./upgrade/analysis.md) holds: the impact view of an upgrade. |
| **The list** | The applications or reports ranked by places; a click opens one. |

**Back to …**, at the top, returns to where the search came from — same object, same form or section, same tab.

---

## Who uses it \{#usage\}

An application and a report say in their heading **Last used … · n user(s)**, or **Not used since …** — the first day the history knows. A click opens **Who uses it**: each user and version with their last use. The figures come from JD Edwards' object usage tracking, as collected over time: they reach further back than JD Edwards' own table, which is purged. Nothing is shown when no usage was ever collected for that JD Edwards.

---

## Actions \{#actions\}

| Button | Does |
|---|---|
| **Create its endpoints…** | On an application: opens [Create from…](./ais/create-from.md) of the AIS connector on it, to build the endpoints and the screen that read and save its records. |
| **Refresh from JDE** | Reads the object again from the JD Edwards specifications — a job of a few seconds that runs in a window on the page; the page then shows the new content without leaving the object. |

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry; the functions it reads need the permissions `plugin:nomajde.xref:*`. **Refresh from JDE** needs the right to run the job that reads one object again.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Before changing a table or a business view, open it and read the **Applications** and **Reports** tabs with **Only the customer's own objects** ticked: that is the list of what to test.
- During an upgrade, tick **Only the applications of the upgrade analysis** to see what a change of Oracle reaches in the customer's code.
- Look at **Who uses it** before retrofitting a modified report: nobody may have run it for years.
- A form's **UDOs** tab lists what the users built on it — queries, grid formats, personal forms, form extensions, the pages and service requests that open it: what to check again when the form changes with a release.
- The assistant knows the object open on the page: ask it *Where is this object used?* or *What would a change to the table F0101 touch?* — see [AI assistant](./ai-assistant.md).
- To review the user defined objects one by one, choose the **UDOs** chip: each line gives the type, and a word of the name narrows the list.
