## Nomajde — User Management
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/user-management/

Add, edit and provision JD Edwards users from a single grid — SQL writes the user master and display preferences, AIS REST provisions the security record and the password.

The **User Management** screen is the JD Edwards user master, condensed into one editable grid. One line per JDE account. From a single page the security administrator can add a new user, change their JDE attributes (language, country, date format, …), reset the password, attach roles and declare environments.

It is the entry point for every user-related security operation — what the JDE *P0092 Work With User Profiles*, *P98OWSEC Work With User Security* and parts of *P95921* do, on one screen.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each JDE user:

- **The user master, editable on the grid.** Add a new user, change the language, swap the date format — all inline. The screen owns the same data as the JDE *Work With User Profiles* form.
- **Full provisioning, end to end.** A new user requires a SQL write on the user master *and* an AIS REST call to create the JDE security record and set the password. Nomajde chains the two on a single save — no manual *Work With User Security* step.
- **Password reset in one click.** The *Reset Password* button on the dialog calls the JDE AIS endpoint directly; the new password is active on the user's next sign-on.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **User** | `ULUSER` — JDE user ID. | The sign-on user. |
| **Alpha name** | `ABALPH` — Address Book alpha name. | Friendly name pulled from the Address Book record. |
| **Language** | `ULLNGP` — preferred language code. | Drives the language of the JDE forms. |
| **Date format** | `ULFRMT` — date format pattern. | Controls how dates are typed and rendered (DMY, MDY, …). |
| **Country** | `ULCTR` — country code. | Default country for new transactions entered by the user. |
| **Address number**, **Date separator**, **Decimal separator** | `ULAN8`, `ULDSEP`, `ULDECF`. | The Address Book number, and how dates and numbers are written. |

The hidden JDE attributes carried on the row (output queue, job queue, message logging, user type, user group, audit columns) are kept on the row so the edit dialog opens with the full picture.

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add** in the toolbar to register a new JDE user, or double-click a row to edit an existing one. The dialog has three tabs. The *Assignments* and *Environments* tabs are hidden on **Add** — they appear once the user record exists.

### Tab 1 — Default

The user identification and the JDE display preferences. Every field corresponds to a column on the JDE user master.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **User** | JDE sign-on user. Mandatory. Cannot be changed after creation. |
| **Alpha name** | Friendly name pulled from the Address Book — appears on every report and form. |
| **Language** | Preferred language code (F, E, S, …). Drives the language of the JDE forms. |
| **Country** | Country code — default country for new transactions. |
| **Address number** | The user's Address Book number. |
| **Date format** | Day / month / year ordering (`DMY`, `MDY`, `YMD`, …). |
| **Date separator** | The character between day, month and year (`/`, `-`, `.`). |
| **Decimal separator** | Decimal character (`,` or `.`). |

The language, the country, the date format, the date separator and the decimal separator are the user's display preferences. Saving a change writes these five and who changed them: the other display preferences of the user — company, currency, time zone, time format… — are left as they are. Creating a user writes the whole preferences row.

The hidden JDE fields (output queue, job queue, message logging defaults) carry standard values populated by Nomajde — typically `QPRINT`, `*NOLIST`, severity `00`.

### Tab 2 — Assignments

Nested table listing the roles attached to the user — the same data the *Role Relationships* screen edits, scoped to this user. Each row carries the role, the effective date and the expiration date.

Add a row to attach a role; double-click to extend the date window; delete to revoke. Hidden on **Add**.

### Tab 3 — Environments

Nested table listing the environments the user can sign on to (`PD910`, `PY910`, `DV910`, `CRP910`, …), with the display sequence. The default environments are populated automatically when the user is created — adjust here if a specific entry has to be added or removed. Hidden on **Add**.

---

## What runs on save

Adding a JDE user is not just a SQL insert. Nomajde chains the SQL writes and the AIS REST calls so the operator never has to switch screen.

| Step | Channel | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **SQL** | Writes the user identification row in the JDE user master. |
| 2 | **SQL** | Writes the display preferences: the whole row for a new user — also for a user who has none yet —, only the five the form shows for a change. |
| 3 | **AIS REST** | Authenticates the Nomajde service account against AIS to obtain a token for the next two calls. |
| 4 | **AIS REST** | Checks whether the user already has a JDE security record, then creates one if missing — this is what makes the user known to the JDE sign-on layer. |
| 5 | **AIS REST** | Sets the initial password. The new account is ready on the next sign-on. |

If any step fails, the chain stops and the operator is notified — there is no half-provisioned user to clean up.

---

## Reset Password

The **Reset Password** button on the dialog calls the JDE AIS *change password* endpoint directly. The administrator enters the new password once, clicks the button, and the change is active on the user's next sign-on. The same flow can be used to unlock an account whose password has expired.

---

## Change tracking

Edits on this screen are **captured into the active [change package](../../nomaflow/change-packages.md)** under the `Users` entity. Each create, update or delete becomes a reviewable entry, so a user change made in a development environment can be reviewed, approved and promoted to production as a bundle — without re-keying it on the target.

Capture is automatic whenever a draft package is open for the application; nothing changes in how you edit. See [Change packages](../../nomaflow/change-packages.md) for the review-and-promote workflow.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Onboard via *Add*, not via SQL.** A direct SQL insert into the user master skips the AIS security record provisioning — the user appears in the table but cannot sign on. The five-step save chain is what makes the new user usable.
- **Excel upload** for SI-delivered user lists — the upload runs the same five-step chain for every row, so 50 new users are provisioned in a single import.
- **Reset Password** is the right tool when an operator reports a forgotten password. It is also what the help desk uses for the *unlock* request — a fresh password resets the failed-attempt counter on the JDE side.
- **Keep the Assignments and Environments tabs in sync.** A user without an environment cannot sign on; a user without a role has no rights. The default environments populate automatically, but the role attachment is a manual step on the *Assignments* tab.

---

## Nomajde — Role Management
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/role-management/

Maintain JD Edwards users and roles in one place — descriptions, attached roles, environments, and the security workbench import workflow.

The **Role Management** screen is the editor for JD Edwards users and roles. JDE stores the description of each user and each role in the same table — the screen lets you maintain both from a single grid. One line per `(User or Role)`.

Open a row to edit the description, attach roles, set the environments, run the security workbench import. The actions that JDE normally splits across the *User Profile*, *Role Description* and *Security Workbench* forms are collapsed into one dialog.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each user or role in the JDE security catalogue:

- **One screen for users and roles.** JDE stores user and role descriptions in the same table; this page does too — a role and a user both appear in the grid, sortable side by side.
- **One dialog for the whole maintenance.** Editing a row gives access to the description, the attached roles, the environments and the security workbench import — without navigating between three separate JDE forms.
- **Bulk-friendly.** Standard grid actions (add, edit, delete) plus the upload action of Nomajde — useful when onboarding a new role definition delivered by the system integrator as a spreadsheet.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **User / Role** | `AUUSER` — JDE identifier. | Either a sign-on user ID or a role ID — JDE stores both in the same table. |
| **Description** | `AUROLEDESC` — friendly label. | The label that surfaces on JDE forms and on the Nomajde reports. |
| **Sequence** | `AUSEQNO` — sequence number. | Precedence when a user holds several roles — the role with the highest sequence is read first. |

Other JDE attributes carried on the row but hidden by default: language, e-mail, last login, intensive-user flag, action / inactive marker, and the audit columns (program, job, date, time).

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add** in the toolbar to register a new user or role, or double-click a row to edit. The dialog has four tabs. The *Roles*, *Assignments* and *Environments* tabs are hidden on **Add** — they appear only after the user / role record exists.

### Tab 1 — Default

The user / role identification and the JDE display preferences (language, country, date format, decimal separator, currency, time zone). All four columns shown on the grid live here; the JDE display attributes are below.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **User / Role** | The JDE identifier — the sign-on user for a user, the role ID for a role. Mandatory. |
| **Description** | Friendly label that surfaces on JDE forms and in the Nomajde reports. |
| **Sequence** | Precedence when the same user holds several roles — highest sequence first. |

The JDE display fields (language, country, date format, decimal separator, currency, time zone, time format, OMW logging, right-to-left, intensive user) keep their JDE semantics. Leave them empty to inherit the JDE default, or set them per user when the deployment guidelines require it.

### Tab 2 — Roles

Nested table listing the roles attached to the user (or the parent roles of the role being edited). Add a row to attach a role, with effective and expiration dates. Hidden on **Add**.

The toolbar of the Roles tab carries two workflow buttons — *Import Security* and *Merge Roles* — that automate the bulk of the JDE security-cloning work in a single click. Both apply across three JDE catalogues:

| Catalogue | What it carries |
|---|---|
| **Security Workbench** | Application, action, row, column, processing-option, tab, exit, hyper-exit, external-call security. |
| **UDO Security** | User-Defined Object security — saved queries, watch lists, personal forms, advanced queries, E1 Pages. |
| **Menu Filtering** | The Solution Explorer task variants the user is allowed to launch. |

Each workflow walks through the three catalogues, deleting the target rows first and inserting the source rows next — a delete-then-insert per catalogue, six steps in total.

#### Import Security — clone a reference user / role

The button copies the **full security setup** of a single source user or role into the target. The target's prior security is removed first — the result is an exact clone.

| Step | Catalogue | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Security Workbench | Removes every existing workbench entry on the target. |
| 2 | Security Workbench | Copies every workbench entry from the source onto the target, line for line. |
| 3 | UDO Security | Removes every existing UDO entry on the target. |
| 4 | UDO Security | Copies every UDO entry from the source — a fresh row identifier is allocated so the target's rows do not collide with the source's. |
| 5 | Menu Filtering | Removes every existing menu-filter entry on the target. |
| 6 | Menu Filtering | Copies every menu-filter entry from the source. |

After the six steps run, the target user / role has the **same security as the source** — same applications, same action grants, same UDO permissions, same Solution Explorer view.

#### Merge Roles — combine the inherited roles into one consolidated set

The button looks at **every active role relationship** on the target (the *Role Relationships* attached to the row) and consolidates the security setups of all source roles into the target. Where two source roles grant a flag (e.g. *Run*), the merged result takes the most-permissive value. The target's prior security is removed first.

| Use Merge Roles when | What you get |
|---|---|
| A role inherits from three source roles and you want a single flat row set instead of resolving the inheritance at every sign-on. | A consolidated *Security Workbench* on the target — JDE no longer has to compute the union at sign-on time. |
| You are about to retire two of the source roles and want to keep the combined access on the target only. | The same effective rights, expressed on the target. After the merge, remove the inheritance from *Role Relationships*. |
| The security workbench grows beyond what a JDE sign-on can comfortably resolve on the fly. | Flatten the hierarchy once, get faster sign-ons and an easier-to-audit row set. |

Both buttons are idempotent — running them twice does not duplicate the result. They both keep the audit columns on the inserted rows (the Nomajde user, the JDE program ID, the timestamp), so the *Audit Trail* picks up the change.

:::caution[Destructive on the target]
*Import Security* and *Merge Roles* both **delete the target's existing rows** before inserting. Always run them on a freshly created user / role, or after confirming the target's current security is no longer needed.
:::

### Tab 3 — Assignments

The reverse view of the Roles tab. Lists the records where the current user / role is the **source** of a role inheritance — that is, every user or role that inherits security from this one. Hidden on **Add**.

Edit a row to extend the effective-date window or to revoke the inheritance.

### Tab 4 — Environments

Nested table listing the environments declared for the user (`PD`, `PY`, `DV`, `CRP`, …). Each environment carries the role under which the user runs there and the date window during which the access is valid. Hidden on **Add**.

When the user record is created (the **Add** flow), Nomajde automatically populates the default environments from the JDE configuration — no manual entry needed on day one.

---

## On save — what runs in the background

Saving a new user / role chains four JDE inserts in one go:

1. **Insert New Role** — writes the user / role identification row.
2. **Get Default Environments** — fetches the default environment list from the JDE configuration.
3. **Insert Default Environments** — populates the *Environments* tab with the defaults.
4. **Insert Display Preferences** — writes the display preferences row (language, country, date format…) tied to the user / role.

The four steps run as a single save — there is no half-created record to clean up if any step fails.

### Server-side security re-merge

Every save on a child role (a role that's *included by* other parent roles) triggers a server-side merge step that re-derives the parents' F00950 / F00950W / F9006 rows from the new child state. Without this, a permission change on a child would only surface in production after every parent that includes it was opened + re-saved by hand.

The re-merge runs through a `call_plugin` action (`nomajde.security:j_remerge_security` with `scope = "child_role"`) wired onto every role-edit screen. It's transparent in normal use — the operator just saves; the merge runs as part of the same write transaction.

When the role-edit screen is **change-tracked** (the standard configuration for promotion-target environments), the same merge also lands as a `CALL_PLUGIN` entry in the [active change package](../../nomaflow/change-packages.md) with `change_replay = true`, so the re-merge re-runs on the target environment after the package's row writes land.

For batch re-merge across every change captured in the draft package (typical when several child roles were touched together), the bundled [`nomajde-remerge-security`](../../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security) Nomaflow job runs the same plugin with `scope = "package"`. Wire it as a post-apply step on the contributing screens so it runs once on the target after every captured row lands.

For a full system re-merge — recovery after a security-table re-import, or a known-bad merge — the [`nomajde-remerge-security-all`](../../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security-all) job runs the same plugin with `scope = "all"`. Use sparingly; the full pass writes every parent's rows again.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Use *Import Security* to onboard a new user** by cloning a reference one — much faster than rebuilding the workbench by hand.
- **The Sequence column matters** when a user holds several roles — JDE resolves the effective rights in sequence order, the highest sequence first: the first rule found for an object decides. Give the highest sequence to the role whose rules must prevail.
- **Maintain users and roles in the same place.** JDE stores both in *F00926*; the screen surfaces both. Apply your own naming convention (e.g. `*_USER` for users, `*_ROLE` for roles) to keep them visually separate on the grid.
- **Check *Nomasx-1 → Conflicts → Summary by User*** after onboarding a user, to confirm the attached roles do not create SoD conflicts.
- **Simulate a role before giving it**: [Security simulation](./security-simulation.md) shows, with *Roles added*, what the user would gain, object by object — nothing is written.

---

## Nomajde — Role Relationships
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/role-relationships/

Maintain the JD Edwards role-inheritance graph in a single grid — pair source and target roles, set effective and expiration dates, bulk-upload from Excel.

The **Role Relationships** screen maintains the JD Edwards role-inheritance graph. One line per `(FROM Role, TO Role, Effective Date)`. Each row says: *the TO role inherits the security setup of the FROM role, during this date window*.

It is the screen the security team opens to grant a junior role the rights of a senior one — or to extend the effective window of an inheritance that is about to expire.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each role-inheritance line:

- **Inheritance, in plain rows.** A relationship row says: *FROM Role grants its security setup to TO Role, between Effective Date and Expiration Date*. The TO Role can be a junior role or a user — JDE treats both the same way.
- **Date-driven access windows.** Effective and Expiration dates make the inheritance temporary by default. Expirations that fall in the next 30 days surface in amber; expirations in the past in red — both call for review.
- **Bulk-loadable.** The screen supports Excel upload — when the SI delivers a new bundle of role relationships for a roll-out, import the file instead of typing 200 rows by hand.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **FROM Role** | `RLFRROLE` — source role. | The role that *contributes* its security setup. |
| **TO Role** | `RLTOROLE` — target role or user. | The role or user that *inherits* the security. JDE treats users and roles in the same table. |
| **Effective Date** | `RLEFFDATE` — start date. | Day the inheritance starts. |
| **Expiration Date** | `RLEXPIRDATE` — end date. | Day the inheritance ends. Empty means no end date. |
| **FU Role 1** | `RLFUROLE1` — secondary role. | Optional second role mixed into the inheritance — used for *role mixes* (the FROM role plus a side role). |

Internal JDE fields kept on the row but hidden: role type, system role flag, default role flag, FU roles 2 to 9, plus the audit columns.

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add** in the toolbar to register a new relationship, or double-click a row to edit one. The dialog is a single form with the five visible fields.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **TO Role** | The user or role that receives the security inheritance. Mandatory. |
| **FROM Role** | The role that contributes its security. Mandatory. |
| **Effective Date** | Start of the inheritance window. Mandatory. |
| **Expiration Date** | End of the window. Leave empty for an open-ended inheritance. |
| **FU Role 1** | Optional second role to mix into the inheritance — used in rare role-blend setups. |

The triple `(TO Role, FROM Role, Effective Date)` is the unique key — JDE uses it to look up the inheritance at sign-on time.

---

## Change tracking

Assignments edited here are **captured into the active [change package](../../nomaflow/change-packages.md)** under the `assignments` entity. Each link added or removed becomes a reviewable entry, so an assignment change promotes from development to production as a reviewed bundle.

A parent role's effective security derives from these assignments, so wire the [`nomajde-remerge-security`](../../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security) job as a post-apply step on this screen — the impacted parents are then re-merged on the target after the assignment writes land.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Always set an Expiration Date** unless the relationship is genuinely permanent. Time-boxed inheritances surface on the dashboard before they expire — a much safer pattern than open-ended grants.
- **Use the Excel upload** for SI-delivered bundles. The standard *Add* flow handles single rows; the upload is meant for the dozen or two dozen rows that ship with a new module.
- **Sort by *Expiration Date* ascending** to bring the next expirations to the top — the natural list for the monthly access-review.
- **Check *Nomasx-1 → Conflicts → Summary by Role*** after granting a new inheritance — combining two roles often creates a SoD conflict that was not visible on either role alone.

---

## Nomajde — Environments
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/environments/

Maintain the JD Edwards environment list per user and per role — production, test, development, conference room, with the order in which they appear at sign-on.

The **Environments** screen lists, for each user and each role, the JDE environments they are entitled to sign on to. One line per `(User or Role, Environment)`. The screen drives the environment picker JDE shows at sign-on.

Maintain the production / test / development / conference-room assignments here, in one grid, instead of opening the JDE *User Environment Revisions* form for every account.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each user or role:

- **The sign-on list.** Each row says: *this user / role is entitled to sign on to this environment, with this display order*. JDE uses the list to populate the environment picker at sign-on.
- **Inheritance-aware.** The *Is parent* indicator turns green when the row applies to a role that is the source of an inheritance — meaning the environment list is propagated to other users via *Role Relationships*.
- **Bulk-loadable.** When a new environment is added to the JDE estate, the new assignments can be uploaded from Excel rather than typed account by account.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **User / Role** | `LLUSER` — JDE identifier. | The user or the role the environment applies to. |
| **Environment** | `LLLL` — environment code. | The JDE environment (`PD910`, `PY910`, `DV910`, `CRP910`, …). |
| **Sequence** | `LLSEQ` — display order. | Order in which environments appear in the JDE sign-on picker. |
| **Menu** | `LLMNI` — initial menu. Hidden by default. | The JDE menu the user lands on after sign-on for this environment. |
| **Is parent** | `IS_PARENT` — `Y` / `N`. Green dot when `Y`. | `Y` when the user / role is the source of at least one role relationship — the environment list is inherited by downstream users. |

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add** in the toolbar to declare a new environment assignment, or double-click a row to edit. The dialog is a single form.

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| **User / Role** | The user or role the assignment is for. Mandatory. |
| **Environment** | The JDE environment code — the lookup is filtered by the selected user / role. Mandatory. |
| **Sequence** | Display order on the sign-on screen. Lower number first. |

The *Initial menu* and the *Is parent* indicator are kept on the row but are not editable from the dialog — they are derived attributes.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Set the *Sequence* deliberately.** The first environment in the list is the JDE default — pick `PD910` for an end user and `DV910` for a developer.
- **Attach the environments on the role, not on each user.** When a user inherits from a role (see *Role Relationships*), they automatically pick up the role's environments — much easier to maintain.
- **A *Is parent* green dot** signals an environment list that propagates to many downstream users. Edits to that row affect everyone who inherits — review the impact before saving.
- **Use the Excel upload** when adding a brand-new environment (e.g. a new test environment for a roll-out) — generate the assignments offline and import in one go.

---

## Nomajde — Security Workbench
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/security-workbench/

Maintain every JD Edwards security entry — application, action, row, column, processing-option, tab, exit, image — on a single grid with inline edit.

The **Security Workbench** screen is the single editor for every JD Edwards security entry. One line per `(Security Type, User / Role, Object)`. The same data the JDE *P00950 Work With User / Role Security* form maintains — but on one grid, with filters, sort and bulk edits.

Add, change or remove an entry directly on the row. The dialog adapts its fields to the security type: Object Name and Action flags for application security, Data Item for column security, From / Thru actions for action security, etc.

---

## At a glance

---

## Goal of the view

For each security entry that exists in JDE:

- **Every security type in one place.** Application security, action security, row security, column security, processing-option security, tab security — instead of separate forms in the JDE security workbench, every type sits on one grid filtered by *Type*.
- **The action flags side by side.** *Run*, *View*, *Add*, *Change*, *Delete* — the per-row grant / deny indicators are visible without opening the row.
- **The dialog adapts.** Only the fields that apply to the selected security type are shown — Object Name for application security, Data Item for column security, From / Thru action codes for action security. No clutter.

---

## Columns

| Column | Source | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **Category** | `SEC_TYPE` — broad category. | `OBJECTS`, `ALIAS` or `OTHERS` — groups the JDE security types into the three buckets the dialog uses to decide which fields to show. |
| **Type** | `FSSETY` — specific security type code. | The JDE security type: `1` for application, `2` for column, `3` for processing option, `4` for row, `5` for tab, `6` / `7` / `9` for processing-option variants, `A` for action, `S` for solution explorer, etc. |
| **User / Role** | `FSUSER` — JDE identifier. | The user or role the entry applies to. |
| **Object** | `FSOBNM` — object name. | The application, form or table the entry applies to. |
| **Data Item** | `FSDTAI` — data item alias. | The data dictionary item (for column and action security). |
| **From / Thru** | `FSFRDV`, `FSTHDV` — action / version range. | The action code range (for action security). |
| **Run / View / Add / Change / Delete** | `FSRUN`, `FSVWYN`, `FSA`, `FSCHNG`, `FSDLT` — `Y` / `N` flags. Displayed as green / red dots. | Per-action grant or deny. A dash means the action does not apply to the security type on that row. |

Additional JDE flags carried on the row but hidden by default: install, OK, copy, update, attention markers, system code, owner display, function name, function number, exit ID, table ID, text ID, path — and the audit columns (program, job, date, time).

---

## Edit dialog

Click **Add** in the toolbar to register a new security entry, or double-click a row to edit. The dialog has one tab, three columns wide. The fields shown depend on the *Type* — the dialog hides the columns that do not apply.

| Field | When it appears |
|---|---|
| **Category** | Always — sets the broad category (`OBJECTS`, `ALIAS`, `OTHERS`). |
| **Type** | Always — the specific JDE security type. Mandatory. |
| **User / Role** | Always. Mandatory. The lookup filters by the *Category*. |
| **Object** | When *Category* is `ALIAS`, `OBJECTS` or `OTHERS`. Mandatory for most types. |
| **Data Item** | When *Category* is `ALIAS` or `OTHERS` and the type is column, action, row or similar. |
| **From action** | Action-security types — the start of the action range. |
| **Thru action** | When *Type* = `4` (row security on alias) — the end of the action range. |
| **Run** | Types that grant *run* (`3`, `6`, `7`, `9`, `A`, `B`, `M`, `S`). |
| **View** | Types that grant *view* (`2`, `4`, `5`, `7`, `8`, `9`, `A`, `G`, `I`, `K`, `U`). |
| **Add / Change / Delete** | Action-security types — turn the row into a grant or a deny. |
| **OK / Copy / Update / Attention** | Object-level action codes for specific JDE types. |

The unique key is the full combination — JDE allows several rows for the same `(User, Object)` when the security type differs.

---

## Bulk edit on the grid

The security workbench is the screen where the security administrator spends most of their time — and most of the work is repetitive: copy an entry to ten more users, flip *View* from `Y` to `N` on every action row of an application, deny a sensitive form across a whole role family. Nomajde supports this directly on the grid.

| Pattern | When to use it |
|---|---|
| **Multi-select** | Tick the rows that need the same change (e.g. set *View* to `N` on five application-security entries for the same role), then edit the column on one of the ticked rows — the change is written to every selected row in a single save. |
| **Copy to user / role** | Right-click a row, pick *Copy to user* or *Copy to role*, choose the target list — the same security entry is inserted for every target. Use this to extend a single grant to a set of users without retyping. |
| **Excel upload** | Export the grid (filtered as needed), edit hundreds of rows offline, then re-import via the toolbar's upload action. The standard *Add* dialog handles single rows; the upload is meant for the bundles that ship with a new module. |

Every bulk action follows the same row-level validation as the single-row edit — a missing required field or an invalid flag combination stops the save, and the operator sees which row failed.

---

## Dynamic columns and filters

The security workbench table holds 35+ columns, but only a subset applies to any single security type. The grid takes advantage of this by **hiding the columns that do not apply** to the rows currently visible.

| When the filter is | The columns that surface | The columns that hide |
|---|---|---|
| *Type = 1* (Application security) | Object, Run, View, Add, Change, Delete | Data Item, From / Thru action |
| *Type = 2* (Column security) | Object, Data Item, View, Change | Run, Add, Delete, From / Thru |
| *Type = 3 / 6 / 7 / 9* (Processing options) | Object, Run, View | Add, Change, Delete, Data Item |
| *Type = 4* (Row security) | Object, Data Item, From / Thru, View, Add, Change, Delete | (all action columns visible) |
| *Type = A* (Action security) | Object, Data Item, From action, Add, Change | View, Thru action |

The same logic drives the **edit dialog**: when the type is `2` (column security), the dialog only shows the fields meaningful for column security; when the type is `1` (application security), it switches to the application columns. There is never a stale, unused field to ignore.

Column visibility can also be overridden manually from the *Columns* button on the toolbar — useful when an administrator wants a specific column visible across all types for an audit export.

---

## Change tracking

Security changes on this screen are **captured into the active [change package](../../nomaflow/change-packages.md)** under the `security` entity. Every grant, revoke or bulk edit becomes a reviewable entry, so a workbench change can be promoted from development to production as a reviewed bundle instead of being re-applied by hand.

This is what makes a JDE security promotion repeatable: pair it with the [`nomajde-remerge-security`](../../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security) job, wired as a post-apply step, so the impacted parent roles are re-derived on the target once the bundle's rows land.

---

## Tips & best practices

- **Filter on *Type*** first — the screen carries every JDE security type, and the right filter (e.g. *Type = 1* for application security) collapses both the rows and the visible columns to a focused view.
- **Multi-select before bulk edit.** Hold *Shift* to select a range or *Ctrl* to pick individual rows, then edit any column — the change applies to every selected row.
- **Use *Copy to user / role*** to extend a row to a list of targets. Faster than retyping, and the copies carry the standard audit columns automatically.
- **Excel upload** for SI-delivered security bundles. The standard *Add* flow handles single rows; the upload is meant for the dozens of rows that ship with a new module.
- **A deny on *All Actions* with `User = *PUBLIC` plus targeted grants on roles** is the standard JDE pattern. The grid makes it easy to read whether the deny is in place for every object.
- **After bulk changes**, run *Nomasx-1 → Applications → Rights* to confirm the effective rights match the intent — the workbench shows what is configured, *Rights* shows what JDE will compute at sign-on.
- **Before and after a change**, [Security simulation](./security-simulation.md) gives what a user or role would be allowed, object by object, with a what-if that writes nothing; its [Consistency](./workbench-consistency.md) tab lists the lines of this grid that serve nothing or contradict each other.

---

## Nomajde — Security simulation
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/security-simulation/

Security Maintenance → Security simulation in Nomajde: what a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne user, role or *PUBLIC may run, add, change and delete on the applications and reports of a module, a system code or a list of objects, the rule that decides each right, and a what-if (roles added or taken away, rules tried) that is never written to JD Edwards.

**Security Maintenance → Security simulation** answers the question the Security Workbench cannot answer at a glance: *what would this person be allowed to do?* A JD Edwards EnterpriseOne security grows line by line — on users, on roles, on `*PUBLIC`, on one object or on `*ALL` — and the result is hard to read from the lines themselves. The page evaluates them the way JD Edwards does and gives, for each application and report, what may be **run, added, changed and deleted**, with the rule that decides. A **what-if** tries roles and rules before anyone writes them.

Nothing on the page writes to JD Edwards. The test cases are kept in Nomajde's own database.

The page has four tabs:

| Tab | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Simulate** | A user, a role or `*PUBLIC` on a module, a system code or a list of objects; the what-if. This page. |
| **Secure a module** | The [Security Workbench lines that secure a whole module](./secure-a-module.md) for a role, proposed and never written. |
| **Consistency** | The [Security Workbench read for what does not add up](./workbench-consistency.md): twelve checks, each finding with what to do. |
| **Test cases** | [Expectations replayed against the security](./security-test-cases.md) after every change, with five samples to adapt. |

---

## At a glance

---

## Simulate \{#simulate\}

### Who \{#who\}

**User, role or \*PUBLIC** lists the users and the roles of JD Edwards (a role is marked *(role)*), and `*PUBLIC`.

| Choice | What is evaluated |
|---|---|
| A **user** | The user's own lines, then the lines of every role the user holds today — assignments already effective and not expired — then `*PUBLIC`. This is what the user gets when signing on with `*ALL`, the default sign-on role that combines all the roles assigned to them. |
| A **role** | The role's own lines, then `*PUBLIC`. |
| **\*PUBLIC** | The `*PUBLIC` lines alone: what anybody gets that no other line overrides. |

### What \{#what\}

Fill one of three fields; **Simulate** reads the security for them.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| **Module** | A licence component as Nomasx-1 defines it (*Settings → Licences → JD Edwards → System codes*), listed by name with its system codes and the number of applications and reports: every object of those system codes, and the objects reclassified into the module. Without these settings, a line says so and a system code is picked instead. |
| **or one system code** | One system code, with its description and how many applications and reports it holds. Picking a module clears the system code, and the other way round. |
| **or objects (comma separated)** | Named objects, for example `P4210, R42565`. When filled, they take precedence over the module and the system code. |

Only the interactive applications and the reports of the Object Librarian are listed. Beyond 5,000 objects the list is cut and a banner asks to narrow it.

### The answer \{#answer\}

Figures above the list: **objects** (with who and how many roles were read), **can run**, **closed**, and with a what-if **changed by the what-if**; under *can run* and *closed*, *before: n* gives the figure without the what-if.

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Object**, **Description**, **System**, **Type** | The application (`APPL`) or report (`UBE`) and its system code. |
| **Run**, **Add**, **Change**, **Delete** | *yes* or **NO** for each right. Hovering a value shows the rule that decides that right. |
| **Run decided by** | The line that decides the right to run, as *who on what* — `SALESORDER on P4210`, `BUYER on *ALL` — or *no rule*. |
| **What changes** | With a what-if only: the rights that differ, as `run: no → yes`. |

The grid has the usual search, filters, columns and **Export**.

---

## How it is decided \{#rule\}

Under the list, **How it is decided** restates the rule the page applies:

- JD Edwards **allows what no rule forbids**: an object no line names is allowed (*no rule*).
- The **user's own lines** come first, then the **roles'**, from the **highest sequence** first, then **`*PUBLIC`**. The first level that says something about a right decides it.
- At one level, the **most precise line wins**: a line on the object before a line on `*ALL`, a line on a form or a version before a line on the whole object.

---

## What-if \{#what-if\}

The **What if… (nothing is written)** panel tries a change before it is made:

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Roles added** | Roles the user would hold in addition, picked one at a time; each appears as a chip, **×** takes it back. |
| **Roles taken away** | Roles the user would no longer hold. |
| **Rules tried** | **Add a rule** adds a line: *for* (user, role or `*PUBLIC`), *object* (`*ALL` when left empty), *right* (run, add, change, delete, or all four), *allow* or *deny*. **Remove** takes it away. |

**Simulate** then gives the answer as it would be: the figures show *before: n*, and the **What changes** column marks each right that moves. Nothing is written to JD Edwards: the roles and the rules tried stay on the page.

---

## Save as a test case \{#save\}

Under an answer, **Save as a test case** with a name keeps it as a [test case](./security-test-cases.md): every object and every right becomes an expectation — four per object. A case of the same name is replaced.

The expectations are taken from **the security as it is**, not from the what-if: a what-if is a hypothesis, not a fact to keep. Once the change is made in the Security Workbench, simulate again and save.

---

## Opening the page on someone \{#link\}

The page reads its address: `…/app/nomajde/secsim?who=JSMITH&sy=42` opens it on user `JSMITH` and system code 42 and simulates at once; `&objects=P4210,P0411` names objects instead of a system code. A link of this kind fits in a ticket or a mail asking *"may this person do this?"*.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page is in the **Security Maintenance** folder of the Nomajde menu. The predefined roles **Security administrator** and **Administrator** hold it (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). The connection used to read JD Edwards needs read access to the Security Workbench (`F00950`), the profiles (`F0092`), the roles and their sequence (`F00926`), the role assignments (`F95921`) and the Object Librarian (`F9860`). The modules come from the licence settings of Nomasx-1; without them, the page works by system code or by objects.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- **Simulate before writing.** A role about to be given, a `*PUBLIC` line about to be closed: the what-if shows what moves, object by object, before the Security Workbench is touched.
- **Read *Run decided by*** when an answer surprises: the line that decides is named, so the fix goes to the right user, role or `*ALL` line.
- **Check the role sequence** when a user holds roles that disagree: the role with the highest sequence is read first.
- **Save the answer as a test case** once the security is right, and replay it after every change: [Test cases](./security-test-cases.md).
- **Run [Consistency](./workbench-consistency.md)** first on a security inherited from years of changes: lines for nobody or that say nothing new make every simulation harder to read.

---

## Nomajde — Secure a module
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/secure-a-module/

Security simulation → Secure a module in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Security Workbench lines (type 3 to run, type 1 for add / change / delete) that open a whole module for a role and close it for everybody else, proposed only where the security does not already say so, never written — reviewed, exported and loaded in the Security Workbench.

The **Secure a module** tab of [Security simulation](./security-simulation.md) prepares the security of a whole module in JD Edwards EnterpriseOne. Pick a module, the role it is opened for and with what rights: the page **proposes the Security Workbench lines** that do it — for every application and report of the module, and only where the security as it is does not already say so.

Nothing is written. The lines are reviewed, exported from the list and loaded in the Security Workbench.

---

## At a glance

---

## What to fill in \{#fields\}

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Module** | A licence component as Nomasx-1 defines it, by name with its system codes and number of objects — every application and report of those system codes, and the objects reclassified into it. See [Simulate → What](./security-simulation.md#what). |
| **or one system code** | One system code instead of a module. |
| **Opened for (role or user)** | The role the module is opened for — or a user, although lines on a role are easier to keep. |
| **With** | **every right**, **everything but delete**, or **run only (inquiry)**. |
| **Closed for everybody else (\*PUBLIC)** | Ticked by default: the module is closed for `*PUBLIC`, so that only the roles opened explicitly reach it. |

**Propose the lines** reads the security of the role and of `*PUBLIC` and builds the plan.

---

## The lines proposed \{#plan\}

Figures: **objects in the module**, **lines to add** (orange when there are some), **closing lines**, **opening lines**, **action lines**, and **objects already right** — those for which nothing is needed.

The list gives each line as the Security Workbench stores it (`F00950`):

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **FSSETY** | The security type: **3** for application security (run), **1** for action security (add / change / delete). |
| **FSUSER** | `*PUBLIC` for a closing line, the role for an opening or an action line. |
| **FSOBNM**, **Description** | The application or report. |
| **FSRUN** | On a type 3 line: `N` to close, `Y` to open. |
| **FSA**, **FSCHNG**, **FSDLT**, **FSIOK** | On a type 1 line: add, change, delete, and OK, as **With** asks. |
| **Why** | *closed for everybody*, *opened for the role*, or *the role's actions*. |

Under the list, the page recalls the next steps: review the lines, export them (**Export**, above the list), load them in the Security Workbench, then simulate the role on the module and save the answer as a test case.

---

## Only what is missing \{#only-missing\}

A line is proposed only where the security as it is would not give the expected result:

- An object `*PUBLIC` already may not run — because a `*PUBLIC` line closes `*ALL`, or one closes the object — gets **no closing line**.
- An object the role may already run gets **no opening line**; its actions get a line only when they differ from what **With** asks.
- Proposing the plan again once its lines are loaded proposes **nothing more**, and a banner says *The security already says all of this: no line to add.*

Beyond 5,000 objects the list is cut and a banner asks to narrow it.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The tab is part of the Security simulation page, in the **Security Maintenance** folder; the predefined roles **Security administrator** and **Administrator** hold it (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). Writing the lines is done in the [Security Workbench](./security-workbench.md), with the rights of that screen.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- **Close `*ALL` for `*PUBLIC` once** rather than every object one by one: a security closed by default makes every module plan shorter. [Consistency](./workbench-consistency.md) says when it is not.
- **Review before loading**: the plan is a proposal on the security as it is when it is read; a line written meanwhile changes it.
- **Then check the result**: simulate the role on the module, save the answer as a [test case](./security-test-cases.md), and replay it after every later change.

---

## Nomajde — Security Workbench consistency
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/workbench-consistency/

Security simulation → Consistency in Nomajde: twelve checks on the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Security Workbench, roles and role assignments — security open by default, lines for nobody or on nothing, lines that say nothing new, row security that cannot work, roles with the same sequence, assignments not in effect — each finding with what to do. Nothing is changed.

The **Consistency** tab of [Security simulation](./security-simulation.md) reads the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Security Workbench for what does not add up. A security that grew over years holds lines nobody would write again: lines for users who left, lines that repeat what another line says, row security that restricts nothing. Twelve checks read the workbench (`F00950`), the profiles (`F0092`), the roles and their sequence (`F00926`) and the role assignments (`F95921`), and list each line to review **with what to do**.

Nothing is changed: the corrections are made in the [Security Workbench](./security-workbench.md) and the Security Maintenance screens.

---

## At a glance

---

## Reading the workbench \{#read\}

**Read the workbench** runs the twelve checks. The figures:

| Figure | Content |
|---|---|
| **to review** | How many findings, with how many of high, medium and low severity. |
| **lines read** | How many Security Workbench lines were read. |
| **in the workbench** | Findings on the lines of the workbench (the first six checks). |
| **in row security** | Findings on row security. |
| **roles and assignments** | Findings on the roles and their assignments. |

The list gives one row per finding: **Finding**, **Severity**, **User / role**, **Object**, **Detail** (the line in words) and **What to do**. It is sorted by severity; each check lists 2,000 findings at most, while the figures count them all. When every check comes back empty, a banner says *Nothing to review*. When the Object Librarian cannot be read, a banner says that objects that do not exist were not checked; the other checks still run.

---

## The twelve checks \{#checks\}

### Security Workbench lines \{#checks-workbench\}

| Finding | Severity | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **The security is open by default** — no `*PUBLIC` line closes `*ALL` | high | Close `*ALL` for `*PUBLIC` (type 3, run `N`), then open what each role needs: until then every application nobody named is allowed. |
| **A line for a user or role that no longer exists** | high | Delete it: it applies to nobody. |
| **A line on an object that does not exist** | medium | Delete it, or correct the object name: it secures nothing. |
| **A line that says nothing new** — the same role already says so on `*ALL`, or `*PUBLIC` does | low | Delete it: fewer lines, same security. |
| **Actions given on what cannot be run** — add, change or delete on an application the same user or role may not run | low | Delete the action line, or open the application. |
| **Security written on a user** — application, action or row security on a user rather than a role | medium | Move these lines to a role and give the role: lines on a user are forgotten when the person changes job. |

### Row security \{#checks-rows\}

| Finding | Severity | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Row security: from is after thru** | high | Correct the range: as written it holds no value. |
| **Row security: ranges that overlap and disagree** — two ranges of one table and data item, for the same user or role, that overlap and say different things | medium | Make the ranges distinct. |
| **Row security that restricts nothing** — ranges that allow, while nothing is forbidden on that item for anybody | medium | Add the line that forbids (usually `*PUBLIC` on the whole range), or delete these: JD Edwards allows what no rule forbids. |

### Roles and assignments \{#checks-roles\}

| Finding | Severity | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Roles with the same sequence** | medium | Give each role its own sequence number: between two equal ones, which is read first is not defined. |
| **A role with no line** | low | Give it its security or delete it: it adds nothing to whoever holds it. |
| **An assignment not in effect** — expired, or not yet effective | low | Delete the expired ones; check the dates of those not yet effective. |

---

## Access \{#access\}

The tab is part of the Security simulation page, in the **Security Maintenance** folder; the predefined roles **Security administrator** and **Administrator** hold it (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). The connection used to read JD Edwards needs read access to `F00950`, `F0092`, `F00926`, `F95921` and the Object Librarian (`F9860`).

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- **Start with the high findings**: a security open by default changes the meaning of every other line.
- **Clean before simulating**: lines that say nothing new or apply to nobody make a [simulation](./security-simulation.md) longer to read without changing its answer.
- **Export the list** (**Export**, above the list) to share the review with the people who own the roles.
- **Replay the [test cases](./security-test-cases.md)** after a clean-up: deleting a line that looked useless must not change what any role is allowed.

---

## Nomajde — Security test cases
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/security-maintenance/security-test-cases/

Security simulation → Test cases in Nomajde: JD Edwards EnterpriseOne security expectations (this role may run P4210, may not delete in P0411) saved as cases, replayed against the security as it is after every change, with what no longer holds and the rule that now decides; five sample cases to adapt and an editor for each case.

The **Test cases** tab of [Security simulation](./security-simulation.md) keeps the non-regression of a JD Edwards EnterpriseOne security project. A case is a list of **expectations** about one user, role or `*PUBLIC` — *may run P4210*, *may not delete in P0411* — and **Run all** replays every case against the security as it is now. After a change in the Security Workbench, a role merge or a promotion, the list says what no longer holds and which rule now decides.

Cases are kept in Nomajde's own database; replaying them only reads JD Edwards.

---

## At a glance

---

## The list of cases \{#list\}

**Run all** replays every case; **Add the samples** adds the [sample cases](#samples). The tab title shows how many cases there are.

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Case** | The name given when the case was saved. |
| **About** | The user, role or `*PUBLIC` the expectations are about. |
| **Expectations** | How many expectations the case holds. |
| **Last run** | When the case was last replayed, or *never*. |
| **Passed** / **Failed** | What the last run gave: the failed count is red when an expectation broke, green at 0. |
| — | **Run** replays this case, **Edit** opens the [editor](#edit), **Delete** removes the case and its expectations. |

A case is made in three ways: [saved from a simulation](./security-simulation.md#save) (every object and right of the answer becomes an expectation), added from the samples, or written by hand in the editor from an existing case.

---

## What no longer holds \{#failures\}

After **Run** or **Run all**, a banner says *Every expectation holds.*, or the list **What no longer holds** opens under the cases, with how many lines:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Case** | The case the expectation belongs to. |
| **Object**, **Right** | The object and the right — run, add, change or delete. |
| **Expected** | What the case expects: *yes* or **NO**. |
| **The security says** | What the security as it is gives now. |
| **Decided by** | The line that decides now, as *who on what* — or *no rule* when nothing forbids it. |

The user is replayed with the roles held on the day of the run, as for a [simulation](./security-simulation.md#rule). The passed and failed counts are kept on the case.

---

## Sample cases \{#samples\}

**Add the samples** adds five cases written for typical roles. Each names a **placeholder role**, to replace with one of yours:

| Sample | About | What it expects |
|---|---|---|
| Accounts payable clerk | `APCLERK` | Enters vouchers (`P0411`: run and add), never deletes them; does not pay (`P0413M`), does not maintain suppliers (`P04012`) nor post to the ledger (`P0911`). |
| Sales order entry | `SALESORDER` | Enters orders (`P4210`: run and add); does not maintain customers (`P03013`), prices (`P4106`) nor credit (`P03B11`). |
| Buyer | `BUYER` | Enters purchase orders (`P4310`: run and add); does not receive goods (`P4312`), enter vouchers (`P0411`) nor maintain suppliers (`P04012`). |
| Inquiry only | `INQUIRY` | Opens `P0411` and `P4210` and changes nothing: add, change and delete refused. |
| Nobody but administrators manages security | `*PUBLIC` | Nobody opens the security applications (`P00950`, `P0092`, `P95921`, `P98OWSEC`). Keep `*PUBLIC`, or pick an ordinary role. |

A sample already added — changed or not — is never overwritten: adding the samples again only adds those missing, or says *The samples are already there.* Until its role is replaced, a sample fails or speaks of a role JD Edwards does not have.

---

## Editing a case \{#edit\}

**Edit** on a row opens the case above the list.

| Field | Use |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The case's name; it can be changed, as long as no other case has it. |
| **About (user, role or \*PUBLIC)** | Who the case is about. When it is not a user or a role of this JD Edwards — the placeholder role of a sample — a warning says so: pick one of yours. |
| **Note** | Free text; the samples explain there what the role is meant to do. |
| Expectations | One line each: **Object**, **Form** (optional, for an expectation on one form), the **right** (run, add, change, delete) and **allowed** or **refused**. **Remove** takes the line away; **Add an expectation** adds one. |

**Save the case** replaces the case as a whole, its expectations included; lines without an object are dropped. **Cancel** closes the editor without saving.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The tab is part of the Security simulation page, in the **Security Maintenance** folder; the predefined roles **Security administrator** and **Administrator** hold it (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). Saving, editing and deleting a case writes only to Nomajde's database.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- **One case per role**, named after what the role is for: a failed expectation then points at one role.
- **Keep the refusals.** The expectations that matter most are often the *NO*: a supplier maintenance that an accounts payable clerk must not reach, a security application that nobody but the administrators may open.
- **Run all after every change** to the Security Workbench, after [Re-merge security](../jobs.md#remerge) and after a promotion of security to another environment.
- **Start from the samples**: replace the placeholder role, adapt the objects to the applications the customer uses, then add the expectations specific to the business.

## Nomajde — Back to standard
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/development/back-to-standard/

Development → Back to standard in Nomajde: the standard JD Edwards EnterpriseOne objects a path code holds as changed, and the copies made of standard objects, compared record by record with Oracle's own in the pristine path code — which can go back to standard as they are, which differ and by what, which differ and are never run — with the OMW project that holds each one and the retrofit days saved at each upgrade.

**Development → Back to standard** answers a question every JD Edwards EnterpriseOne customer meets before an upgrade: of all the standard objects changed over the years, **which changes still matter?** Each changed object, and each copy of a standard object, costs retrofit days at every upgrade. The page lists them, compares each one with Oracle's own object in the pristine path code (`PS920`, Oracle's objects as delivered) or in another path code, and sorts them: **those that can go back to standard as they are**, **those that differ, and by what**, and **those that differ but that nobody runs**. JD Edwards is only read.

---

## At a glance

---

## What is compared \{#scope\}

The comparison takes, for one path code (`PD920` for instance):

- **the standard objects it holds as changed** — those the Object Librarian flags as changed in that path code;
- **the copies of standard objects** — an object the customer added that kept the application id of a standard object of the same type. A copy is compared with **its original**: a copy that adds nothing can be replaced by the standard object, and a copy has to be retrofitted like a changed object when Oracle changes its original.

Each object is compared with the same object — or, for a copy, with its original — in the path code named as reference: usually the pristine one, or any other path code.

### Record by record \{#records\}

The comparison reads the **specifications** of the object in the two path codes and matches them record by record: each record is identified inside the object by a few values (a form and a control, an index and its rank, a section…). Two records with the same identification are the same when their values and their specification are the same. What is compared:

| Object | Records compared |
|---|---|
| Table | Its columns, its indexes and the columns of each index. |
| Business view | Its specification. |
| Data structure | Its specification, named mappings included. |
| Business function | Its functions and their specifications. |
| Application | The application, its forms, the controls of each form, the texts of the forms, the event rules. |
| Report | Its sections and objects, its texts, the event rules — those of the report itself (its versions hold overrides only). |
| Named event rules | Their specification. |

**Not compared, and said so on each object**: the C source of a business function (its functions and their data structures are compared, not its code), the data dictionary, the processing option texts, a report's versions.

### A copy under its original's names \{#copies\}

A copy carries names of its own: `P550101` for `P0101`, its forms `W550101A` for `W0101A`, a table's own column prefix. Before a copy is compared with its original, these names are put back to the original's — in the identifications, the values and the specifications —, so that **a name alone is never a difference**. The opened row says so: *A copy of P0101, compared with it under the original's names.*

---

## The page \{#page\}

The heading names the path code, the path code it was compared with and the date of the comparison. When several path codes were compared, a list next to the buttons switches from one to the other.

| Button | Does |
|---|---|
| **Compare a path code** / **Compare again** | Opens the [comparison job](#job), with the path code and the reference already filled in. **Compare a path code** before the first comparison, **Compare again** after. Shows only to those who may run the job. |
| **Read again** | Reads the list again — after a comparison, for instance. |

Before the first comparison, the page says so: the comparison reads every standard object the path code holds as changed and compares it with the path code named, read-only, in a few minutes.

### The figures \{#figures\}

| Figure | Counts |
|---|---|
| **identical to the standard** | The objects every record of which is the same as the standard's: *can go back as they are* — or, when the [upgrade analysis](../upgrade/analysis.md) exists for the path code, the days of retrofit they save at each upgrade. |
| **differ and nobody runs them** | The applications and reports that differ and that no user ran, with the days they save. A dash, with *the usage is not known for this path code*, when the upgrade analysis has no usage for it. |
| **differ** | The objects with at least one record added, removed or changed. |
| **not in the path code compared with** | The objects the reference path code holds no specification of: nothing to compare them with. |

### The five views \{#views\}

Five cards above the list choose what it shows, each with its count. The view chosen is kept for the next visit.

| View | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Can go back as they are** | The objects identical to the standard: only the "changed" flag is left. |
| **Changed, never run** | The applications and reports that differ and that no user ran — a change that serves nobody. Empty when the usage is not known. |
| **Differ** | What was changed, record by record. |
| **Not in the standard** | The objects with nothing to compare with — absent from the reference path code, or without a specification in either. |
| **All** | Every object compared. |

### The list \{#list\}

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Object** | The object's name. |
| **Copy of** | For a copy, its original. |
| **What it is** | The object's description. |
| **Type** | Its type (`APPL`, `UBE`, `TBLE`, `BSFN`…). |
| **Compared with the standard** | **Identical**, **Differs** with its counts (`+` added, `−` removed, `~` changed), **Not in the standard** or **No specification**. |
| **Where it differs** | The kinds of records that differ, with their number: *Form controls (5), Event rules (2)*. |
| **OMW project** | The OMW projects that hold the object, with their description — why it was changed, when the project says it. A user's default project is left out when the object sits in another one. |
| **Last run**, **Users** | Its last use and its users, from the upgrade analysis. |
| **Retrofit days** | The days of retrofit the upgrade analysis gives it, when it is to retrofit. |

The list has the usual search, filters, grouping and columns, and exports to Excel.

---

## What differs, and by what \{#detail\}

Opening a row compares the object **now**, in the two path codes, and shows what was found:

- the verdict in one line: how many records were **added**, **removed** and **changed**, how many are the same, the schemas read and the OMW project that holds it;
- for an identical object, that the standard object can be taken back — or, for a copy, that it adds nothing to its original and that the standard object can be used in its place;
- one block per kind of record that differs — **Table columns**, **Indexes**, **Index columns**, **Business view**, **Data structure**, **Named mappings**, **Functions**, **Application**, **Forms**, **Form controls**, **Form texts**, **Report sections and objects**, **Report texts**, **Event rules**, **Named event rules** — with:
  - **Added by you**: the records only the path code examined holds;
  - **Removed by you — in the standard only**: the records only the reference holds;
  - **Changed**: each record identified in words (*form W4210A · control 12 · event 13*), its values as *standard → yours*, and, when its specification differs, **the lines that differ** — removed in red, added in green.

A long list is cut and the rest counted (*… and 12 more*); a long difference stops after 120 lines (*… and 40 more line(s)*).

---

## The comparison job \{#job\}

The job **Compare with the standard** (`nomajde-standard-compare`, menu **Jobs**) makes the comparison of one path code and keeps the verdict of every object; what the page lists is what the last run kept. Comparing a path code again replaces what it held. It takes a few minutes — 350 objects in under a minute on a demonstration system.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Path code to examine** | `PD920` | The path code whose changed objects and copies are compared. |
| **Path code to compare with** | `PS920` | The reference: `PS920` for Oracle's objects as delivered, or another path code. |

The job is read-only on JD Edwards: it reads the specifications of the two path codes, runs no Oracle batch and adds nothing to JD Edwards. A path code cannot be compared with itself. It has no schedule: run it before an upgrade, or after a clean-up, to see where things stand.

Opening a row does not need the job again: the comparison of that object is made on the spot.

### A JD Edwards behind a database link \{#dblink\}

When Liberty reaches the JD Edwards libraries through a database link, the job and the page follow the JD Edwards pool: each table is read with its library from the pool's **Schemas** and that library's link from its **Database links**, under the same key — `OL` for the Object Librarian, `SY` for the OMW tables, `CO` for the central objects of both path codes. A library with no link is read locally. The specifications are stored as BLOBs, which the usual driver cannot read through a link: behind a `CO` link they are read by the thick Oracle driver, by itself — nothing to set. See [Schema and DB-link tokens](../../framework/connectors.md#schema-and-db-link-tokens).

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page is in the **Development** folder of the Nomajde menu. The predefined roles **Developer** and **Administrator** hold it, and may run the comparison job (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). The buttons that open the job show only to those who may run it. The connection used to read JD Edwards needs read access to the Object Librarian, the central objects of the two path codes and the OMW tables.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Start with **Can go back as they are**: each line is an object to take back from the standard at no cost, and the retrofit days it saves at every upgrade.
- Run the [upgrade analysis](../upgrade/analysis.md) of the same path code first: the last use, the users and the retrofit days come from it, and so does the **Changed, never run** view.
- Read the **OMW project** before deciding: its description often says why the object was changed, and who to ask.
- The reference need not be the pristine path code: the job accepts any path code to compare with.
- A difference made only of a copy's own names is not shown: what remains after the names are put back is a real change.

---

- [Object Management Workbench](../master-data/delivered-screens.md#omw) — the OMW projects, their objects and their log.
- [Cross Reference](../cross-reference.md) — where an object is used before taking it back.

## Nomajde — JDE Health Check
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/jde-servers/

Monitoring → JDE Health Check in Nomajde: every health check of the JD Edwards enterprise, web and REST servers seen by Server Manager — state, health, failed checks, action taken — over a period, the history of a server, the overview figures and the job that collects them.

**Monitoring → JDE Health Check** lists the health checks of the JD Edwards servers, newest first: one row per instance and per check, with its state in Server Manager, the health result, the checks that failed and the action taken. The checks come from the [`nomajde-jde-health`](#job) job, which queries Server Manager every five minutes once enabled.

---

## At a glance

---

## The grid \{#grid\}

The grid is read-only and lists every check kept, newest first. It opens on the checks of the last 7 days: the period on **Checked at**, in the advanced filters, widens or narrows that window (*All dates* shows every check kept, see `keep_days` in [Parameters](#parameters)).

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Host** | The Server Manager agent host of the instance. |
| **Instance** | The instance name in Server Manager. |
| **Server type** | `entserver` (enterprise server), `webserver` (HTML server) or `restserver` (AIS server). |
| **State** | The state reported by Server Manager, e.g. `RUNNING`. |
| **Health** | `passed`, `failed` (a check did not pass, or its enterprise server is not healthy), `down` (the instance is not running) or `error` (Server Manager could not be queried for it, or the instance is unknown to Server Manager). |
| **Failed checks** | The Server Manager checks that did not pass, among the ones monitored (see [Parameters](#parameters)). |
| **Enterprise server** | For an instance declared in a group, the enterprise server it depends on. |
| **Action** | `stopped` when the check stopped the instance, `stop failed` when the stop was refused. |
| **Detail** | The error message, or the reason of a failure inherited from the enterprise server. |
| **Checked at** | The time of the check. |

The **Host**, **Instance**, **Server type** and **Health** columns can be filtered too. With a check every five minutes, an instance adds 288 rows a day: to follow a single server, filter on its instance or open its history.

## The history of an instance \{#history\}

Opening a row shows the instance in a dialog. The **General** tab repeats the fields of the grid; the **History** tab lists every check kept for that instance, most recent first: time, state, health, failed checks, enterprise server, action, detail.

---

## On the overview \{#overview\}

The Nomajde [Overview](../home.md) leads here from its *The platform* group, and shows the last run of the `nomajde-jde-health` job among its jobs. For the state of the instances at this moment, see [Platform synthesis](../synthesis.md).

---

## The collection job \{#job\}

The `nomajde-jde-health` job checks the servers through the Server Manager REST API. It ships **disabled**, scheduled every five minutes (Europe/Paris).

1. In **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools**, open the `jde_server_manager` pool and set the Server Manager address with its account (`jde_admin`) and its password — see [the Server Manager connection](./server-manager.md#connection).
2. In **Nomaflow → Jobs**, adjust the parameters of `nomajde-jde-health` if needed, then enable it.
3. **Jobs → Check the JDE servers** in the Nomajde menu runs the check at once, without waiting for the schedule.

Each run asks Server Manager for the list of instances and runs its health check on each running instance. The run **fails** — and triggers the job's alerts — when an instance did not pass; the rows are written beforehand, so the grid shows the failure.

### Parameters \{#parameters\}

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `checks` | `UBE, BSFN, Port Test, Login, Interactive App, OVR` | The Server Manager checks that count; the others are ignored. Blank: every check counts. |
| `groups` | blank | The instances that depend on an enterprise server, as JSON: `{"<host>-<enterprise server>": ["<host>-<instance>", …]}`. When the enterprise server is down or not healthy, its instances are marked failed without being checked. When set, only the instances named here are monitored. |
| `auto_stop` | `false` | `true` stops a running instance that failed, and the running instances of a failed enterprise server. |
| `keep_days` | `30` | The number of days of checks kept; older rows are removed at each run. |

Details of the job: [`nomajde-jde-health`](../../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-jde-health).

## Nomajde — Server Manager
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/server-manager/

Monitoring → Server Manager in Nomajde: seven screens that read the JD Edwards Server Manager console live — instances, connected users, enterprise servers, server processes, business function calls and errors, web and AIS servers with their Java memory, JDBj caches — with advanced filters, pick-lists, starting, stopping and restarting an instance and clearing a cache from a row, and the catalogue of Server Manager REST services behind them.

**Monitoring → Server Manager** shows what the JD Edwards Server Manager console knows, in seven Nomajde grids: the instances and their state, who is connected, the load of the enterprise servers and of their processes, the business function calls and errors, the Java memory of the web and AIS servers, the JDBj caches of the HTML servers. A row's menu starts, stops or restarts an instance, or clears a cache. The screens read the console **live** each time they are opened or refreshed; nothing is stored in Nomajde.

For the health of the servers over time — checks every five minutes, availability, alerts — see [JDE Health Check](./jde-servers.md); to watch the instances and restart one that fails, see the *Instances watch* job in [Jobs](../jobs.md).
