## At a glance

---

## The screens \{#screens\}

Every screen loads when opened and only reads; the row actions below are the only changes made from them. Each one asks the console for its instances, then reads every **running** instance of the right kind together: one grid covers the whole platform. An instance that is stopped, or that the console refuses to answer for, keeps a row whose **Note** column says why — `not running (STOPPED)` for example.

| Menu entry | What it lists | Main columns |
|---|---|---|
| **Instances** (*JDE instances*) | Every instance the console manages. | Instance, Type, State, Tools release, Host, JDE home. |
| **Connected users** | The web and AIS sessions — and, on request, the enterprise server processes each user is connected to. | User, Session, Instance, Environment, Role, From, Open applications, Signed in at, Idle (seconds), Last active, Process. |
| **Enterprise servers** | One row per enterprise server. | Instance, Host, Up for, Network jobs, Kernel jobs, Zombie processes, Security kernel users, Call object users, CPU, Memory. |
| **Server processes** | Each kernel and network listener of the enterprise servers. | Process, Process id, Instance, Kind, Process state (*Running* or *Zombie*, from the console's own status of the process), Users, Connected, Outstanding requests, Messages received, Memory, CPU, Threads, Database connections, Open transactions, Started, Last message. |
| **Business functions** | The business function calls seen by each web server. | Business function, Calls, Average (ms), Longest (ms), Timeouts, Application errors, System errors, Total (ms), Shortest (ms), Instance, Enterprise server. |
| **Web and AIS servers** | Each web and AIS node. | Instance, Node, Type, Up for, Online users, Sign-in, Java heap used (MB), Java heap maximum (MB), Java heap used (percent). |
| **JDBj caches** | Each JDBj cache of the HTML servers. | Instance, Node, Cache, Items, Accesses, Hits, Misses, Hit ratio. |

Figures are numbers: they sort, total and export as such. **JDBj caches**, **Server processes** and **Business functions** hold many lines per server: they open **grouped by instance**, so that several web or enterprise servers read apart — **Group** in the toolbar ungroups them.

### Connected users \{#users\}

The **Show** dropdown above the grid chooses between **Sessions** — the web and AIS sessions, the default — and **Sessions and server processes**, which adds the enterprise server processes each user is connected to. The grid is empty when nobody is signed in.

---

## Starting, stopping and restarting an instance \{#start-stop\}

The **Instances** screen (*JDE instances*) has three row actions in each row's menu (**···**). Each one asks for a confirmation first, then reads the list again.

| Row action | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Start this instance** | Sent to Server Manager as it is. Server Manager starts the instance; refresh the list to follow its state. |
| **Stop this instance** | Sent to Server Manager as it is. Its users are disconnected and what they were doing is lost. |
| **Restart this instance** | Liberty stops the instance, waits until Server Manager says it is stopped, starts it and waits until it runs — a few minutes. An instance that does not stop is **not** started again; an instance that does not come back says so. In both cases the message gives the state it was left in, to look at in Server Manager. An instance found stopped is simply started. |

Everything goes through Server Manager's REST API: nothing is installed on the JD Edwards servers.

The **Instances watch** job asks every enterprise, HTML and AIS server for its state and for the console's own health checks, keeps what is wrong and alerts; it can also restart an instance whose checks fail, within guards. It is described in [Jobs](../jobs.md).

---

## Clearing a cache \{#actions\}

Three screens clear a cache from a row's menu (**···**). Each action asks for a confirmation first, and has its own permission.

| Screen | Row action | Clears |
|---|---|---|
| **Web and AIS servers** | **Clear data caches** | On an HTML server, its form extension, personalized form and search group caches; on an AIS server, its orchestration, form and data service and read data caches. |
| **Web and AIS servers** | **Clear JDBj caches** | Every JDBj cache of an HTML server — data dictionary, menus, security, serialized objects… On an AIS server's line, the action says it belongs to an HTML server. |
| **Enterprise servers** | **Clear a table's cache…** | Asks for the table and the environment (a name, or `ALL`); the answer says how many processes were cleared. |
| **JDBj caches** | **Clear this cache**, **Clear every cache of this server** | The cache of the row, or every JDBj cache of its server. The list is read again afterwards. |

---

## Filters \{#filters\}

Nothing is typed above the grids: the columns are in the **advanced filters**, with the same operators as any Nomajde grid. Where the values are known the filter is a pick-list:

| Filter | Values |
|---|---|
| **State** | `RUNNING`, `STOPPED`, `UNKNOWN`. |
| **Session** (Connected users) | `Web session`, `AIS session`, `Enterprise server process`. |
| **Kind** (Server processes) | `Kernel Process`, `Network Listener`. |
| **Instance** | The instances of the console, listed live with their type. |

A filter applies to the rows the console returned: it narrows what is shown, not what is asked from the console.

---

## The Server Manager connection \{#connection\}

The screens use the `jde_server_manager` connector, the one the [health check](./jde-servers.md#job) already uses. The connector holds no address and no account: it names the **`jde_server_manager` pool**, where the console is set once. In **Liberty Next → Administer → Pools**, open that pool (kind *HTTP server (an API)*) and set the address of the console's REST service with its account (`jde_admin` by default), its password and whether the TLS certificate is checked. The account's rights in Server Manager decide what it may read.

At installation the pool can be filled from the server's environment instead: `JDE_SM_URL` (the address with its account) and `JDE_SM_VERIFY_SSL` (`true` by default). See [Pools](../../framework/connectors.md#pools).

---

## The catalogue of Server Manager services \{#catalogue\}

Beyond the screens, the connector carries a catalogue of the Server Manager REST services, written from Oracle's guide: each endpoint has its parameters explained, and its own permission, so that a role can be given one service and not the others. They can be called from the connector's **Test** tab, a screen action, a job step or the [AI assistant](../../framework/ai-assistant.md).

| Heading | Content |
|---|---|
| **Monitoring** | Instances, homes and agents, path codes, WebLogic domains and servers, components and their versions, INI configuration, log files. |
| **Runtime Metrics** | Enterprise server activity and processes, business function statistics, Java memory, JDBj connections and caches, connected users, user sessions. |
| **Manage and Update Operations** | Start or stop an instance, every instance or a WebLogic server, refresh the environments, clear the data caches. |
| **Server Group**, **User Log Configuration**, others | Server groups, saved configurations, the log level of a user. |

The services that **change the platform** — start and stop an instance, start and stop every instance, start and stop a WebLogic server, refresh the environments, change a log level, clear the data caches, the JDBj caches or a table's cache — are marked as such: the AI assistant never calls one without showing a card to approve first, and only for a user allowed to change data through it.

Provisioning (create, register or delete an instance), passwords, TLS, users and groups, save and restore, and the updates of the agents and of the console are left out of the catalogue on purpose.

---

## Access \{#access\}

Each screen shows to the roles that hold its menu entry. **Start this instance** and **Stop this instance** call the services `sm_startinstance` and `stopinstance` and need their API endpoint permission; **Restart this instance** runs with `plugin:nomajde.instances:*`, which the predefined roles **Platform operator** and **Administrator** hold. A raw service of the catalogue needs the permission `api:jde_server_manager:<service>` (rule type **API endpoint** in a role's *Beyond the menus* rules): grant the reading ones widely, those that change the platform — the cache clearing of the row menus included — to the platform team only.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Start with **Instances**: an instance that is not `RUNNING` explains an empty line in the other screens.
- Prefer **Restart this instance** to a stop followed by a start: it waits for the stop to be over, where a start sent too early does nothing.
- In **Server processes**, sort on **Outstanding requests** or **CPU** to find the kernel that holds a queue; sort on **Process state** to bring together the *Zombie* processes — those that ended without being cleaned up.
- In **Business functions**, sort on **System errors** or **Timeouts** after a deployment: a function that fails on one web server only points at that server.
- **Web and AIS servers** — a heap used close to its maximum over several refreshes is the signal to look at before the users call.
- **JDBj caches** — a low **Hit ratio** just after a restart is normal; one that stays low points at a cache too small for what is used. Clear a cache after changing what it holds in JD Edwards (security, menus, data dictionary) rather than restarting the server.

---

- [Performance](./performance.md) and [Platform analysis](./platform-analysis.md) — the same console read as advice and as an analysis.

## Nomajde — Architecture
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/architecture/

Monitoring → Architecture in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform drawn from what is found — Server Manager's instances by tier and host, the application server and its version, the database, the machines connected to it — with a dashed outline for what Server Manager does not declare, lines drawn only on evidence, a card that opens its details, and a download as SVG.

**Monitoring → Architecture** draws the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform **from what is found**, not from a drawing kept by hand: the instances Server Manager declares, grouped by tier and by host, the database the JD Edwards connection points at, and the machines the database sees connected. What only the database side shows has a dashed outline; a line between two cards is drawn only when something proves it. The page reads Server Manager and the database live, each time it is opened or **Read again** is clicked, and changes nothing.

The same diagram is the **Architecture** tab of the [Platform synthesis](../synthesis.md).

---

## At a glance

---

## The figures and the sources \{#figures\}

Five figures head the page: **instances running** (out of those Server Manager declares), **hosts in Server Manager**, **database**, **not declared in Server Manager** (amber when there is one) and **links with their evidence**.

Under them, each source of the diagram says whether it was read: **Server Manager instances**, **Business function calls**, **JD Edwards pool**, **Database instance**, **Database sessions** — *read*, *not read* or *not read on this database*. A source that did not answer is named in a warning with the reason, and the rest is still drawn.

What the page read is kept while the browser session lasts: opening it again draws it at once, and the header says when it was read (*Read at 14:02*). **Read again** reads anew. The Monitoring pages — Platform synthesis, Architecture, Platform analysis, Performance and Database audit — share their readings: what one page has read, the others draw at once, and what one page reads again is fresh in the others. The readings are kept per user, in the browser's memory only: reloading the browser reads again.

---

## The diagram \{#diagram\}

One column per tier, left to right — a tier with nothing in it is not drawn:

| Tier | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Web and AIS** | The web servers and the AIS servers, and the **application server** they run in — WebLogic or WebSphere, with its version (*Application server · WebLogic 14.1.1*). |
| **Enterprise servers** | The enterprise servers. |
| **Database** | The database the JD Edwards connection points at: its product (Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, Db2 for i…) and version, its sessions. |
| **Other database clients** | The other machines connected to the database — a tool, an interface: the busiest ones one by one, the rest gathered on one card (*12 other machines*). |
| **Other servers** | The instances of another type. |
| **Administration** | The Server Manager console. |

Inside a tier, the cards sit on their **host**: a machine is one host whatever a source calls it (`ENT01.example.com`, `ent01` and `EXAMPLE\ENT01` are the same machine). Each card gives its name, its kind, its state — **Running**, **To review**, **Stopped**, **Not known** — and a key fact (version, home, sessions).

### What Server Manager does not declare \{#undeclared\}

Server Manager declares servers, not databases. What the database side shows and the console does not list is drawn with a **dashed outline**: the database server when its host is none of the console's hosts, a machine that runs JD Edwards kernels without being an instance, the other machines connected to the database. The figure **not declared in Server Manager** counts them: a machine nobody declared is often the first thing an audit asks about.

### The lines \{#lines\}

A line is drawn **only on evidence**, and says which:

| Line | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Blue — **business function calls** | A web server's own counters of the calls it sent to an enterprise server (*4,803 calls*). |
| Purple — **database sessions** | The sessions open on the database at this moment, by machine (*42 sessions*). |

Nothing is drawn because it is usual: two servers without a line are servers between which nothing was measured.

### A card's details \{#details\}

A click on a card opens, on the right, what is known of it: its **State**, whether it is **Declared in Server Manager** (*no — found on the database side only* for a dashed card), its **Host**, its **Tier**, then its own facts (version, home, type, port, sessions, programs, accounts…), and **Its lines** — each line from or to it, with its evidence. A second click closes it. The **−** / **+** buttons zoom the diagram.

---

## Download and keep \{#download\}

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Download as SVG** | Reads the platform again and saves the picture as an SVG file (`jde-architecture.svg`), at the size of a landscape report page. |
| **Keep for the audit report** | Reads the platform again and keeps that reading for the licence audit report of the application on this JD Edwards pool: the report draws it on its architecture page, in its own language — unless a picture was put there by hand. Only the last reading is kept. |

The line under the header says what is kept: *Nothing is kept for the audit report yet*, or the date of the reading kept and its pool.

---

## When a source does not answer \{#partial\}

The diagram is drawn from what was read:

- **Server Manager does not answer** — the servers shown are those the database sessions name, and the page says that what is declared is not known;
- **the database sessions are not read** — who connects to the database is not shown;
- **the database is none of Oracle, SQL Server and Db2** — the database audit is not read, but the pool still says where the database is;
- **nothing answers** — the page says that neither Server Manager nor the database answered.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry and the permissions `plugin:nomajde.architecture:*`. The predefined roles **Platform operator** and **Administrator** hold both (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)). It reads Server Manager through the `jde_server_manager` pool (see [Server Manager](./server-manager.md#connection)) and the JD Edwards database, with the statements the [Database audit](./database-audit.md) already sends: no new statement, no AWR, no ASH.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- A dashed card deserves a question: a machine that runs kernels or holds sessions on the database without being declared is either forgotten in Server Manager or not JD Edwards at all.
- Read the page at a busy hour: the database sessions are those of the moment, and a quiet platform draws fewer lines.
- Keep a reading for the audit report once the platform is complete — after a restart, servers not yet called draw no line.

## Nomajde — Platform analysis
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/platform-analysis/

Monitoring → Platform analysis in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne servers as Server Manager measures them now — six figures, what the figures say, the instances, the web and AIS nodes, the enterprise server processes, the business functions — and an instance's INI settings, read or compared with another's.

**Monitoring → Platform analysis** reads what Server Manager measures now and reads it as an analysis: the figures, then **what the figures say** — the points to review first —, then the details by subject in four tabs. The figures are those of the console at the moment the page is read.

What the page read is kept while the browser session lasts: opening it again draws it at once, and the header says when it was read (*Read at 14:02*). **Read again** reads anew. The Monitoring pages — Platform synthesis, Architecture, Platform analysis, Performance and Database audit — share their readings: what one page has read, the others draw at once, and what one page reads again is fresh in the others. The readings are kept per user, in the browser's memory only: reloading the browser reads again.

---

## At a glance

---

## The four tabs \{#tabs\}

Each tab says, beside its description, how many of its points are to review.

| Tab | Content |
|---|---|
| **Overview** | Six figures — **instances running**, **server processes**, **zombie processes**, **sessions**, **business function calls**, **of them in error** —, **What the figures say** and the list of **Instances** (instance, type, state, version). |
| **Servers** | The **Web and AIS** nodes — up for, users online, Java heap used against its maximum, with a bar — and the enterprise server **Processes**: waiting requests, open transactions, database connections, threads, memory, users; the busiest first. |
| **Business functions** | Calls, average and longest time, timeouts, system and application errors; the ones in error or the slowest first. |
| **INI settings** | An instance's INI, read or compared with another's. |

---

## What the figures say \{#findings\}

Each line names its area and is marked amber (to review), blue (to know) or green (nothing to flag):

- an instance that is not running;
- zombie processes on an enterprise server — to review with its logs;
- a kernel with requests waiting, or many transactions open;
- a business function that times out, fails, or is far slower than the others' median;
- a Java heap above 80 % of its maximum, a web server restarted a moment ago.

An area with nothing to flag says so: *The 4 instances are running.*

---

## INI settings \{#ini\}

Pick **An instance**, optionally another under **Compared with**, then **Read its INI**. Alone, the INI is listed by section and setting; compared, only the settings that differ are listed, with the value of each instance. **Find a section or a setting…** narrows the list as you type. Server Manager takes a few seconds to answer an INI; the result stays in place when you switch tabs.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry and the permissions `plugin:nomajde.platform:*`. It reads Server Manager through the `jde_server_manager` connector for the user: the permissions of the [Server Manager services](./server-manager.md#catalogue) do not apply here.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Read the **Overview** tab after a deployment or a restart: an amber line is where to start.
- Compare the INI of two enterprise servers that should be identical: a difference is often the cause of a behaviour seen on one server only.
- The server log files are not read — the console only lists the signed-in user's own logs.

## Nomajde — Performance
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/performance/

Monitoring → Performance in Nomajde: what slows the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform down now, read live from Server Manager, the database and the cross reference — a short list of advice, the heaviest first, each with what was measured, what it means and what to do.

**Monitoring → Performance** answers one question: **what slows the JD Edwards platform down now, and what to look at first?** The page reads Server Manager, the database and the cross reference — live, read-only, in about seven seconds — and turns the figures into a short list of advice, the heaviest first. Each line says what was measured, what it means and what to do.

---

## At a glance

---

## The figures \{#figures\}

Nine figures head the page: **business function calls**, **seconds spent in them**, **ms per call**, **timeouts**, **requests waiting**, **% Java heap, highest**, **% cache hits, lowest**, **% database cache hits** and **sessions blocked**. A figure turns amber or red past its threshold.

What the page read is kept while the browser session lasts: opening it again draws it at once, and the header says when it was read (*Read at 14:02*). **Read again**, at the top right, reads everything once more. The Monitoring pages — Platform synthesis, Architecture, Platform analysis, Performance and Database audit — share their readings: what one page has read, the others draw at once, and what one page reads again is fresh in the others. The readings are kept per user, in the browser's memory only: reloading the browser reads again.

---

## The advice \{#advice\}

The lines are grouped by weight — **To act on first**, **To review**, **To know** — and each one names its area.

| Area | What is flagged |
|---|---|
| **Business functions** | A function that timed out, failed on the system side, takes most of the time measured, is slow at each call, or had one long wait. The line lists the applications and reports whose event rules call it, from the [cross reference](../cross-reference.md). |
| **Enterprise server** | A server step such as `init-remote-env` (opening the user's environment at sign-in), a kernel with requests waiting, a process that keeps transactions open, zombie processes. |
| **Web and AIS** | A Java heap close to its maximum. |
| **Caches** | A JDBj cache that answers too rarely. |
| **Database** | Blocked sessions, unusable indexes, a low cache hit ratio, statements parsed from scratch, a statement slow at each execution (its schema, its tables, who sends it, its text), redo logs that switch too often, missing or stale statistics, CPU held back by the Resource Manager, and the three largest waits. |

An area read with nothing to flag is named under the list (*Nothing to flag: …*): silence is not "not read". A source that did not answer is said in a warning; the rest of the page is still read.

### Details \{#details\}

Most lines carry a **Details** button, at their right: it reads, live, the rows behind the figure and shows them under the line, in a grid with search, filters, columns and export. **Hide** closes them.

| Line | What **Details** lists |
|---|---|
| Tables never analysed, or with stale statistics | Each table: owner, table, its description, rows, last analysis, state of its statistics. |
| Unusable indexes | Each index, its table and its type. |
| Blocked sessions | The sessions waiting, and who blocks them: session, user, program, machine, wait. |
| A slow statement | Its full text and the plan the database runs it with. |
| Low database cache hit ratio | The statements that read the disk most. |
| Statements parsed from scratch | The statements sent with their values written in the text. |
| Redo logs switching too often | The switches by hour. |
| A business function | Who calls it: the applications and reports whose event rules name it, up to 200 places. |
| Zombie processes, kernel with requests waiting, open transactions | The processes of the enterprise server named — the zombies themselves when Server Manager says which they are, otherwise every process of the server. |
| Java heap, server step, cache | The nodes, the business function calls or the caches of the server named. |

A database detail is read from Oracle, SQL Server and Db2 (Db2 for i included), each in its own words; a line a database has no rows for says *This detail is not read on this database.* On an IBM i, which counts the jobs waiting on a lock without saying for how long, the line gives how many jobs wait and how many hold them. Like the rest of the page, **Details** only reads: on Oracle, no AWR, no ASH.

---

## How to read the page \{#limits\}

The box at the bottom of the page states its limits:

- every figure is the present moment or a counter since the servers started: there is no history yet, so the page says what is slow, not since when;
- the thresholds: a function is flagged from a share of the time measured or a time per call, a Java heap from 80 %, a cache under 80 % of hits, a statement from a time per execution, the database cache under 90 %;
- the timeouts are the business functions' own counters — the enterprise server's log files are not reachable through Server Manager;
- the database is read from its own counters — on Oracle without the Diagnostics Pack: no AWR, no ASH.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry and the permissions `plugin:nomajde.performance:*`; **Details** needs nothing more. It reads Server Manager through the `jde_server_manager` pool (see [Server Manager](./server-manager.md#connection)) and the JD Edwards database.

The assistant is told what the page shows — the heaviest advice — and offers its own questions: *What should I look at first, and why?* See [AI assistant](../ai-assistant.md).

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Start with **To act on first**: one business function that takes a large share of the time is where users feel an improvement most.
- Open the callers of a slow function in the [cross reference](../cross-reference.md) to know which screens and reports are affected.
- After a restart, the counters start from zero: read the page again once the platform has worked for a while.
- **Details** first, for the rows behind a line; then [Platform analysis](./platform-analysis.md) (servers, processes, functions, INI) or [Database audit](./database-audit.md) for the whole picture.

---

## Nomajde — Database audit
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/database-audit/

Monitoring → Database audit in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne database read live from its own dictionary — Oracle, SQL Server, Db2 for Linux / UNIX / Windows or Db2 for i (IBM i) — the way an audit reads it — the instance and its parameters, what the figures say, then size, tablespaces, the largest tables, activity, the most expensive statements, sessions, redo logs, objects and statistics — without any Diagnostics or Tuning Pack view.

**Monitoring → Database audit** reads the JD Edwards database live from its own dictionary, the way an audit reads it: what the instance is, what the figures say, then nine sections in four tabs. It is read-only. Four databases are read — **Oracle**, **SQL Server**, **Db2 for Linux / UNIX / Windows** and **Db2 for i** (IBM i, AS/400) — with the same sections and the same rules, each in its own words: see [Per database](#databases). On another database, the page says the database the JD Edwards pool is on and reads nothing.

On Oracle, no AWR, ASH, ADDM or SQL-monitor view is read: they belong to packs licensed separately, and reading them would itself count as a use. The activity figures therefore count since the instance started.

---

## At a glance

---

## The four tabs \{#tabs\}

Each tab says, beside its description, how many of its points are to review.

| Tab | Sections |
|---|---|
| **Overview** | **The instance** — version, instance, database, mode, platform and the parameters that matter (`control_management_pack_access`, `cursor_sharing`, `db_block_size`, `open_cursors`, `processes`, `sga_target`, `undo_retention`…) — and **What the figures say**. |
| **Storage** | **Size** by what each owner holds — business data, control tables, central objects, system, object librarian, data dictionary, Oracle, other —; **Tablespaces** with what they use and may grow to; **The largest tables**, their indexes and LOBs counted in, with their description from the Object Librarian. |
| **Activity** | **Activity** — five figures on one strip: cache hit ratio, hard parses, executions, commits, sorts on disk —; **Where time was waited** beside **Sessions** by program — JDE kernels, JDE batches, web / AIS servers, tools; **Redo logs** and their switches hour by hour, across the page; **The most expensive statements** and who sends them, last. |
| **Objects** | **Objects and statistics** — invalid objects, unusable indexes, JDE tables never analysed or with stale statistics. |

---

## What the figures say \{#findings\}

| Flagged | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A tablespace above 85 % | Of what it may grow to. |
| NOARCHIVELOG | No recovery to a point in time. |
| Redo logs with one member, or switching too often | A lost file is a lost log; the logs are small for the activity. |
| A short cache, hard parses | The buffer cache is short for what is read; statements are not shared. |
| Tools connected to the database | Sessions of programs other than JD Edwards. |
| Invalid objects, unusable indexes, statistics never taken or stale | On the JD Edwards owners. |
| `control_management_pack_access` | Whether the Diagnostics / Tuning packs' features may be used — a licence exposure if they are not held. |

These are Oracle's rules; the other databases follow the same ones in their own words, with a few of their own — see [Per database](#databases).

---

## What the page keeps \{#kept\}

What the page read is kept while the browser session lasts: opening it again draws it at once, and the header says when it was read — *Read at 14:02*, with the day when the reading is older than today. **Read again** reads every section anew.

The Monitoring pages share their readings: once [Platform synthesis](../synthesis.md) is read, this page reads only the two sections the synthesis does not show, and what one page reads again is fresh in the others. The readings are kept per user, in the browser's memory only: reloading the browser reads again.

---

## Per database \{#databases\}

The database is the one the JD Edwards pool points at; its type decides the reading. The tabs and the rules stay the same; the sections and the columns take the database's own words, in both languages, on the page and in the [platform report](../synthesis.md#report). A section the database has nothing of says so (*SQL Server has nothing of this kind.*); a section that fails shows the database's own message, and the others are still read.

The pool must be of the database's type, and Liberty Next must carry that database's driver — see the pool's [Database stage](../../framework/connectors.md#pool-stages).

### Oracle \{#oracle\}

The sections described above, from the `v$` and `dba_` views. The account needs to read them.

### SQL Server \{#sql-server\}

A JD Edwards on SQL Server is several databases — the business data and the control tables in one, the system tables, the server map, the Object Librarian and the data dictionary in another, each path code's central objects in its own. An owner is therefore a database **and** a schema: the pool's schemas name a table of another database than the pool's own as `DATABASE.SCHEMA` (`JDE_PRODUCTION.PRODDTA`); a plain name is a schema of the pool's database.

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **The instance** | Version, edition, collation, the settings that matter (`max server memory (MB)`…), and the JD Edwards databases with their **Recovery**, **Compatibility**, **Read committed snapshot**, automatic statistics, **Auto shrink**, **Auto close** and **Page verify**. |
| **Size** | Per **Database.schema**. |
| **Data files** | In place of the tablespaces: how full each file is of what it may grow to — its own limit, or the room left on its volume. |
| **The largest tables** | With their **Statistics** date. |
| **Transaction logs** | One per database: **Recovery**, size, **Used %**, what it **Waits on**, **Last log backup**, **Virtual files**. |
| **Activity** | Cache, **Batches compiled** in place of the hard parses, the page life, the waits. |
| **The most expensive statements** | Those still in the plan cache. |
| **Objects and statistics** | **Disabled indexes**, statistics **Never computed** or **Stale** — SQL Server has no invalid object. |

Its own rules flag `max server memory` not set, a JD Edwards database with auto shrink, auto close, automatic statistics off or a page verify other than `CHECKSUM`, a transaction log 80 % full, a log in full recovery never backed up or not for more than 24 hours, a database in SIMPLE recovery, and a log cut in more than 1 000 virtual files.

The account needs `VIEW SERVER STATE` and to be a user of the JD Edwards databases.

### Db2 for Linux, UNIX and Windows \{#db2\}

The same sections, from the monitor functions and the catalog: the tablespaces, the **Transaction log** and the log files archived per hour, the buffer pools and the package cache (**Not in the package cache** in place of the hard parses, **Sort overflows** for the sorts on disk), the time waited by cause, lock waits, **Indexes to rebuild**, the tables **Used, never analysed**. Its own rules flag circular logging, automatic statistics off, the self-tuning memory off, a log nearly full, and deadlocks or lock timeouts since the database was activated.

The account needs to run the monitor functions (`SQLADM` or `DBADM`) and to read the catalog.

### Db2 for i (IBM i) \{#db2-for-i\}

On an IBM i, the database is the system: there is no instance, tablespace, redo log or buffer cache. The sections keep their place and show what the system has instead:

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **The system** | Its release and PTF levels, processors, memory, the last IPL, the system values that matter. |
| **Libraries** | The size per library — the pool's schemas name them. |
| **Disk pools (ASP)** | How full each disk pool is. |
| **The largest files** | With their **Deleted rows** and **Last used** date. |
| **Journals** | Their **Receivers**, who manages them, whether they delete their receivers, the files journaled, and the receivers attached per hour. |
| **Activity** | **Processor in use**, **Active jobs**, **Jobs in the system**, temporary storage; **Memory pools** with their faults in place of the waits. |
| **What the jobs run now** | The statements the active jobs run at this moment. The plan cache is read only through a procedure that writes a file, which this reading never runs. |
| **Jobs** | The active jobs, by name, client address and user. |
| **Indexes and deleted rows** | **Indexes not valid**, the files **To reorganise**, the **Indexes the system advises**. |

Its own rules flag a journal that is not active, a journal that keeps its receivers on line, files holding many deleted rows, and the indexes the system advises. A figure counts since the last IPL.

The account needs to read the `QSYS2` services; the statement a job runs and the locks of another job ask for more (`*JOBCTL`, or the function usage `QIBM_DB_SQLADM`).
---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry and the permission `plugin:nomajde.dbaudit:j_db_audit`. It reads the database through the JD Edwards database connection; what the account needs is said for each database under [Per database](#databases).

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Read the **Overview** tab first: the amber lines are the points an auditor would raise.
- On Oracle, check `control_management_pack_access` on every database of the platform: `NONE` keeps the packs' features out of reach.
- On SQL Server, write in the pool's schemas the `DATABASE.SCHEMA` of each library that is not in the pool's own database: the largest tables, the disabled indexes and the statistics are read only for the databases the pool names.
- The activity figures count since the database started (since the last IPL on an IBM i): compare two readings a few days apart rather than one reading after a restart.

## Nomajde — Server sizes
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/server-sizes/

Monitoring → Server sizes in Nomajde: one line per machine of the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform — processors, physical cores, memory, disk, processor family, virtualisation, cluster and a note — stated by you, never collected on the machines. List the servers adds a line per machine found; what is left empty is measured by the database or taken from Oracle's published minimum on OCI. Feeds Platform synthesis, the OCI target and Nomasx-1's processor licence count.

**Monitoring → Server sizes** holds the size of each machine of the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform: its processors, physical cores, memory and disk. Nothing is collected on the machines — Server Manager says what a server *uses*, not how large the machine is — so the size is **stated**, one line per machine. What is left empty is filled from what the database says of its own server, else from a **standard configuration**.

These sizes are what the [Capacity](../synthesis.md#capacity) and [Improvements](../synthesis.md#improvements) tabs of Platform synthesis read, and what the [OCI target](./oci-target.md) sizes production from. With the processor family, the virtualisation and the cluster, they are also what Nomasx-1 counts the **processor licences** on — see [Processor licences](#processor-licences).

---

## At a glance

---

## The grid \{#grid\}

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Server** | The machine's name. It is matched with the names the [Architecture](./architecture.md) reading finds without the case, the DNS domain or a port: `JDEENT01.example.com`, `jdeent01` and `jdeent01:6017` are one machine. |
| **Role** | *Database server*, *Enterprise server*, *Web and AIS server*, *Deployment server*, *Several roles on one machine*, *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)* or *Other*. |
| **Processors (threads, vCPU)** | What the system counts as processors. |
| **Physical cores** | The cores of the machine. |
| **Memory (GB)** | The machine's memory. |
| **Disk (GB)** | The machine's disk. |
| **Processor family** | The chip, with Oracle's core factor in its name (*Intel Xeon, AMD EPYC / Opteron, desktop and laptop chips — 0.5*, *IBM POWER6 and later — 1*…). |
| **Virtualisation** | *Physical machine*, *Hardware partition (accepted by Oracle)*, *VMware virtual machine* or *Other virtual machine*. |
| **Cluster** | The virtualisation cluster the machine belongs to. |
| **Note** | Free text — where the figures come from, for example. |
| **Changed by**, **Changed on** | Who saved the line last, and when. Read-only. |

**Add row** adds a machine by hand; the grid's usual tools — **Bulk edit**, filters, export — apply.

---

## List the servers \{#list\}

**List the servers** adds a line for each machine the architecture reading finds that has none yet, with its name and its role; the sizes are left for you to type. A line that exists is never changed, so the action can be run again after a new server is installed.

A machine the reading does not show — a deployment server, typically — is added by hand with **Add row**, with its role. It then counts with the others, marked *stated only — the architecture reading does not show it* in Platform synthesis.

---

## Where each figure comes from \{#origin\}

Each figure is taken, field by field, from the first source that has it:

| Origin | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **stated** | The value typed in this grid. A stated value always wins. |
| **measured by the database** | For the database server only: the processors, cores and memory the database — Oracle, SQL Server or Db2 — reports of its own host. |
| **standard configuration** | Oracle's published minimum for JD Edwards EnterpriseOne 9.2 on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (One-Click Provisioning), per role the machine carries: 2 cores and 30 GB per server; the disk by role — 50 GB for the database, 75 GB for an enterprise server, 20 GB for a web or AIS server, 30 GB more for the application server, 100 GB for Server Manager, 210 GB for a deployment server. |
| **counted from the other figure** | When only one of processors and cores is known, the other follows it — two processors per core. |

A machine that carries several roles adds up the standard of each role it carries. The **Role** column says what a machine carries when the reading does not show it; *Several roles on one machine* keeps what the reading found.

The standard configuration is a floor to start from, not a sizing: Platform synthesis and the OCI target say how many machines still rest on it.

A line of role *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)* is not a machine of the platform: Platform synthesis and the OCI target leave it out. It is stated for the processor licences only.

---

## Edit dialog \{#edit\}

A double click on a line, or **Add row**, opens the form, in two tabs of two columns: **Size** and **Processor licences**.

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Server** | Required. The name as the architecture reading shows it, or the machine's own name for a machine added by hand. |
| **Role** | From the list of roles; it decides the standard configuration of what is left empty. |
| **Processors (threads, vCPU)**, **Physical cores** | One of the two is enough: the other is counted from it. |
| **Memory (GB)**, **Disk (GB)** | Empty when not known. |
| **Note** | Optional. |

The **Processor licences** tab holds what the licence count needs:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Processor family** | From Oracle's *Processor Core Factor Table*; each choice names its factor. Empty is read as Intel / AMD (0.5). |
| **Virtualisation** | Empty is read as *Physical machine*. |
| **Cluster** | For a virtual machine: the cluster it runs on. For a physical host of that cluster: the same name, with the role *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)*. |

---

## Processor licences \{#processor-licences\}

Nomasx-1 reads these lines to count the licences of a product sold per processor — the database, Oracle Data Integrator, Oracle Analytics Server — on the machines where it runs, by Oracle's rule:

- **cores × core factor**: the physical cores of the machine (its processors when no core is stated) times the factor of its processor family; the cores are added up before the factor is applied, and the result is rounded up once;
- **a hardware partition** counts the cores given to the partition;
- **a virtual machine that is not a hardware partition** (*VMware virtual machine*, *Other virtual machine*) counts **every physical host of its cluster**, whatever the size of the virtual machine — the lines of that cluster whose role is *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)*. A cluster is counted once, however many machines of the product run on it;
- a cluster whose hosts are not stated cannot be counted: Nomasx-1 says so, and keeps the virtual machine's own cores as a floor.

The count is a reading of Oracle's rules, an assumption to discuss — never a certified position. See the Nomasx-1 [licence pages](../../nomasx1/licenses/odi.md#processors).

---

## Access \{#access\}

The screen shows to the roles that hold its menu entry; saving a line needs the right to change it (`edit:nomajde:server_sizes`), and **List the servers** the functions `plugin:nomajde.sizing:*`. The predefined roles **Platform operator** and **Administrator** hold them (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)).

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Run **List the servers** first, then type the sizes from the virtualisation console or the system: the names then match the reading.
- Write in **Note** where the figures come from (the hypervisor, an inventory, a date): a sizing is discussed on its sources.
- Add the deployment server by hand: the reading does not see it, the OCI target counts one.
- For the database server, leave the sizes empty if the database is Oracle, SQL Server or Db2: its own figures are taken.
- Behind a VMware cluster, state each physical host once, with its cores, its processor family, the role *Physical host of a cluster (hypervisor)* and the cluster's name: without them, the licence count is only a floor.

---

## Nomajde — OCI target
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/monitoring/oci-target/

Monitoring → OCI target in Nomajde: the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform proposed on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and its estimated cost — your choices (currency, BYOL or licence included, database edition, high availability, disaster recovery, non-production platforms), the estimate per platform and line by line with Oracle's part numbers, the rules it rests on, the dated price list and the OCI target PDF. An estimate, not a quotation.

**Monitoring → OCI target** proposes the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne platform on **Oracle Cloud Infrastructure** and says what it would cost. The target starts from what the platform is today — the machines the [Architecture](./architecture.md) reading finds and their size as stated in [Server sizes](./server-sizes.md) — and is priced with Oracle's public price list. Each choice made on the page (currency, database licence, high availability…) is applied at once.

:::warning[An estimate, not a quotation]
The figures are Oracle's public list prices, pay as you go, without discount or commitment. They are not contractual. The page says so at its top, on its diagram and above its table; the PDF says it on its cover, above and under its table and at the foot of every page.
:::

---

## At a glance

---

## The target \{#target\}

The proposal keeps the three tiers of JD Edwards apart, on Linux virtual machines, with the database on Base Database Service:

| Tier | Proposed as |
|---|---|
| **Web and AIS** | Virtual machines carrying the web and AIS instances. |
| **Enterprise servers** | Virtual machines carrying the enterprise servers. |
| **Database** | **Base Database Service**, billed per ECPU, with its storage and its backups in object storage. |
| **Administration** | A deployment server (Windows) and Server Manager on a small machine of its own (optional), **shared by every platform**. |

**Production** is sized like for like from what each server is today: a physical core is an OCPU (one core with its two threads, that is 2 vCPU), the memory is kept, and no server goes below Oracle's published minimum for JD Edwards on OCI (2 OCPU, 30 GB). A machine that carries several tiers today is divided between them in proportion to their standard size. Each **non-production** platform is one web server, one enterprise server and one database, at that minimum, running all month.

The figures behind production come from [Server sizes](./server-sizes.md): stated, measured by the database, or the standard configuration. A server without a stated or measured size is named in [What the estimate rests on](#rests-on).

---

## Your choices \{#choices\}

| Choice | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Currency** | The currencies of Oracle's price list. | EUR |
| **Database licence** | **your own licences (BYOL)** or **licence included**. | BYOL |
| **Database edition** | Standard Edition, Enterprise Edition, Enterprise Edition High Performance. | Enterprise Edition |
| **Non-production platforms** | From 0 to 12. | 1 |
| **High availability** | Web and enterprise servers doubled behind a load balancer, and a standby database (Data Guard) in the same region. | Off |
| **Disaster recovery site** | A standby database of the same size in a second region; the application servers' disks are replicated there and the servers are started only when needed — their processors are not billed until then. | Off |

Standard Edition has no Data Guard: with high availability or a recovery site, no standby database is proposed and the protection of the database rests on its backups. With your own licences, the database licences held must cover the ECPU proposed — Oracle's conversion ratio is in its *Universal Credits Service Descriptions*, to check against the contract.

The page remembers the choices in the browser. **Read again** reads the platform again; a choice changed only recomputes the estimate.

---

## The estimate \{#estimate\}

Two figures first — **a month, estimated** and **a year, estimated** — then one per platform: *Production*, *Non-production 1*, *Non-production 2*…, *Shared by every platform* and, with a recovery site, *Disaster recovery site*.

**Production as proposed** draws the production platform: the tiers from left to right, each machine with its OCPU and memory (the database with its ECPU), the administration servers, and the second region when there is one.

**The estimate, line by line** lists, per platform, what is billed:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **What is billed** | Virtual machines, disks, Windows licence, Base Database Service (edition and licence), database storage, database backups, load balancer, replicated disks. |
| **Quantity** | For example `2 × 2 OCPU, 30 GB`, `16 ECPU (32 GB)`, `256 GB`. |
| **Oracle part** | Oracle's part numbers for the line (`B97384 + B97385` for a virtual machine's OCPU and memory). |
| **A month** | The month's amount; the platform's heading carries its total, the last line the total of all. |

---

## What the estimate rests on \{#rests-on\}

Under the table, every rule that applies to this target is written out:

- the like-for-like sizing and Oracle's minimum per server;
- how the database is sized: 4 ECPU stand for a core and bring 8 GB of memory, so its size is the larger of what its cores and its memory ask, never below 8 ECPU;
- its storage — twice its size today, in steps of 256 GB — and its backups in object storage, twice its size;
- the servers whose size is neither stated nor measured, by name, with the advice to state them;
- the sizing does not look at the load: the peaks kept by the snapshots ([Platform synthesis → Capacity](../synthesis.md#capacity)) tell whether a tier can be reduced or must grow;
- high availability, the recovery site and the non-production platforms when chosen;
- the shared servers — Server Manager's lines can be left out of the total when it runs on another server;
- a month counts 744 hours, disks are at balanced performance, virtual machines are the standard x86 shape (E5);
- **what is left out**: network (VPN or FastConnect, data sent out beyond the free allowance), Oracle support for the JD Edwards and database licences, the JD Edwards licences themselves, migration work, free allowances.

**State the server sizes** opens [Server sizes](./server-sizes.md).

---

## The prices \{#prices\}

The prices come from a dated file shipped with the application: the foot of the page names the list in use (*Oracle's public price list of 2026-11-02 — as shipped with the application*, or *fetched on …*). **Fetch the prices again** reads Oracle's public price list and keeps it; the page is computed again with it. It is the only call the page makes outside, and it sends nothing about the platform.

---

## Get it as a document \{#document\}

**Get it as a document (PDF)** writes the OCI target as a PDF, with the choices made on the page and in the page's language: the estimate per platform and line by line with Oracle's part numbers, the servers proposed, production drawn on a landscape page, and every rule the estimate rests on.

The same document is on the **Reports** page (*JD Edwards on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure — target and estimate*), where the language, the customer name written on the cover and each choice are asked as parameters. The [Platform synthesis](../synthesis.md#report) report can also carry the OCI target as one of its chapters.

---

## Access \{#access\}

The page shows to the roles that hold its menu entry and reads with `plugin:nomajde.oci:*`; the PDF needs the right to run the application's reports. The predefined roles **Platform operator** and **Administrator** hold both (see [Predefined roles](../overview.md#roles)).

It reads Server Manager through the `jde_server_manager` pool (see [Server Manager](./server-manager.md#connection)) and the JD Edwards database. A source that does not answer is said in a warning (*Not read — …*).

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- State the size of every server in [Server sizes](./server-sizes.md) before sharing an estimate: a target built on the standard configuration only says what the minimum would cost.
- Turn on the *Platform snapshot* job (see [Jobs](../jobs.md)) a few weeks before a sizing: the peaks it keeps tell whether production can be reduced or must grow.
- Compare the options rather than one figure: BYOL against licence included, with and without high availability.
- Fetch the prices again before a meeting: Oracle changes its list.

## Nomajde — Jobs
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/jobs/

The Jobs folder of the Nomajde menu: re-merge the JD Edwards security, refresh the data dictionary of the Explorer models, check the JD Edwards servers, keep the platform's figures, watch the instances and restart them when told, mail the platform synthesis and the weekly upgrade report, compare a path code with the standard — run on demand with a live log; and the AIS jobs that run a report or export a table from Nomaflow.

The **Jobs** folder, at the bottom of the Nomajde menu, runs the JD Edwards maintenance jobs on demand without opening Nomaflow. Each entry opens the job's page: its parameters, **Run**, the log followed live, the previous runs with who ran them. See [Run a job from an application's menu](../nomaflow/jobs/run-from-menu.md).

---

## Re-merge security (change package) \{#remerge\}

Re-merges the JD Edwards security — Security Workbench, UDO security, menu filtering — of the parent roles touched by the active change package, each parent once. Run it after applying a package that changed roles or role relationships. Details: [`nomajde-remerge-security`](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security).

## Re-merge security (all roles) \{#remerge-all\}

Re-merges the security of every active parent role, whatever the change package — after a bulk import, or to recover from a missed re-merge. On a large instance it takes several minutes. Details: [`nomajde-remerge-security-all`](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-remerge-security-all).

## Refresh data dictionary (Explorer models) \{#dictionary\}

Creates the dictionary entries the [Data Explorer](./data-explorer.md) models lack, from the JD Edwards data dictionary (F9200 / F9202 / F9210: description, type, decimals, UDC lookup), one scan per table. The labels show at once: no restart.

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Explorer model (blank = every model)** | One of the Nomajde models, or blank for all. |

The log lists, per model, the tables scanned and the entries created.

## Check the JDE servers \{#jde-health\}

Runs the health check of the JD Edwards servers through Server Manager at once, without waiting for the five-minute schedule, and records the result shown in [Monitoring → JDE Health Check](./monitoring/jde-servers.md). The run fails when an instance did not pass. Details: [`nomajde-jde-health`](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-jde-health).

## Platform snapshot \{#platform-snapshot\}

Keeps the platform's figures of the moment, so that their trend can be read in the **Capacity** tab of the [Platform synthesis](./synthesis.md): users online, sessions, instances running, response time and timeouts of the business functions, requests waiting, the enterprise servers' processor and memory in use and their kernels, the Java heap of the web and AIS instances (used and its maximum), cache, the database's sessions, blocked sessions, load and size, and the day's batch jobs — in error and waiting included. One row per figure in the Nomajde database, kept **400 days**.

Hourly as shipped, **off** until it is turned on. A source that does not answer leaves its figures out of that snapshot and is named in the run; the run fails only when nothing could be read. Read-only on JD Edwards.

## Instances watch \{#instances-watch\}

Watches the JD Edwards instances through Server Manager — every enterprise server, HTML server and AIS server — every **15 minutes** as shipped, **off** until it is turned on. Everything goes through Server Manager's REST API: nothing is installed on the JD Edwards servers.

### What it checks \{#instances-watch-checks\}

For each instance: its state, and for a running instance the console's own health checks (the port, the login, an application, a report…). An instance is **ok**, **unhealthy** (a check failed, with the console's message), **stopped**, or **not checked** (its health could not be read). What is wrong is kept in the Nomajde database for 90 days, and **the run fails** when something is still wrong at its end — the message names each instance and why — so the job's alert goes out.

The console's check of an enterprise server runs a report each time: keep the schedule reasonable.

### Restart and start: two questions \{#instances-watch-cure\}

The job can also cure. Two questions at launch, both **no** as shipped:

| Question | When **yes** |
|---|---|
| **Restart an instance whose health checks fail** | An unhealthy instance is stopped, Server Manager is asked until it says it is stopped, then it is started and asked until it runs. An instance that does not stop is not started again. |
| **Start an instance found stopped** | A stopped instance is started — leave it on **no** when instances are stopped on purpose. |

Each wait lasts up to five minutes. The same restart is the row action **Restart this instance** of the *JDE instances* screen — see [Server Manager](./monitoring/server-manager.md).

### Guard rails \{#instances-watch-guards\}

A restart is never repeated in a loop:

- **at most one instance per run**, enterprise servers first; the others are left for the next run, and the run says so;
- an instance restarted or started — or whose restart failed — **less than an hour ago** is not restarted a second time: the restart did not cure it, the run fails and says that a person must look.

### Health checks that count \{#instances-watch-checks-that-count\}

**Health checks that count (blank: all — e.g. Login, Port Test, BSFN)** names the checks to follow, separated by commas. Leave out a check that fails for a reason a restart does not cure — a certificate, a report server that is not installed: it would otherwise mark the instance unhealthy at every run.

---

## Documents by mail \{#reports\}

Two jobs make a PDF document — in French or in English — and send it by mail with the file attached. Both are **off** as shipped: turn them on once the mail settings are in place, or run them by hand. The same documents come from a button on their page and from the **Reports** page.

### Platform synthesis report \{#report-platform\}

The platform synthesis as a document: a summary, what needs attention, the architecture on a landscape page with each server's size, the capacity, what could be improved, what each analysis says — and, when asked, the target on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure with its estimate (see [OCI target](./monitoring/oci-target.md)). A source that did not answer is named in the document. Monthly as shipped (the 1st at 07:00), mailed to the users of the **Platform operator** role. The same document is **Get the report (PDF)** on the [Platform synthesis](./synthesis.md) page.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Language** | `fr` | `fr` or `en`. |
| **Customer name on the cover** | blank | Written on the cover. |
| **With the OCI estimate** | `no` | `yes` adds the OCI target and its estimate. |

### Weekly upgrade report \{#report-upgrade\}

Not the list of the objects: **what moved this week, and what comes next** — see [Weekly upgrade report](./upgrade/analysis.md#weekly-report). The job first keeps the week's figures, so that each report says what moved since the last one, then makes the document and mails it to the users of the **Developer** role. Every Monday at 07:00 as shipped. The same document is **Weekly report (PDF)** on [Prepare for upgrade](./upgrade/analysis.md).

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Language** | `fr` | `fr` or `en`. |
| **Path code (blank: the one analysed last)** | blank | The upgrade analysis the report reads. |
| **Customer name on the cover** | blank | Written on the cover. |

## Upgrade and tests \{#upgrade-tests\}

The two jobs of the upgrade analysis are started from the **Prepare for upgrade** page, with **Load Oracle's list** and **Run the analysis** — see [Prepare for upgrade](./upgrade/analysis.md#steps). **Tests → Run the tests** sits in the Tests folder of the menu — see [Non-regression tests](./tests.md#job).

## Compare with the standard \{#standard-compare\}

Compares every standard object a path code holds as changed, and every copy of a standard object, with Oracle's own in another path code — `PS920`, Oracle's objects as delivered, or any other —, record by record, and keeps the verdict of each: which are identical and can go back to standard, which differ and by how much. The result is read on [Back to standard](./development/back-to-standard.md), whose **Compare again** button opens this job with its values filled in.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Path code to examine** | `PD920` | The path code whose changed objects and copies are compared. |
| **Path code to compare with (PS920: Oracle's objects as delivered — or another)** | `PS920` | The reference. |

No schedule: run it when needed, before an upgrade for instance. Read-only on JD Edwards; comparing a path code again replaces what was kept for it.

---

## JD Edwards AIS jobs \{#ais\}

Two jobs reach JD Edwards through its AIS server (connector `ais_connection`). They are not in the Nomajde menu: they are run from **Nomaflow → Jobs** with **Run with parameters**, or copied into a job of their own with fixed parameters and a schedule.

| Job | What it does | Parameters asked at launch |
|---|---|---|
| [`nomajde-ais-report`](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-ais-report) | Runs a JD Edwards report (UBE) and waits until it is done; the run fails when the report ends in error or is still running after the time limit. | **Report**, **Version** (`XJDE0001` by default), **Queue**, **Processing options (JSON)**. |
| [`nomajde-ais-export`](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#nomajde-ais-export) | Exports a table or a business view to an xlsx file of the run, with AIS's column titles as headers; the file is sent to whoever started the run and stays downloadable from the run detail. | **Table** or **Business view**, **Columns**, **Conditions (JSON)**, **Max rows** (`5000` by default). |

The same AIS calls — and a few more: count rows, call a business function, run an orchestration, start or stop the scheduler — are available as Python steps of a job and as screen actions: see [the AIS steps](../nomaflow/bundled-jobs.md#ais-steps). Two of them keep several forms open in one JD Edwards session — a flow over several forms, one row of a grid: see [Several forms in one session](./ais/services.md#flow).

---

## Who may run them \{#access\}

An entry shows to whoever may run the job: a role that sets the entry — or its folder — to **Read and change**, or that holds the `job:<id>` permission (rule type **Job** in its *Beyond the menus* rules). **Read** alone never shows it: reading never starts anything. Each person who may run the job sees every run of it, not only their own. As shipped, the **Platform operator** role runs *Platform snapshot*, *Instances watch* and *Platform synthesis report*; the **Developer** role runs *Weekly upgrade report* and *Compare with the standard*; the **Administrator** runs them all — see [Predefined roles](./overview.md#roles).

---

## Nomajde — Non-regression tests
Source: https://docs.nomana-it.fr/liberty/nomajde/tests/

The Tests folder of Nomajde: non-regression tests for JD Edwards played through the AIS server — cases drawn as a flow of calls (a form, a data query, a business function), what each call must answer, a reference run recorded before a change and compared after an ESU, a tools release or an upgrade; results, the job that plays a suite and its Excel report.

The **Tests** folder checks that JD Edwards **still behaves the same** after a change — an ESU, a tools release, an upgrade, a package build. A test calls JD Edwards the way an integration does, through the AIS server: it opens a form, reads a table, runs a business function, and compares the answer with what is expected and with a **reference run** recorded before the change.

Nothing is installed in JD Edwards, and no script is written: a case is built by picking calls in a list and letting JD Edwards' own answer fill in what to expect.

---

## At a glance

---

## The three entries \{#entries\}

| Menu entry | Use |
|---|---|
| **Tests → Results** | How the last runs went: cases passed, failed, changed or never played, the last runs of each suite as bars, each case with its last results. |
| **Tests → Cases** | The suites and their cases, drawn and edited as flows of calls. |
| **Tests → Run the tests** | The job that plays a suite — on demand here, or on a schedule. |

**Results** and **Cases** are the test pages of Liberty Next, described in full in [Tests](../framework/build/tests.md); this page covers what is specific to JD Edwards.

---

## A case, step by step \{#case\}

A **suite** holds **cases**; a case is a sequence of **steps**; a step is one call to JD Edwards with what is expected of its answer.

1. In **Tests → Cases**, pick the suite and choose **New case**. Say what it checks, and tick *This case changes data* when one of its steps writes in JD Edwards.
2. The **+** on the flow adds a step. Pick the **Endpoint called** in the list of the AIS connector: one of the [catalogue's services](./ais/services.md) — a table read, a business function — or an endpoint made with [Create from…](./ais/create-from.md) for a form, a report or an orchestration.
3. Fill the **Parameters**: one labelled field per parameter of the endpoint, with its help.
4. **Fill from the answer** plays the call now and proposes what to expect — the number of rows and the values of the first row, by JD Edwards alias (`AN8`, `ALPH`). Keep the lines that must stay true, delete the others.
5. **Save**, then **Run this case**.

What a step can expect:

| Expectation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **The call** *must work* / *must be refused* | A refusal is a valid expectation: a table that does not exist, a value the form rejects. **The refusal says** checks the message. |
| **Rows, at least / exactly / at most** | The number of rows returned. |
| **The first row holds** | Values of the first row, by column name. |
| **A warning says** | A warning of JD Edwards (*Duplicate Address Book record*) reported with the answer. |

A value read at one step — an address number just created — can be kept and given to the next steps. A step marked *Played even after a failure (a cleanup)* always runs: this is how a case that writes removes what it created.

---

## Reference and comparison \{#reference\}

Expectations say what must be true. The **reference** catches what nobody thought of writing down: the columns of a form, the labels of a grid, the values of a set-up table.

1. **Before the change**, record the reference: **Record the reference** on the Cases page, or the job with *record*. Each step keeps the parts of its answer it was asked to keep.
2. **After the change**, run the suite again. Each case ends as:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Passed** | Every expectation holds and nothing differs from the reference. |
| **Changed** | The expectations hold, but a kept value differs from the reference — a column gone, a new one, another value. The difference is listed value by value. |
| **Failed** | An expectation is not met, or the call failed. |
| **Skipped** | The case writes on JD Edwards and the run did not allow it. |

A *Changed* is not always a defect — an update may legitimately add a column — but it is always something to read. Record the reference again once the change is accepted.

---

## The job \{#job\}

**Tests → Run the tests** plays a suite outside the page — on demand, or on a schedule after each package deployment.

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Suite** | `smoke` | The suite to play, among the suites of the AIS connector. |
| **Compare with the reference, or record it** | compare | *compare* checks the cases and reports what differs; *record* keeps the run as the new reference. |
| **Only these cases** | blank | Case identifiers separated by commas; blank plays them all. |
| **Cases that write on JDE** | no | *yes* also plays the cases marked as changing data. |

The run **fails** when a case fails or has changed, which triggers the job's alerts. Its files hold an Excel report, one line per step: case, label, case status, step, endpoint, step status, duration and what was found. The results also appear in **Tests → Results**.

---

## The suite shipped \{#smoke\}

Nomajde ships a first suite, **smoke** — *JDE — what must keep working* — made of reading cases any JD Edwards answers:

| Case | Checks |
|---|---|
| `ais-is-up` | AIS answers and says what it runs. |
| `udc-types-of-system-00` | The UDC types of system 00 are read from `F0004`. |
| `address-book-form` | The Address Book search form opens and still has its columns. |
| `unknown-table-is-refused` | A table that does not exist is refused, not answered empty. |

Use it to check the connection, then add the cases that matter to the business: the forms the users live in, the business functions the interfaces call, the set-up tables an update must not touch.

---

## Access \{#access\}

| To | A role needs |
|---|---|
| See the suites and the results | **See the test suites and their results** |
| Play a case or a suite | **Play the tests (and see them)** |
| Write suites, cases and steps | **Write the tests: suites, cases, steps (and play them)** |
| Run the job from the menu | The job's permission |

The three test permissions are in a role's *Beyond the menus* rules, type **Tests**: a functional team can write and play the tests without being administrators. Every call runs under the JD Edwards account of the AIS connector: JD Edwards security applies to that account.

---

## Tips & best practices \{#tips\}

- Record the reference on the environment that will be changed, **just before** the change.
- Prefer many small reading cases to a few long ones: a failure then names what broke.
- Keep the writing cases apart, each with its cleanup step, and play them on a test environment.
- Schedule the job after the nightly package deployment: a regression is known in the morning, with the difference listed.
- The AI assistant knows the procedure: ask it to *check that JDE still behaves the same after a change*.

---

## Related

- [Tests](../framework/build/tests.md) — the Cases page in full; [Test results](../monitoring/test-results.md).
- [JD Edwards services (AIS)](./ais/services.md) and [Create from…](./ais/create-from.md) — the calls a step can make.
- [Prepare for upgrade](./upgrade/analysis.md) — what to retrofit before the tests are played.
